arxiv_record.abstract:
We introduce DavIR, a model-based data selection method for post-training
Large Language Models. DavIR generalizes Reducible Holdout Loss to core-set
selection problem of causal language modeling, and quantifies the learnability
of a given datum with respect to a pre-trained LLM based on relative reduction
in loss during fine-tuning, a metric we show to be closely related to the
implicit reward model described in Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We
show that 6% of Alpaca dataset selected with DavIR can steer both the LLaMA and
Gemma model family to produce superior performance compared to the same models
trained on the full 52K dataset. We also show that Alpaca dataset compressed
with DavIR can be combined with GSM8K dataset to effectively balance
open-domain freeform QA and mathematical reasoning capabilities. Finally, we
apply the DavIR objective to DPO and develop a normalized DavIR-DPO objective
which improves alignment performance of Zephyr-7B-SFT model by 8% (relative) on
AlpacaEval, compared against training on vanilla DPO objective.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on learnability-based SFT selection and balancing conversational and mathematical capabilities. v2 additionally claims a normalized RHO generalization linked to implicit rewards, effectiveness across LLaMA and Gemma, broad superiority over selection methods, and an approximately 8% relative improvement from DavIR-DPO. These substantially expand the claimed contribution and applicability.

C2.justification: v2 develops a sequential-context explanation for length bias and interprets backbone-mismatch results as evidence of model-dependent learnability. Its limitations now identify failed GSM8K compression, with competing explanations involving reasoning capabilities and cross-entropy's suitability. It also explains that learnability selection does not ensure quality or diversity. These replace much of v1's future-work discussion about generation, augmentation and mixture proportions.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the single human annotator's characteristics and comparison instructions, greedy decoding, and reuse of the published AlpaGasus subset rather than fresh ChatGPT scoring. These are limited disclosures, not demonstrated changes to the earlier experiments. Some earlier details, including the explicit GPT-4 judging temperature of zero, are no longer stated; comprehensive training hyperparameters remain absent.

E1.justification: v2 adds human-curated LIMA data for subset training, UltraFeedback preference pairs for the new alignment task, and MBPP data for length-correlation diagnostics. It also evaluates new experiments on the AlpacaEval benchmark described in Appendix E. These extend the represented data and task coverage beyond v1's Alpaca selection, mixed instruction evaluation and GSM8K mixing.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated EL2N, forgetting-score and DataInf comparators in Table 6, vanilla DPO in Table 8, and multiple DPO variants in the length-correlation comparison of Table 3. The latter are diagnostic comparisons, not end-to-end performance evaluations. RHO-LM corresponds to v1's existing unnormalized loss-difference variant; full-data, random and ChatGPT-selection comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Added protocols include Gemma-2B subset-size comparisons, controls that mismatch selection and retraining backbones, and Zephyr-7B-SFT preference training with ordinary and length-controlled AlpacaEval metrics. Table 6 evaluates Gemma against GPT-4, distinct from the earlier Text-Davinci-003 comparisons. These are substantial new experimental designs, without establishing that retained LLaMA experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands length-bias diagnostics across datasets, models and DPO objectives (Tables 1–3), tests model dependence through backbone mismatches (Table 7), and investigates failed GSM8K compression (Figure 5). It adds selected-example cases in Table 11. Earlier normalization and category analyses remain, while v1's loss-versus-ranking scatterplots are removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests. v2 Appendix E introduces 1,000 bootstrap samples from the 805-question AlpacaEval dataset, 95% confidence intervals in Table 12 and t-test p-values in Table 13. These quantify evaluation-question resampling, not repeated training runs or additional seeds.

E6.justification: The original LLaMA curves and appendix overlap/category counts are largely retained, but substantial new results appear. Table 6 reports Gemma win rates of 20.2 for DavIR with 6,000 examples versus 18.3 for full-data training. New Table 8 reports length-controlled win rates of 61.83 for DavIR-DPO versus 57.23 for vanilla DPO. LIMA compression, correlation, model-mismatch and GSM8K failure results are also added.

M1.justification: The normalized SFT selection formula and full-data reference-model procedure are retained despite renaming. However, v2 introduces DavIR-DPO, a new preference-training objective that normalizes preferred and rejected responses' log-probability ratios by their reference-model losses (Section 3.2, Equation 4). This substantially extends the method beyond selecting SFT data.

P1.justification: Beyond the LoBaSS-to-DavIR rename and author-information changes, the abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around RHO, length dependence and implicit rewards. Experiments are reorganized into SFT and DPO sections with new thematic subsections, conclusion and limitations change order, and the appendix is reorganized into Sections A–E.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, with substantially redrawn and relabeled performance plots. The workflow diagram is removed and algorithm pseudocode is added; the loss-ranking scatterplots disappear. Numerous new comparison and statistical tables and a GSM8K failure plot are introduced, while existing appendix tables and sunburst charts are relocated and reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 repositions the method as a normalized adaptation of RHO connected to DPO, rather than principally introducing a novel learnability criterion. Related work expands substantially into implicit rewards, preference-optimization variants and classical coreset selection, including RETRIEVE, CRAIG, EL2N and influence methods. This changes both the cited literature and the account of the work's novelty.

T1.justification: v2 adds a formal connection between loss-reduction scoring and the Bradley–Terry/DPO implicit-reward representation (Section 3.1, Equation 2), then defines a normalized preference-learning objective in Equation 4. This extends the mathematical formulation beyond SFT subset scoring. The denominator-invariance proof itself is retained from v1 Appendix A.2 as Proposition 1 in v2 Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow comparative validation through additional selection baselines, an independent model family, backbone-mismatch controls and an explicit GSM8K failure analysis. These help establish where the method works and qualify its applicability. The gains are tempered by overclaims: Table 6 contradicts consistent superiority over full-data training, and t-tests on bootstrap replicates provide weaker significance evidence than claimed. Nevertheless, the added controlled comparisons, clearer research positioning and concrete limitations substantially improve the paper's overall evidential value.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same model-dependent data-selection work, renamed from LoBaSS to DavIR. The normalized SFT score, original experiments, proof and appendix analyses can be matched across versions. The complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Gemma comparisons, length-correlation measurements, model-mismatch experiments, GSM8K compression tests and Zephyr preference-training results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLaMA-7B/13B fine-tuning experiments, GPT-4 and human evaluations, Alpaca/GSM8K mixing results, and analyses of selected examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in traditional natural language processing tasks but struggle with problems that require complex domain-specific calculations or simulations. While equipping LLMs with external tools to build LLM-based agents can enhance their capabilities, existing approaches lack the flexibility to address diverse and ever-evolving user queries in open domains. Currently, there is also no existing dataset that evaluates LLMs on open-domain knowledge that requires tools to solve. To this end, we introduce OpenAct benchmark to evaluate the open-domain task-solving capability, which is built on human expert consultation and repositories in GitHub. It comprises 339 questions spanning 7 diverse domains that need to be solved with domain-specific methods. In our experiments, even state-of-the-art LLMs and LLM-based agents demonstrate unsatisfactory success rates, underscoring the need for a novel approach. Furthermore, we present OpenAgent, a novel LLM-based agent system that can tackle evolving queries in open domains through autonomously integrating specialized tools from GitHub. OpenAgent employs 1) a hierarchical framework where specialized agents handle specific tasks and can assign tasks to inferior agents, 2) a bi-level experience learning mechanism to learn from both humans' and its own experiences to tackle tool flaws. Experiments demonstrate its superior effectiveness and efficiency, which significantly outperforms baselines. Our data and code are open-source at https://github.com/OpenBMB/OpenAct.

C1.justification: V1 principally claims successful autonomous GitHub tool extension and learning from human experience. V2 makes OpenAct a central benchmark contribution, claims a gap in existing open-domain evaluation, and adds claims of superiority over baselines and experimental validation of hierarchy and bi-level experience learning.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of the ablations, hint dependence, application difficulty, and failures from unnecessary tool use. Its new limitations section identifies GitHub-specific applicability, reproducibility problems from changing repositories, and Docker resource demands. Earlier repository-selection and configuration failure explanations are largely retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds benchmark construction and validation procedures, repository/domain/difficulty inventories, Apply and Judge prompts, CPU and base-image disclosures, and a stated code/data release link. Conversely, v1's complete query list and several specialized prompts, including Issues/PR judgment and experience summarization, are no longer supplied in the PDF.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from four repositories in four domains to OpenAct's 21 repositories across seven domains, retaining the original four while adding network analysis, security analysis, visualization, and additional specialized tasks. V2 also systematically evaluates explicit, implicit, and absent repository hints: 113 base queries produce 339 variants.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates only GitAgent. V2 Table 3 adds actual comparisons against vanilla LLMs, ReAct, and ReAct+Summary using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, plus GPT-4-based XAgent. ReAct receives the same available actions as OpenAgent.

E3.justification: OpenAgent's settings change from gpt-4-32k at temperature 0.6 to gpt-4-0125-preview and gpt-3.5-turbo-16k at 0.7, with an explicit zero-shot setting. V2 replaces phase-level success checking with GPT-4-judged answer matching and a completeness rubric, and introduces a 120-case judging validation and a 51-query experience-reuse experiment.

E4.justification: V2 adds Issues/PR removal and cross-task experience ablations, controlled repository-hint comparisons, setup/application difficulty analyses, and human-versus-GPT-4 judging validation. V1's stored-repository retrieval-accuracy and API/token-cost analyses disappear. Most execution case studies are retained, chiefly in Appendix E.

E5.justification: V1 Section 3.1 specifies five runs per query and says averages and standard deviations are reported, although Table 2 displays only point values. V2 omits repeated-run counts and provides no variability estimates. This changes statistical documentation without establishing that the actual number of runs decreased.

E6.justification: V1's four-repository phase results and 69.4% headline success rate are replaced by extensive new benchmark results. V2 Table 3 reports OpenAgent averages of 47.3% for GPT-4 and 17.1% for GPT-3.5; Table 4 reports 40.3% without Issues/PRs. These are results under changed tasks and settings, not directly comparable performance changes from v1.

M1.justification: Hierarchical decomposition, Issues/PR consultation, and stored environments and experience already exist in v1; their renamed presentation does not establish new components. A concrete procedural refinement appears in the setup prompt: v1 Figure 16 forbids creating a Dockerfile, whereas v2 Appendix A.3 permits creating one when the default base image causes errors.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and method narrative are extensively rewritten, and GitAgent becomes OpenAgent. Related work moves earlier, benchmark construction precedes the method, detailed procedures and case studies move into appendices, and dedicated limitations and evaluation-validation sections are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. V2 adds benchmark-positioning, construction, performance, and judging-agreement graphics and reorganizes tables around domains, baselines, and ablations. Original case-study diagrams are largely relocated or reformatted, while the cost plot and query-list figures disappear.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around domain-knowledge, tool-use, repository-level, and open-ended benchmarks. Section 2 and Table 1 introduce comparisons with works including ScienceQA, SciEval, SWE-Bench, ML-Bench, and SUPER, reframing the contribution as a benchmark and agent system rather than primarily a tool-extension method.

T1.justification: V2 recasts v1's descriptive action-observation and hierarchical-decomposition equations in recursive agent notation. This does not introduce a substantive mathematical result or change the underlying formal relationships. Neither version supplies theorems, proofs, or mathematical guarantees.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical coverage and absence of baseline comparisons and component ablations. Broader task coverage, comparisons with matched available actions, experience-learning tests, and human checks of automated judging strengthen the evidence for effectiveness. These gains outweigh omitted run-count/cost information and the inconsistency between Section 3.4's completeness rubric and Appendix A.6's judging instructions, which still weaken reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GitHub tool-integration research, with GitAgent renamed OpenAgent and substantial retained procedures and examples. All 22 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison despite extensive revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original OpenAct evaluations, baseline comparisons, experience-learning ablations, difficulty analyses, and human validation of automated judging.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on 30 queries across four repositories, including phase success rates, stored-repository retrieval accuracy, API/token costs, and execution case studies.

arxiv_record.abstract: The generation of toxic content by large language models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge for the safe deployment of language technology. We propose a novel framework for implicit knowledge editing and controlled text generation by fine-tuning LLMs with a prototype-based contrastive perplexity objective. Central to our method is the construction of hard negatives - toxic outputs that are generated through adversarial paraphrasing to be semantically similar and model probability to their non-toxic counterparts. By training on these challenging and realistic pairs, our approach ensures robust and stable contrastive optimization. Experimental results in the domain of detoxification demonstrate that our method significantly reduces toxic generation while maintaining strong performance on downstream tasks such as commonsense reasoning and reading comprehension. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of exploiting hard negatives for attribute-aware fine-tuning.
arxiv_record.authors: Tassilo Klein, Moin Nabi
arxiv_record.title: Contrastive Perplexity for Controlled Generation: An Application in Detoxifying Large Language Models

C1.justification: The central claim of detoxification while preserving general utility remains. v3 gives prototype-based learning and hard negatives greater prominence and adds the abstract's claim that these pairs ensure robust, stable optimization. This strengthens a methodological claim while retaining the principal application and contribution.

C2.justification: v3 Sections 7–8 add substantive limitations concerning generator and corpus coverage, residual toxicity, adversarial bypasses, English-only evaluation, and demographic bias. Section 5.3 newly interprets positive-only training as encouraging input repetition and negative-only training as producing degenerate outputs. These considerably expand the account of mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 adds a source-code link, NVIDIA A10G hardware, approximately 1.5-hour Mistral training time, an estimated 2,500 GPU-hour experimentation budget, LoRA target layers in Table 9, and the judge prompt in Appendix A.3/Figure 5. These substantially expand reproducibility information. LoRA rank and scaling are retained, while v1's exact all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding-checkpoint identification is omitted.

E1.justification: v3 adds WikiText2 for open-domain fluency evaluation in Section 5.4. SafeNLP detoxification, white-box and black-box tasks, and the ten downstream utility benchmarks are retained. The demographic breakdown analyzes populations already represented in SafeNLP.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds reported comparisons with CHRT using GPT-2 and Mistral-7b, Model Arithmetic, and additional GPT-2 variants. Table 4 adds PPO, DPO, and SimPO comparisons using Mistral-7b. These substantially expand comparison methods beyond v1's principal comparisons with underlying language models; DPO's earlier citation alone was not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The reported negative-weight settings change from β in {0, 0.5, 3.5} to direct α in {1, 1.1}. New protocols include dist-n diversity metrics, perplexity evaluation on held-out sets with 0/50/75/100% toxicity, and Qwen-2.5-7b judging with randomized candidate order. The existing generation settings and downstream benchmark shot counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 Section 5.3 adds positive-only and negative-only loss ablations and tests one versus seven samples per contrastive set. Section 5.4 adds fluency, diversity, and toxicity-mixture analyses; Appendix A.2 adds results for 13 demographic groups. The earlier embedding visualization and qualitative examples are retained, with the embedding analysis moved into the main text.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without a repeated-run count. v3 Section 4.1 first specifies five fine-tunings with different random seeds and adds extensive ± reporting in experimental tables. The meaning of ± is not defined. This establishes substantially changed uncertainty reporting, without establishing an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Reported CP toxicity values change, including Falcon-7b from 30.6% to 36.6% and Mistral-7b from 4.7% to 4.3% in Table 1. Black-box and instruction-tuned results also change, and v3 adds comparator, ablation, fluency, diversity, judge-preference, and demographic results. Changed method specifications and run reporting prevent treating these revisions as controlled same-setting gains or losses. v1 Table 4's downstream utility values are unchanged in v3 Table 6.

M1.justification: The stated training objective changes materially: v1 Section 2.2 uses exp(|ϕ(x)−c|/τ), whereas v3 Section 3.2 uses exp(−|ϕ(x)−c|)/τ. This reverses the distance preference and changes temperature dependence. Prototype averaging and the paraphrase-generation procedure remain. The PDFs establish a changed method specification but do not resolve which implementation produced each result.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting, including a new communication metaphor and expanded prototype-based explanations. The document gains dedicated related-work, limitations, and ethics sections; results are reorganized, and the embedding analysis moves from the appendix into the main text.

P2.justification: v3 redraws Figure 1 and expands experimental tables with additional comparators and uncertainty columns. It adds ablation, perplexity, demographic, and LoRA tables plus judge-preference and prompt figures. The instruction-tuning comparison is incorporated into a diversity table, while the algorithm and resized embedding visualization move into the main text. The utility table and qualitative examples are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds an extensive Previous work section covering controlled decoding, preference optimization, knowledge editing, paraphrasing, and hard-negative learning. It develops explicit distinctions from approaches including CMD, GPT-Detox, Model Arithmetic, and LongLLMLingua, with numerous additional citations. v1's explicit identification of the loss as an InfoNCE variant and its corresponding citation are removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical definition of the central contrastive score is substantively revised through the exponential sign and temperature placement. These formulas are non-equivalent. In v3 Equations 3–4, the common 1/τ factor cancels from the normalized score, contradicting the accompanying explanation that it affects learning dynamics. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs resolving these issues.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited competitive comparisons, absent component ablations, and missing run-variability reporting. The ablations expose degenerate low-toxicity solutions, while generation-quality checks, demographic results, explicit limitations, and implementation details make the claims more assessable. Important weaknesses remain: the revised temperature cancels mathematically, Algorithm 1 retains an objective-sign inconsistency, and ± values are undefined. Nevertheless, the added empirical scrutiny and transparency provide a substantial net improvement over v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Contrastive Perplexity research. Their main text and appendices are readable, and visual inspection resolves extraction issues in equations, figures, and tables. The substantial revision supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original detoxification results, comparator experiments, component ablations, generation-quality evaluations, and demographic analyses, alongside retained results.

before.justification: v1 reports original detoxification experiments, downstream utility measurements, embedding analysis, and qualitative outputs in the main text and appendix.

arxiv_record.abstract: Attributed Question Answering (AQA) has attracted wide attention, but there are still several limitations in evaluating the attributions, including lacking fine-grained attribution categories, relying on manual annotations, and failing to compare attributions with only subtle differences. To bridge these gaps, we introduce Complex Attributed Question Answering (CAQA), a large-scale benchmark containing comprehensive attribution categories, automatically generated using Knowledge Graphs (KGs), and complex attribution scenarios. We have conducted extensive experiments to verify the effectiveness of CAQA, including the benchmarking of 25 automatic evaluators, their comparison with human evaluators, the testing of LLM evaluators fine-tuned by CAQA and so on. These experiments also lead to a series of important findings that can benefit the future research of AQA. All the codes and data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/HuuuNan/CAQA-Benchmark.
arxiv_record.authors: Nan Hu, Jiaoyan Chen, Yike Wu, Guilin Qi, Hongru Wang, Sheng Bi, Yongrui Chen, Tongtong Wu and Jeff Z. Pan
arxiv_record.title: Can LLMs Evaluate Complex Attribution in QA? Automatic Benchmarking using Knowledge Graphs

C1.justification: The introduction extends headline findings to few-shot evaluation and distinguishes GPT weaknesses in concatenation/intersection from open-model weaknesses in union. The central contributions—automatic KG-based CAQA construction and its usefulness for assessing and training attribution evaluators—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations involving keyword co-occurrence, CoT decomposition errors and annotators' missing domain knowledge. It also discusses fact-level evaluation failures and explicitly limits coverage of lengthy answers, mathematical, temporal, spatial and domain-specific reasoning. V1 offers much narrower interpretation and limitations.

D1.justification: V2 adds code/data access information, licensing, annotation guidelines and filtering procedures, few-shot/CoT/FACTSCORES prompts, and the ALCE augmentation recipe. It documents vLLM, revised inference hardware and the 3,000-example GPT evaluation limit. However, v1's explicit GPT snapshot identifiers are omitted.

E1.justification: V2 augments whole-answer attribution classification with atomic-fact support estimation and explicit KG-to-text fidelity assessment. The underlying sources remain GrailQA/WebQuestionsSP over Freebase and ALCE; ALCE-FineGrained expands the earlier ALCE-derived evaluation without introducing a new domain.

E2.justification: Tables 5, 15 and 16 substantially expand evaluated comparators with LLaMA-3/3.1, Gemma-2, Phi-3, Qwen-2.5, GPT-4o variants and CoT evaluators. The ALCE comparison adds CAQA-trained T5-11B and further-adapted Vicuna. V1's separate LLaMA-2-chat rows are absent from v2's full results.

E3.justification: V2 introduces few-shot protocols, FACTSCORES evaluation and adaptation using 800 GPT-4-labeled/edited ALCE examples. Four-category ALCE annotations increase from 50 to 215, and AutoIS comparisons now merge negative labels into a binary category. The main-text CAQA human-check count changes from 600 to 300, while Appendix H describes larger annotation pools. Table 4 also revises complexity-group counts while retaining the total dataset size.

E4.justification: New analyses include a 100-example generated-text audit, fact-level evaluation of 200 partially supportive cases, sensitivity to demonstration count, CoT comparisons, domain adaptation and an attribution-error analysis of 234 Vicuna-generated examples. The earlier complexity analysis and ALCE case studies are retained or reorganized.

E5.justification: V2 adds inter-annotator reliability reporting: Fleiss' kappa of 0.780 and 0.748 in Appendix H, and Cohen's kappa of 0.758 for the text audit. V1's automatic-versus-human kappa of 0.65 is no longer reported, while Pearson correlation remains 0.97. Model scores still lack repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive few-shot, CoT, fact-level and adaptation results, including CAQA versus human FACTSCORES of 0.62 versus 0.58. Existing entries also change: zero-shot Vicuna-13B overall F1 is 0.143 in v1 Table 5 and 0.405 in v2 Table 16, whereas several fine-tuned rows remain identical. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core generator retains query extension, subgraph editing and ChatGPT verbalization. Appendix E.3 adds an auxiliary CoT evaluator that decomposes answers into atomic facts, classifies each fact and aggregates the classifications into an attribution label.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and evaluation narrative are extensively rewritten. Benchmark construction is reorganized into four subsections, appendices expand from A–D to A–I, and the narrative and results rename insufficient as partially supportive. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the opening illustration with a construction-pipeline figure and a category-example table, combines category and complexity results into broader tables, and adds several experimental tables and annotation-guideline figures. Complexity examples move to Appendix Table 17, while the earlier ALCE case study reappears as Table 18.

R1.justification: V2 adds AttributionBench, discussion of unanswerable-question attribution, and relevant newer model and evaluation literature. Table 1 separates AttrEval-Gen from AttrEval-Sim, and the positioning explicitly acknowledges extrapolatory/irrelevant equivalence. These refine the comparison with prior work while preserving the original research framing.

T1.justification: Table 3 corrects the formal path-extension expression: the added edge now connects to the original head e0, rather than v1's inconsistent e1 reference. The underlying logical operators and intended query structures remain stable, and neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through generated-text audits, fact-level human comparisons and a fairer AutoIS comparison using matched binary labels and T5 architecture. Diagnostic experiments, annotation guidelines and access information address important weaknesses in v1's validation and reproducibility. Unexplained complexity-count revisions and omitted GPT snapshot identifiers remain drawbacks, but the net quality gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAQA research and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. Renaming, relocation and substantial expansion do not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original model evaluations, fact-level attribution results, human validation studies and supplementary experiments (Tables 5–8 and Appendices A, E–H).

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluator experiments on CAQA and ALCE-Manual, plus comparisons with human annotations (Tables 5–7 and Section 6).

arxiv_record.abstract: Creating lyrics and melodies for the vocal track in a symbolic format, known as song composition, demands expert musical knowledge of melody, an advanced understanding of lyrics, and precise alignment between them. Despite achievements in sub-tasks such as lyric generation, lyric-to-melody, and melody-to-lyric, etc, a unified model for song composition has not yet been achieved. In this paper, we introduce SongComposer, a pioneering step towards a unified song composition model that can readily create symbolic lyrics and melodies following instructions. SongComposer is a music-specialized large language model (LLM) that, for the first time, integrates the capability of simultaneously composing lyrics and melodies into LLMs by leveraging three key innovations: 1) a flexible tuple format for word-level alignment of lyrics and melodies, 2) an extended tokenizer vocabulary for song notes, with scalar initialization based on musical knowledge to capture rhythm, and 3) a multi-stage pipeline that captures musical structure, starting with motif-level melody patterns and progressing to phrase-level structure for improved coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SongComposer outperforms advanced LLMs, including GPT-4, in tasks such as lyric-to-melody generation, melody-to-lyric generation, song continuation, and text-to-song creation. Moreover, we will release SongCompose, a large-scale dataset for training, containing paired lyrics and melodies in Chinese and English.

C1.justification: V2's abstract, introduction and conclusion elevate scalar initialization and motif/phrase-aware whole-song composition into central contributions. V1 primarily emphasized symbolic tuples, token efficiency and dataset construction. The revised claims explicitly emphasize structural coherence and repetition while retaining unified generation and superiority over GPT-4.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting initialization to embedding geometry, motif repetition to a diversity tradeoff, and phrase tokens to structural attention. It discusses memorization evidence and adds substantive limitations concerning dependence on singing synthesis, vocal expressiveness and missing accompaniment generation.

D1.justification: V2 documents the 5,120-token limit, All-In-One phrase annotation, text-to-song prompt construction, revised formats and detailed human-evaluation procedures and participant characteristics. Conversely, FL Studio is replaced by an unspecified internal transcription model, while v1's pitch-augmentation, token-budget and evaluation-calibration details are no longer provided.

E1.justification: The reported paired training corpus changes substantially: v1 combines LMD-full, Reddit, OpenCpop, M4Singer and scraped Mandarin songs; v2 describes 8K Chinese/English pairs collected from audio sources, including newly collected English pairs. V2 also explicitly evaluates pure-melody continuation. Both languages and the four headline tasks remain.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 removes the Transformer Baseline and Baichuan 2, replaces Qwen with Qwen 1.5, and adds InternLM 2 and a fine-tuned InternLM 2 control. The melody-to-lyric comparison also gains SongMass and LLaMA 2, which were absent from v1 Table 3.

E3.justification: Validation changes from 1,188 songs, comprising 415 Chinese and 773 English songs, to 100 split equally between languages. Training batch size changes from 8 to 1, and whole-song training replaces the described short-segment approach. V2 introduces repetition metric RR and continuation-based ablation protocols, substantially revising experimental settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds phrase-token and initialization ablations, a motif-repetition threshold sweep, alignment-granularity comparisons, attention/PCA analyses, memorization testing and annotated song case studies. The pretraining-dataset ablation is retained in Appendix D.3 with revised results; v1's duration/note-vocabulary ablation is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's additional experiments continue the point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Objective, subjective and ablation results are extensively revised, and structural and memorization findings are added. SongComposer's continuation MD/BERT score changes from 2.56/0.683 in v1 Table 4 to 2.12/0.662 in v2 Table 3, which adds RR of 1.64. These are results under revised settings, not established same-setting improvements. Separate English/Chinese lyric-to-melody scores disappear.

M1.justification: V1's logarithmic duration discretization and 120-note vocabulary are replaced by beat-based durations, a restricted 36-pitch vocabulary and revised tuples. V2 adds scalar pitch initialization, motif-level training and phrase tokens, and changes the backbone from InternLM-7B to InternLM2-7B (Sections 3.1-3.3 and 4.2).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. Dataset construction moves largely into Appendix A, detailed subjective criteria move into Appendix B, and method, experiments and appendices are reorganized. The title, author list and dataset terminology also change.

P2.justification: V2 merges the objective conversion-task tables, removes language-separated columns and redesigns the continuation table. It removes the two-stage training schematic and adds hierarchical-structure, attention, memorization, embedding and annotated-score figures. Retained diagrams and prompt templates are also relocated or reformatted.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from contrasting SongComposer with acoustic music generation toward positioning it among symbolic composition subtasks and symbolic LLMs. V2 acknowledges ChatMusician and ComposerX and expands task-specific literature, while removing discussions of works including M2UGen, Noise2music and Mousai.

T1.justification: Mathematical changes concern specific constructions: v1's logarithmic duration encoder/decoder equations are replaced by clipped, tempo-dependent beat quantization. V2 also specifies scalar pitch-embedding multipliers and defines RR as total melodic lines divided by unique lines. Neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support for its design choices: the fine-tuned-backbone control and direct alignment, initialization and structural ablations address questions left largely untested by v1's dataset/vocabulary studies. Human-evaluation documentation and explicit limitations also improve transparency. The smaller validation set, loss of language-specific results and unspecified internal transcriber weaken evaluation breadth and reproducibility, but the controlled analyses provide a substantially stronger methodological justification overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SongComposer and retain its symbolic lyric-melody composition framework and four main tasks. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports objective and human-evaluation results, component ablations, attention and embedding analyses, memorization testing, and generated-song case studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original objective comparisons, a 30-participant human evaluation, and dataset and vocabulary ablations in Tables 1-6.

arxiv_record.abstract: Neural machine translation (MT) models achieve strong results across a variety of settings, but it is widely believed that they are highly sensitive to "noisy" inputs, such as spelling errors, abbreviations, and other formatting issues. In this paper, we revisit this insight in light of recent multilingual MT models and large language models (LLMs) applied to machine translation. Somewhat surprisingly, we show through controlled experiments that these models are far more robust to many kinds of noise than previous models, even when they perform similarly on clean data. This is notable because, even though LLMs have more parameters and more complex training processes than past models, none of the open ones we consider use any techniques specifically designed to encourage robustness. Next, we show that similar trends hold for social media translation experiments -- LLMs are more robust to social media text. We include an analysis of the circumstances in which source correction techniques can be used to mitigate the effects of noise. Altogether, we show that robustness to many types of noise has increased.
arxiv_record.authors: Ben Peters and Andr\'e F.T. Martins
arxiv_record.title: Did Translation Models Get More Robust Without Anyone Even Noticing?

program_record.Abstract: Neural machine translation (MT) models achieve strong results across a variety of settings, but it is widely believed that they are highly sensitive to "noisy" inputs, such as spelling errors, abbreviations, and other formatting issues.  In this paper, we revisit this insight in light of recent multilingual MT models and large language models (LLMs) applied to machine translation. Somewhat surprisingly, we show through controlled experiments that these models are far more robust to many kinds of noise than previous models, even when they perform similarly on clean data. This is notable because, even though LLMs have more parameters and more complex training processes than past models, none of the open ones we consider use any techniques specifically designed to encourage robustness. Next, we show that similar trends hold for social media translation experiments -- LLMs are more robust to social media text. We include an analysis of the circumstances in which source correction techniques can be used to mitigate the effects of noise. Altogether, we show that robustness to many types of noise has increased.
program_record.Title: Did Translation Models Get More Robust Without Anyone Even Noticing?

C1.justification: The central claim that modern translation models are more robust remains. However, the mitigation contribution is substantially redefined: v1 emphasizes diminishing correction benefits for stronger models, whereas v2 claims that finetuning or correction lets conventional models exceed GPT-3.5 on three of four noise types, and that correction combined with LLMs surpasses it across the synthetic benchmarks.

C2.justification: V2 attributes robustness more strongly to training data following the OPUSLLM control and reverses v1's interpretation that correction and inherent robustness are not complementary. It adds explanations of deletion difficulty and mitigation data efficiency, plus explicit limitations concerning possible test contamination, high-resource languages, restricted natural-noise domains and exclusively automatic evaluation.

D1.justification: V2 supplies OPUSLLM training settings, detailed mitigation-data construction, revised training/decoding libraries and metric identifiers, and changes the stated code-repository location. Conversely, earlier batch-size, GPU and training-limit disclosures and several explicit checkpoint paths disappear. Keyboard layouts, prompts and MultiLexNorm statistics largely move to appendices rather than becoming new disclosures.

E1.justification: FLORES, MTNT and MultiLexNorm retain their language and domain coverage. Correction training changes from NeuSpell PROB+WORD to synthetically corrupted Tatoeba Challenge text, and the main synthetic mitigation evaluation shifts from English–French to English–Portuguese. These are limited coverage changes within the existing translation and correction tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds OPUSLLM as an architectural comparator and synthetic-noise-finetuned OPUS as a mitigation comparator. It removes MTNT-finetuned NLLB and excludes GPT-3.5 from the MTNT correction comparison. JamSpell remains in intrinsic correction results but disappears from downstream translation comparisons, while ByT5 replaces mT5. TOWER/TI and finetuned OPUS/r/OPUS are matched across renaming.

E3.justification: The main TowerInstruct evaluation changes from 7B to 13B parameters. V2 introduces matched mitigation training with 60% corrupted source tokens, mixed clean/noisy validation and 100k/1m/5m training budgets. For retained MTNT OPUS finetuning, validation changes from every 100 to 500 steps and the learning-rate grid expands. Appendix H adds BLEU and chrF evaluations.

E4.justification: V2 adds the OPUSLLM architecture control, mitigation training-size analysis, synthetic sentence-level benefit/harm analysis and tests of synthetic finetuning on MTNT. V1's GPT-2 perplexity analysis of fluency versus adequacy is removed. The model-size/multilinguality and tokenizer analyses are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Regression slopes remain point estimates without uncertainty reporting; additional scores and language averages do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: Numerous benchmark entries and rankings change, and substantial result sets are added or removed. For example, MTNT English–French changes from Tower-7B scoring 80.65 below GPT-3.5's 81.33 in v1 Table 8 to TI-13B scoring 81.91 above the unchanged GPT-3.5 score in v2 Table 7; this involves a changed model setting. V2 also adds architecture, mitigation, training-size and BLEU/chrF results.

M1.justification: Section 5 replaces the mT5-Large source corrector with ByT5-Small and introduces direct OPUS finetuning on synthetically corrupted translation data. These change the mitigation architecture and training procedures substantially. The underlying perturbation types and COMET-slope approach remain unchanged despite terminology changes.

P1.justification: Beyond local wording and terminology edits, Section 5 is reorganized from source correction into a comparative mitigation narrative. V2 condenses substantial main-text explanations, redistributes technical material into Appendices A–H and adds a dedicated limitations section. This is a substantial structural revision despite the nearly unchanged abstract.

P2.justification: V2 restructures FLORES tables into translation-direction groups with averages, adds a TI-13B curve to Figure 1 and introduces new mitigation tables and plots. V1's fluency scatterplot, correction grid and MTNT correction scatterplots disappear. Several retained tables move to appendices, which also add six BLEU/chrF result tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds Bawden and Sagot's RoCS-MT work and Kwon et al.'s vLLM reference, while removing references associated with deleted components and analyses, including NeuSpell, mT5 and GPT-2. It corrects v1's assertion that no corpus provides noisy sources, cleaned sources and translations. The broader research positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: The COMET-slope construction and the definition of ΔQE are unchanged, and neither version presents theoretical propositions or proofs. Appendix H applies the existing slope construction to BLEU and chrF without introducing a substantive new mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses an important gap in v1 through a matched-data comparison of direct noise finetuning and correction, supported by training-size and sentence-level analyses that clarify when mitigation helps or harms. Architecture controls, alternative metrics and explicit limitations further strengthen the evidence. These gains outweigh the removed comparisons and lost implementation details, although v2 retains inaccurate results prose: its claim that NLLB generally beats TI on keyboard noise contradicts the English-source results in Table 3.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same translation-robustness study and contain readable text, tables and figures. The comparison includes v2's Appendices A–H; v1 ends with references and has no appendices.

after.justification: V2 reports original results on the retained benchmarks and adds architecture controls, synthetic-noise finetuning, training-size experiments and additional metric results.

before.justification: V1 reports original translation experiments on synthetically perturbed FLORES, MTNT and MultiLexNorm, together with tokenizer analyses and source-correction experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Despite the increasing use of large language models (LLMs) for context-grounded tasks like summarization and question-answering, understanding what makes an LLM produce a certain response is challenging. We propose Multi-Level Explanations for Generative Language Models (MExGen), a technique to provide explanations for context-grounded text generation. MExGen assigns scores to parts of the context to quantify their influence on the model's output. It extends attribution methods like LIME and SHAP to LLMs used in context-grounded tasks where (1) inference cost is high, (2) input text is long, and (3) the output is text. We conduct a systematic evaluation, both automated and human, of perturbation-based attribution methods for summarization and question answering. The results show that our framework can provide more faithful explanations of generated output than available alternatives, including LLM self-explanations. We open-source code for MExGen as part of the ICX360 toolkit: https://github$.$com/IBM/ICX360.

C1.justification: The main framework, scalarization, and explanation-fidelity contributions remain. v2 explicitly extends its principal superiority claim to LLM self-explanations, including DeepSeek-V3, while dropping v1's concluding claim that C-LIME outperforms the other MExGen variants.

C2.justification: v2 suggests that larger perturbation subsets explain P-SHAP's advantage at higher deletion fractions, qualifies the self-explanation experiment as testing rankings rather than numerical scores, and proposes independent-party explanations to mitigate obfuscation. Existing limitations concerning locality and perceived versus actual fidelity remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds ICX360 code-access information, detailed inference settings and prompts, self-explanation parsing instructions, expanded algorithm settings, and fuller survey procedures and participant disclosures. Appendix C updates estimated computation from 100–200 to approximately 1000 hours and identifies the original IBM API as unavailable. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate summarization on XSUM and CNN/Daily Mail and context-grounded question answering on SQuAD. Added models and self-explanation comparisons retain these datasets and task requirements.

E2.justification: Section 4.4 and Table 2 introduce prompted LLM self-explanation rankings as a substantial new comparator class, evaluated using DeepSeek-V3 and Granite-3.3. PartitionSHAP and CaptumLIME comparisons remain. Newly discussed methods such as TextGenSHAP are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Summarization samples increase from 100 to 1000 for DistilBART and 500 for API models; SQuAD increases from 200 to 1000 randomly sampled examples. v2 adds model configurations and changes larger-model refinement to the top 25% of sentences, with revised perturbation budgets and neighborhoods. Perturbation curves stop at 20% rather than 50% removal, and scalarizer cross-evaluations replace BART with SUMM as one evaluation measure.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix D.3 and Figure 12 add sentence-level versus mixed-level perturbation curves for MExGen and self-explanations, providing additional evidence about granularity. Existing scalarizer analyses, human granularity preferences, and the unsuccessful BERT-infilling observation are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly reports fixing the random seed for DeepSeek-V3 and Granite-3.3 generation. Standard-error bands and the user study's confidence intervals and statistical tests already existed in v1. No increase in repeated-run counts is documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds Llama-3 and self-explanation results and revises existing scores under changed settings. For Flan-UL2/CNN/DM, v1 Table 2 reports C-LIME 31.7 versus P-SHAP 30.7; v2 Table 1 reports 32.1 versus 33.2, reversing their ranking. These are not same-setting performance changes. The user-study concentration mean and SD also change from 4.32 and 1.48 to 4.39 and 1.47.

M1.justification: The core scalarizers, segmentation, and attribution framework remain. However, v2 Appendix C.3 uses LOO-only sentence-level screening before C-LIME or L-SHAP refinement for larger models; v1 Appendix B specifies algorithm-specific sentence-level attribution for Flan-UL2. This is a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around context-grounded generation. Method exposition is reordered, related work is substantially reorganized, and the appendices separately organize general method details, experimental settings, additional results, and the user study. This exceeds routine wording edits.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, with extensive figure and table relocation and resizing. v2 adds refinement pseudocode, a self-explanation prompt display, new result tables and plots, and a survey scale illustration. Existing perturbation plots are redrawn with reordered panels and shorter axes; retained survey screenshots are rearranged.

R1.justification: Section 2 and the new related-work appendix substantially expand positioning against TextGenSHAP, GiLOT, ContextCite, Inseq, numerical self-explanation methods, and rationalization research. v2 also explicitly positions its self-explanation comparison relative to Fragkathoulas and Chlapanis, beyond v1's narrower discussion.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix B.3 revises the printed L-SHAP definition: the neighborhood explicitly excludes the attributed unit, and the expression includes a 1/(K+1) averaging factor absent from v1 Equation (2). This is a limited mathematical revision; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical assessment and auditability through larger evaluations, a controlled comparison with an important practical alternative—LLM self-explanation—and much fuller implementation and survey documentation. It also acknowledges the P-SHAP exception and removes v1's blanket C-LIME dominance claim. The retired API and some overly broad superiority wording, despite the DeepSeek-V3 LOO tie in Table 2, remain limitations but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MExGen, with readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained content can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports expanded automated evaluations, new comparisons with LLM self-explanations, and the retained user study in Section 5 and Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original automated attribution evaluations on summarization and question answering, plus an 88-participant user study in Section 5 and Appendix D.

arxiv_record.abstract: In real-world services such as ChatGPT, aligning models based on user feedback is crucial for improving model performance. However, due to the simplicity and convenience of providing feedback, users typically offer only basic binary signals, such as 'thumbs-up' or 'thumbs-down'. Most existing alignment research, on the other hand, relies on preference-based approaches that require both positive and negative responses as a pair. We propose Binary Classifier Optimization (BCO), a technique that effectively aligns LLMs using only binary feedback. BCO trains a binary classifier, where the logit serves as an implicit reward, effectively minimizing the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) loss. We demonstrate that the binary cross-entropy loss employed in classifier training acts as an upper bound for the DPO loss. Additionally, a novel reward shift technique further minimizes the gap between the losses. We validate our methodology in two settings: first, on a paired preference dataset, where our method performs on par with DPO; and second, on a Likert-5 scale annotation dataset which stems from real users' queries. Our model consistently demonstrates effective and robust alignment across four base LLMs and three different datasets, showcasing the strength of our approach to learning from binary signals.
arxiv_record.authors: Seungjae Jung, Gunsoo Han, Daniel Wontae Nam and Kyoung-Woon On
arxiv_record.title: Binary Classifier Optimization for Large Language Model Alignment

C1.justification: v1 presents reward shifting and distribution matching as two central contributions, emphasizing robustness to divergent feedback distributions. v2 drops the distribution-matching contribution, foregrounds alleged flaws in KTO's reference point, and claims BCO surpasses KTO while matching DPO on preference datasets and outperforming DPO on HelpSteer2.

C2.justification: v2 introduces explanations based on gradient suppression, KTO's zero-clipped reference point, and differing KL trajectories. These replace v1's distribution-mismatch and density-estimation interpretations. Its new limitations section acknowledges the absence of genuine binary-feedback benchmarks, the distinction between minimizing an upper bound and its underlying objective, and the loss of comparative information when using binary labels.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix C newly specifies sequence, prompt, and completion limits, bfloat16, FlashAttention-2, and HelpSteer2 balancing procedures. Dataset identifiers and processed sample counts are added. The old Nomic-embedding and scikit-learn density-classifier implementation details disappear with UDM. These changes substantially revise the reproducibility information beyond the changed experimental settings.

E1.justification: v2 retains paired UltraFeedback, drops Anthropic-HH, and adds Capybara, HelpSteer2, and MT Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0 LC, and Arena-Hard evaluations. The generator-filtered UltraFeedback binary-feedback simulations and controlled ShareGPT/FLAN prompt-mismatch scenarios from v1 are removed.

E2.justification: v1 cites IPO but reports no evaluations of IPO or NCA. v2 Table 1 directly compares both against BCO, DPO, and KTO across three chat benchmarks and two instruction-tuned models, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: StableLM-2-1.6B and Mistral-7B are replaced by four Llama/Qwen configurations, and the judge changes from GPT-4-0613 to GPT-4o-2024-08-06. Reported SFT batch size changes from 64 to 128, and UltraFeedback alignment learning rate from 1e-6 to 5e-7. New HelpSteer2 protocols specify tied-pair exclusion, matched training prompts, score binarization, class balancing, and dataset-specific training budgets.

E4.justification: The reward-shift error analysis remains. v2 removes the identical-prompt-ratio sensitivity study, RS/UDM combination ablations, classifier-ensemble comparison, and alternative importance-weighting experiments. It adds KL-divergence, KTO reference-point-collapse, and response-length analyses. The appendix's accounting example is replaced by a WordPress example with a different method comparison.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without evaluation-run counts or uncertainty intervals. v2 Figures 1–2 and Table 1 introduce means and standard deviations across three random seeds, and Arena-Hard results include confidence intervals. These are newly reported statistical practices; the PDFs do not establish how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: The UDM results are removed and extensive new preference, HelpSteer2, and chat-benchmark results appear. For example, v2 Table 1 reports Llama Arena-Hard scores of 31.37 for BCO versus 29.50 for DPO, while IPO leads BCO on AlpacaEval, 30.31 versus 28.61. Changed models, data, and evaluation settings prevent interpreting these as performance gains over v1.

M1.justification: v1's final objective combines reward shifting with density-ratio importance weighting and an auxiliary prompt classifier (Equation 11). v2 removes distribution matching and the classifier; its objective (Equation 8) corresponds to v1's BCE+RS or BCO without UDM. This removes a central method component while retaining reward shifting.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. The experimental narrative shifts from component and distribution-matching studies to preference, Likert-feedback, and chat-benchmark evaluations. Proofs and the KTO reference-point definition move between the main text and appendices, and a dedicated limitations section is added.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redesigns performance figures around absolute win rates and error bars, and replaces UDM displays with benchmark tables and KL/reference-point plots. The reward-error plot and general judge template persist with revised presentation, while qualitative-response tables are replaced and reformatted.

R1.justification: The new Section 4.3 develops substantial comparisons with KTO and NCA, and online-versus-offline alignment studies motivate excluding PPO. References supporting distribution matching and the old experimental suite are removed, while new theoretical, dataset, model, and benchmark references reshape the paper's research positioning.

T1.justification: The BCE–DPO upper bound and optimal reward shift are retained. v2 removes the distribution-matching assumptions and importance-sampling/density-ratio derivations, adds BCO/KTO gradient analysis and the average-reward/negative-KL derivation, and replaces v1 Appendix A.2's derivative-based proof with an AM-GM proof in Appendix A.3, correcting the earlier derivative sign error.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the retained reward-shift method: repeated-seed uncertainty reporting makes results more assessable, and Table 1 tests relevant additional baselines on standard chat benchmarks while exposing exceptions to BCO's lead. The corrected optimal-shift proof and explicit limitations also improve rigor. Removing UDM sacrifices targeted distribution-mismatch support, but the remaining method is substantially better validated and its limitations more clearly documented.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Binary Classifier Optimization research. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison, despite substantial changes to the method, experiments, and presentation.

after.justification: v2 reports original alignment experiments across four LLM configurations, chat-benchmark results, training-dynamics analyses, and generated-response examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM alignment experiments, win rates, component ablations, distribution-mismatch studies, and generated-response examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Detecting tricky bugs in plausible programs, those that pass existing test suites yet still contain bugs, remains a significant challenge in software testing. To address this problem, we propose TrickCatcher, an LLM-powered approach to generating test cases for uncovering bugs in plausible programs. TrickCatcher operates in three stages: First, it uses an LLM to generate program variants based on the program under test (PUT) and its specification. Second, it employs an LLM to construct an input generator from the specification for producing test inputs. Finally, these inputs are executed on both the PUT and its program variants to detect inconsistencies in their outputs. We evaluate TrickCatcher on two datasets, TrickyBugs and EvalPlus, which include 366 human-written and 151 AI-generated plausible programs with tricky bugs. TrickCatcher achieves recall, precision, and F1 scores that are 1.80x, 2.65x, and 1.66x those of the state-of-the-art baselines, respectively. Code and data used are available at https://github.com/RinCloud/TrickCatcher.

C1.justification: The central three-component contribution and headline performance claims remain unchanged. v2 drops v1's explicit claims of the most comprehensive evaluation and being the first practically effective method for this problem, modestly narrowing its novelty assertions.

C2.justification: Section 7 adds logical complementarity between buggy variants and the PUT as a mechanism explanation, plus interpretations concerning model generalization. Limitations now discuss data leakage and model coverage while omitting manual-checking subjectivity. The shortened ablation discussion also removes v1's qualifications about filtering and low-k PUT-guided generation.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 and CYaRon, states dataset licenses, and replaces the anonymous replication-package address with a named TrickCatcher GitHub repository. It omits v1's server specifications, random program-selection details, and independent checking by two authors. These are changes in documented reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The datasets, languages, and 366 human-written plus 151 AI-generated buggy PUTs remain unchanged. Section 6.2 adds a bounded test scenario: canonical EvalPlus programs, previously used as reference implementations, are now evaluated as correct PUTs to measure false alarms.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains CHAT, DPP and APR, and the ablation configurations remain equivalent. DirectChatGPT is renamed DirectChat. The added correct-program experiment reuses CHAT and DPP; DeepSeek-V3 is another backend for the proposed approach, not a new competing method.

E3.justification: v2 adds correct-program false-positive testing and a DeepSeek-V3 comparison at k=5 and k=10. For the retained evaluation, it reports Python input-validity checkers for EvalPlus instead of v1's manual checking and corrects the stated F1 formula. These reported changes do not establish that the unchanged main results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial reliability analyses: false alarms on correct programs separated by error source, the fraction of useful variants that remain buggy, and generalization to DeepSeek-V3. The existing ablations, variant-count sensitivity and difficulty analyses are retained; making difficulty a separate RQ does not constitute a new analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly specifies 100 CHAT cases, 10 APR patches, and 100 inputs plus 10 variants for DPP/TrickCatcher, with explicit averaging steps. The 10-choose-4 example yielding 210 combinations already appeared in v1. This expands statistical reporting without establishing increased repetitions.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their numerical results. New findings include 2.57 versus 41.14 average false positives for TrickCatcher/DPP at k=2 on correct programs, 23.2%/15.0% buggy useful variants on TrickyBugs/EvalPlus, and DeepSeek-V3 F1=59.54 at k=5. The introduction corrects DPP's best F1 values to 24.95 and 36.20; v1's preliminary 92.2% oracle-error breakdown is omitted.

M1.justification: AID becomes TrickCatcher, but the three components and Algorithm 1 remain equivalent: PUT-guided variant generation and filtering, generator-based inputs, and oracle selection from outputs disagreeing with the PUT. CYaRon disclosure and testing another LLM do not establish a changed procedure.

P1.justification: The paper is extensively rewritten and reorganized: related work moves forward, evaluation setup and results become separate sections, discussion is added, and taxonomy/repetition material moves into appendices. The title, method terminology and author block also change. These revisions extend well beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: Typesetting, author layout, captions, prompt panels and result callouts are redesigned. Figure 2 is redrawn, Figure 1 moves into the introduction, and existing tables and plots are reformatted or relocated. v1 Figures 5 and 7 become v2 Figures 7 and 8; the false-positive chart and model-comparison table are genuinely new.

R1.justification: v2 removes the dedicated neural test-oracle literature discussion, including TOGA, and the PAL/chain-of-thought grounding. It adds symbolic-execution coverage and references such as B4 and The Counterfeit Conundrum, while organizing the relationship to Differential Prompting around four explicit distinctions. This substantially changes literature coverage and positioning.

T1.justification: v2 corrects v1's erroneous F1 definition, 2TP²/(TP+FP), to the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The problem definition and test-case taxonomy otherwise remain substantively equivalent, with the taxonomy moved to Appendix A. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's practical-reliability evidence came from buggy PUTs using one LLM. v2 adds missing correct-program controls, a second-model evaluation, and quantitative evidence explaining why buggy variants remain useful, substantially strengthening empirical support. The corrected F1 definition and expanded repetition documentation improve auditability. These gains outweigh the omitted hardware/manual-review details and reduced ablation nuance.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable PDFs describe the same work, renamed from AID to TrickCatcher. Algorithms, tables and figures can be matched reliably. Inspection includes v2 Appendices A–B, which relocate or expand material from v1.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds evaluations of correct programs, useful buggy variants, and a second LLM in Sections 6.2 and 7.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original experiments on TrickyBugs and EvalPlus, including baseline comparisons, ablations, and analyses of task difficulty and variant count.

arxiv_record.abstract: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Preference Optimization (PO) are key processes for aligning Language Models (LMs) with human preferences post pre-training. While SFT excels in efficiency and PO in effectiveness, they are often combined sequentially without integrating their optimization objectives. This approach ignores the opportunities to bridge their paradigm gap and take the strengths from both. In this paper, we interpret SFT and PO with two sub-processes -- Preference Estimation and Transition Optimization -- defined at token level within the Markov Decision Process (MDP). This modeling shows that SFT is only a special case of PO with inferior estimation and optimization. PO estimates the model's preference by its entire generation, while SFT only scores model's subsequent predicted tokens based on prior tokens from ground truth answer. These priors deviates from model's distribution, hindering the preference estimation and transition optimization. Building on this view, we introduce Intuitive Fine-Tuning (IFT) to integrate SFT and PO into a single process. Through a temporal residual connection, IFT brings better estimation and optimization by capturing LMs' intuitive sense of its entire answers. But it solely relies on a single policy and the same volume of non-preference-labeled data as SFT. Our experiments show that IFT performs comparably or even superiorly to SFT and some typical PO methods across several tasks, particularly those require generation, reasoning, and fact-following abilities. An explainable Frozen Lake game further validates the effectiveness of IFT for getting competitive policy.

Our experiments show that IFT performs comparably or even superiorly to SFT and some typical PO methods across several tasks, particularly those requires generation, reasoning, and fact-following abilities. C1.justification: The central contributions remain a unified MDP interpretation of alignment and IFT using one policy and positive-only data to obtain competitive alignment efficiently. The shift from RLHF to Preference Optimization terminology and the additional supporting experiments preserve the substantive scope of these claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds an explanation of cumulative summation as addressing missing future-token gradient feedback during parallel computation, and states that slight SFT overfitting can impair subsequent preference optimization. It removes the earlier model-generalization limitation while retaining the limited-data scalability caveat. Most interpretations of generation performance and Frozen Lake are retained.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-access link, Algorithm 1, and an implementation appendix absent from v1. Appendix B specifies optimizer and training settings, lambda 0.2, decay 0.95, checkpoint selection, four A6000 GPUs, runtimes, and Frozen Lake training targets. These are substantial new disclosures, without establishing that retained experiments used changed settings.

E1.justification: v3 adds dedicated TL;DR summarization evaluation, extending the earlier question-answering and general instruction evaluations. It also uses UltraFeedback variants containing newly generated Gemma2/LLaMA3 responses and ArmoRM preference labels. The original benchmarks, ARC generation adaptation, and Frozen Lake remain.

E2.justification: TDPO and SimPO are added to both direct and sequential Mistral comparisons in Tables 2–3, substantially expanding the evaluated comparator set beyond SFT, DPO, and ORPO. Frozen Lake retains its original comparators; v3 explicitly excludes TDPO and SimPO there.

E3.justification: v3 adds Gemma-2B and LLaMA3-8B configurations and a GPT-4-judged TL;DR protocol. Frozen Lake's stated MSE target changes from policy parameters to transition matrices, although Figure 3 retains its parameter-distance title and curves; this establishes a reported metric revision, not a demonstrated rerun. Existing benchmark shot counts and chat-template usage remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C, Table 7 adds a comparison between standard IFT and 'IFT with noisy lambda,' examining a mixing-coefficient variation without specifying its noise construction. The Frozen Lake analysis and comparison of multiple-choice versus generated ARC answers already exist in v1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests for its experiments. Figure 3 retains the same curves without uncertainty bands; the additional tables continue reporting individual scores.

E6.justification: Existing Mistral scores are retained, including IFT's 59.61 Open-LLM average, while substantial new results appear. In v3 Table 3, added SimPO exceeds IFT on direct Alpaca-Eval-2 length-controlled win rate, 20.31 versus 13.27. New entries include TL;DR, Gemma/LLaMA evaluations, and Table 7's noisy-lambda average of 60.56 versus standard IFT's 59.61. The normalized cost table is removed and concrete runtimes are disclosed.

M1.justification: Temporal residual mixing and future-token loss accumulation already appear in v1. v3 adds Algorithm 1 and an undefined 'IFT with noisy lambda' variant. Algorithm 1 multiplies token losses by cumulative-loss weights, whereas Equation 21 presents a summed-loss objective. These discrepancies prevent reliably distinguishing a changed training procedure from expanded or inconsistent documentation.

P1.justification: v3 retitles the paper, rewrites substantial portions of the abstract and method explanation, and changes alignment terminology throughout. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 6, the SFT-to-preference-optimization comparison becomes a separate section, and limitations and appendices receive a more explicit structure.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, Table 1 moves from full-width to column-width presentation, and the benchmark tables gain comparator rows and additional task/resource columns. v3 adds Algorithm 1, a hyperparameter table, and three appendix result tables, while removing v1's normalized cost table. Figure 3 is relocated and recaptioned with its plot retained.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands research positioning through discussion of RAFT, RRHF, SLiC-HF, improved ranking and negative-sample strategies, and TDPO/SimPO regularization. It also adds literature supporting the language-model background and evaluation discussion. These additions extend the substantive comparison with prior alignment research.

T1.justification: v3 replaces the short IFT loss derivation with expectation-based formulations and an argument that the disturbed optimal state remains unchanged in Appendix A.2. New Appendix A.4 explicitly formulates SFT, reward-model/PPO, online/offline DPO, and IFT objectives. The original MDP definitions and Bellman argument are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens empirical scrutiny and reproducibility: TL;DR and additional model evaluations reduce v1's narrow validation, newer baselines reveal important performance tradeoffs, and Appendix B supplies previously missing implementation settings. The loss/pseudocode discrepancy and undefined noisy-lambda variant still limit exact reproduction, and SimPO's stronger Alpaca-Eval-2 results warrant more qualified claims. These weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe IFT, with matching central formulations, experiments, and results. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and rendered figures and tables support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v3 retains those experiments and reports additional baseline, summarization, model, and noisy-lambda results in Tables 2–3 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original Mistral fine-tuning evaluations and Frozen Lake experiments in Section 5, Tables 2 and 4, and Figure 3.

arxiv_record.abstract: Code generation plays a crucial role in various tasks, such as code auto-completion and mathematical reasoning. Previous work has proposed numerous methods to enhance code generation performance, including integrating feedback from the compiler. Inspired by this, we present ReflectionCoder, a novel approach that effectively leverages reflection sequences constructed by integrating compiler feedback to improve one-off code generation performance. Furthermore, we propose reflection self-distillation and dynamically masked distillation to effectively utilize these reflection sequences. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks, i.e., HumanEval (+), MBPP (+), and MultiPL-E, demonstrate that models fine-tuned with our method achieve state-of-the-art performance. Beyond the code domain, we believe this approach can benefit other domains that focus on final results and require long reasoning paths. Code and data are available at https://github.com/SenseLLM/ReflectionCoder.
arxiv_record.authors: Houxing Ren, Mingjie Zhan, Zhongyuan Wu, Aojun Zhou, Junting Pan, Hongsheng Li
arxiv_record.title: ReflectionCoder: Learning from Reflection Sequence for Enhanced One-off Code Generation
