C1.justification: The introduction reframes the dataset-construction contribution around automatically generated reflection data and annotation savings, and drops the explicit claim of improvement without extra instructions. The central claims about reflection self-distillation, dynamic masking, and improved one-off code generation remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations concerning the value of reflection traces, self-generated data, filtering versus test-time reflection, negative-input handling, and loss spikes during masking transitions. It argues that GPT-4 data is not essential and qualifies the earlier GPT-4 dependency as a broader reliance on capable models, with open-source alternatives. The RoPE restriction and DS-1000 limitations are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds concrete prompts for APPS/LiveCodeBench and ClassEval. The Ethics Statement newly documents upstream sources and access links for the existing instruction corpus. Original code/data access, training hyperparameters, hardware, filtering instructions, and training templates are largely retained; several new experiments receive limited implementation detail.

E1.justification: V2 adds APPS and LiveCodeBench script-generation tasks, ClassEval class/function evaluation, and BigCodeBench complex coding tasks. Section 4.5 also adds GSM8K and MATH for training and evaluating mathematical reasoning, extending coverage beyond code. The earlier benchmarks and multilingual coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds O1-Preview while retaining the previous comparators. The new Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct experiment compares distillation with the unmodified model and test-time reflection. The additional coding benchmarks reuse the existing Magicoder-S and OpenCodeInterpreter comparator families.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs vary reflection-data generators, compare training-time distillation with test-time reflection, and introduce Llama-3.1 mathematical reasoning controls. Appendix B.3 specifies zero-shot greedy evaluation and a post-2023-09-01 LiveCodeBench selection. Existing training settings largely persist. Table 11 labels StarCoder as 7B rather than v1's 15B, but retains the scores and 15B description in the prose; an actual model change is unresolved.

E4.justification: V2 adds the 'w/o Reflection Sequence' control, distinguishing the contribution of traces from additional final-answer data. It also adds generator-source comparisons, autonomous enhancement experiments, a negative-input code case study, and training-loss diagnostics in Appendix B.7. The earlier component, masking-order, up-sampling, positional-embedding, and token-masking analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point performance estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-training-run and seed information. The added tables and training-loss curves do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark scores are retained, including DS-33B's 82.9/76.8 on HumanEval/HumanEval+ and 84.1/72.0 on MBPP/MBPP+. V2 adds substantial results in Tables 4-6 and 10, the no-sequence ablation, O1-Preview scores, and loss trajectories. For example, Table 6 reports GSM8K accuracy of 9.9 versus 11.1 and MATH accuracy of 9.6 versus 13.6 without versus with ReflectionCoder; these are new within-v2 comparisons.

M1.justification: The code-generation pipeline, KL objectives, and three masking strategies remain intact. Section 4.5 adds a limited adaptation that treats mathematical chain-of-thought as the reflection sequence and distills it into final-answer generation. The expanded loss-masking explanation largely repeats information already present in v1 Appendix C.

P1.justification: Most shared prose remains recognizable. V2 edits the abstract, contributions, related work, conclusion, and affiliations; separates the two distillation techniques into methodology subsections; and moves GPT-4 data-construction prompts to Appendix A.1. It also adds Ethics and Acknowledgment sections and simplifies some terminology.

P2.justification: The document changes throughout from a single-column to a two-column layout. Figure 1 is substantially simplified, tables and prompt boxes are reformatted, and Figure 4's unchanged plots are stacked vertically. V2 also adds four result tables and Figures 5-6 showing the masking schedule and training losses.

R1.justification: Related work adds InverseCoder and AutoCoder, explicitly distinguishing training on reflection sequences from AutoCoder's use of interaction to obtain training data. V2 also adds references supporting the new models and benchmarks, while removing CodeT5+ and MAmmoTH citations. The overall research positioning remains centered on improving one-off generation through reflection-based training.

T1.justification: Equations 1-2 remain unchanged, but the definition accompanying Equation 2 changes t_prs from tokens of a partly masked reflection sequence to a partly masked reflection instruction. improvement.justification: The no-sequence control addresses an important attribution gap: whether gains arise from reflection traces or merely additional answer data. after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds data-source experiments, autonomous enhancement, mathematical reasoning, additional coding benchmarks, and training-loss analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original code-generation benchmark results and ablations, including multilingual, DS-1000, masking, and positional-embedding experiments in Appendix B.

arxiv_record.abstract:
As LLMs continuously evolve, there is an urgent need for a reliable
evaluation method that delivers trustworthy results promptly. Currently, static
benchmarks suffer from inflexibility and unreliability, leading users to prefer
human voting platforms like Chatbot Arena. However, human evaluations require
significant manual effort. To address this, we propose the Auto-Arena, an
innovative framework that automates the entire evaluation process using
LLM-powered agents. Firstly, an LLM examiner generates questions. Then, two LLM
candidates engage in a multi-round peer battle based on individual questions,
aiming at revealing their true performance differences. Finally, a committee of
LLM judges collaboratively discusses and decides the winner, reducing bias and
enhancing fairness. During the peer battles, we observe intriguing scenarios
where the LLM candidates display competitive behaviors and even learn from the
opponents. In our extensive experiments involving 15 recent LLMs, Auto-Arena
shows a 92.14% correlation with human preferences, surpassing all previous
expert-annotated benchmarks without any manual efforts. As a result, Auto-Arena
offers a promising alternative to current human evaluation platforms for
evaluating LLMs automatically.

C1.justification: The central claims of fully automated evaluation, leading human-preference alignment, language adaptability, and competitive/learning behaviors remain. The introduction recalibrates headline evidence to 15 rather than 17 models, a 5-point rather than 46.4-point peer-battle benefit, and an 11-point rather than 20-point agreement increase.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands explanations of how decentralized follow-up questioning reduces generator bias and contamination concerns. Appendices C–E interpret question realism and generator-swap results, acknowledge unavailable training data behind the contamination proxy, and allow residual self-enhancement bias despite preserved rankings. These add substantive interpretations and qualifications beyond v1's design arguments.

D1.justification: v4 adds contamination-matching thresholds, sampling and volunteer details, model identifiers, selection reasons, licenses, and a $45 tournament/$5-per-model cost estimate. Existing prompts and length controls are retained. The direct code and leaderboard links supplied in v1 are omitted, while the project website remains and a demo link is added.

E1.justification: The main English/Chinese coverage and eight question categories remain. Appendices C–D add focused scenarios involving benchmark web overlap, human identification of synthetic questions, and debates using math questions from MT-Bench, AMC-8, and AGI-Eval. These extend validation within otherwise retained domain coverage.

E2.justification: GPQA joins both principal benchmark comparisons. The new contamination comparison evaluates MMLU, ARC Challenge, and HellaSwag against generated questions. The existing principal comparators remain; v1's MT-Bench Hard and v4's Arena-Hard cite the same work and are matched as one comparator.

E3.justification: The primary/expanded English cohorts change from 7/17 to 9/15 models, with substantial roster changes. v4 adds individual-versus-majority-vote kappa measurements and new protocols using 100-question web-overlap samples, 30-versus-30 math-question comparisons, and two human raters. These substantially revise and extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained peer-battle ablation and behavioral examples, v4 adds a direct committee-discussion ablation, contamination checks, human and model comparisons of synthetic versus real questions, and a question-generator swap testing self-enhancement bias. Appendices C–E substantially broaden the questions tested about reliability and generalizability.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. Bradley–Terry/Elo estimation is retained. New agreement comparisons and revised numerical values change evaluation endpoints and results, rather than uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: v1 reports 96.4%/94.5% correlations for its 7/17-model experiments; v4 reports 91.67%/92.14% for different 9/15-model cohorts. The strongest benchmark changes from LC-AlpacaEval to Arena-Hard in the primary comparison and MT-Bench after expansion. New results include 88.33% without committee discussions and 2%/28% contamination-proxy rates. These are revised or additional results, not same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: v4 Section 2.3 excludes judges from either participant's model family; v1's experimental setup excluded only the participants themselves. This refines committee selection. The three-stage framework, debate actions, prompt templates, reference-guided judging, and majority voting are retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and related work are extensively rewritten. v4 adds an explicit contribution list, moves related work near the end, separates leaderboard construction into its own section, combines component ablations, and reorganizes the appendices. These substantially change the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v4 redraws or reformats the overview, leaderboard plots, and retained behavioral illustrations. Correlation and ablation tables are consolidated, tables and figures increasingly use wrapped layouts, pairwise heatmaps move to Appendix F, and a new majority-vote agreement display appears. Several new comparison and analysis tables are added.

R1.justification: v4 expands research positioning through comparison matrices and citations covering evaluation surveys, GPQA, LLM-Eval, contamination detection, and synthetic evaluation data. It drops the ChatEval and WideDeep discussions and removes v1's assertion that prior multi-model evaluators lack collective discussion, refining the novelty positioning.

T1.justification: v4 makes the specified Swiss pairing count integer-valued, replacing log2(n) with ceil(log2(n)), and adds cost-scaling reasoning in Appendix H. No new theorems or proofs appear. Appendix H's nlog2(n) pairing count for adding one model conflicts with Section 4.1's logarithmic opponent count.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation through a direct committee-removal ablation and targeted contamination, question-realism, and generator-bias tests, addressing important evidentiary gaps in v1. Model-selection and cost documentation also improve transparency. The small math-focused studies and web-overlap proxy support limited conclusions, and model-count and cost-scaling inconsistencies remain, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in support for the framework's central claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Auto-Arena. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison. Renamed and relocated material can be matched despite substantial revisions to the experiments.

after.justification: v4 reports original tournament results and ablations, plus contamination analysis, a human study, and experiments comparing question sources and generators.

before.justification: v1 reports original English and Chinese tournaments, correlations with human preferences, peer-battle ablations, judge-agreement measurements, and behavioral case studies.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performances in complex text generation tasks. However, the contribution of the input prompt to the generated content still remains obscure to humans, underscoring the necessity of understanding the causality between input and output pairs. Existing works for providing prompt-specific explanation often confine model output to be classification or next-word prediction. Few initial attempts aiming to explain the entire language generation often treat input prompt texts independently, ignoring their combinatorial effects on the follow-up generation. In this study, we introduce a counterfactual explanation framework based on Joint Prompt Attribution, JoPA, which aims to explain how a few prompt texts collaboratively influences the LLM's complete generation. Particularly, we formulate the task of prompt attribution for generation interpretation as a combinatorial optimization problem, and introduce a probabilistic algorithm to search for the casual input combination in the discrete space. We define and utilize multiple metrics to evaluate the produced explanations, demonstrating both the faithfulness and efficiency of our framework.
arxiv_record.authors: Yurui Chang, Bochuan Cao, Yujia Wang, Jinghui Chen, Lu Lin

C1.justification: The central claims about joint attribution, efficient probabilistic search, faithfulness and transferability remain. V2's introduction adds an explicit contribution claim concerning potential benefits to model safety and efficiency, modestly extending the claimed applications.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations concerning jailbreak defense, diagnosis of overlooked requests and stability across seeds. The original token-interaction rationale and black-box mechanism limitation remain. Section 5.3 also introduces an erroneous reference to higher SentenceBert scores indicating greater semantic change, contradicting its lower-is-better definition and Table 1.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link and documents details such as 16-bit execution for the 70B experiment and ReAGent's full-output adaptation. Existing software and hardware disclosures remain. The new larger-sample runtime limit is inconsistently documented as 240 hours in A.8 and 200 hours in Table 6.

E1.justification: The original Alpaca, tldr_news and MHC coverage remains. V2 adds AQuA few-shot chain-of-thought reasoning in Appendix A.12 and adversarial jailbreak scenarios involving GCG and random-search prompts in A.4, substantially broadening the evaluated task and input conditions.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds averaged Attention and Last-Attention alongside the retained Random, Captum and Integrated-Gradient baselines. Table 8 adds continuous-mask Gradient optimization, and Figure 9 evaluates ReAGent adapted to explain full outputs. These materially expand the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Section 5.2 changes the stated PR definition from a raw joint-probability ratio to a length-normalized ratio; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. New settings include expanded Alpaca/tldr_news sampling and full MHC evaluation, a 20-instance 16-bit LLaMA-2 70B test, and few-shot reasoning. The convergence experiment extends from 100 to 150 iterations.

E4.justification: The original token-count and gradient-guidance ablations remain in Appendices A.6-A.7. V2 adds continuous-mask optimization analysis, jailbreak detection and token-removal cases, diagnosis of ignored requests, and additional counterfactual response examples in A.4, A.5 and A.10. It also extends the convergence analysis.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates without stated repeated-seed uncertainty. V2 Appendix A.9 and Table 7 report three runs with different seeds and mean plus standard deviation for all evaluated metrics across the three LLaMA-2 7B datasets. This introduces substantive uncertainty reporting without establishing v1's run count.

E6.justification: Most matched Table 1 entries and all Table 2 timings remain unchanged. For the proposed method on LLaMA-2, Alpaca BLEU changes from 0.482 to 0.484, while MHC PR/KL change from 0.710/0.238 to 0.701/0.246. V2 adds extensive results in Tables 4 and 6-8 and Figures 7-9. The PR change cannot be treated as a same-definition performance gain.

M1.justification: Equation (3) and Algorithm 1 retain the binary-mask objective, gradient-guided initialization and sampling, token swaps, and acceptance procedure. Renaming XPrompt to JoPA and applying it to additional scenarios do not establish a changed proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: V2 renames the method and title, adds equal-contribution credit, corrects and condenses prose, and introduces related-work subsections. It moves the main ablation discussion to Appendix A.6 and the existing limitations paragraph to Section 7. Much of the original exposition remains.

P2.justification: V2 expands Table 1 with attention-baseline rows, adds four result tables and three comparison charts, and redraws the convergence plot with a longer iteration axis. Existing case-study figures and ablation plots are relocated and renumbered, while the timing and dataset tables are reformatted.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds substantive distinctions from Archipelago and Diffmask. Additional references support attention explanations, ContextCite, jailbreak testing and reasoning experiments. The central positioning around joint attribution of complete generations and most existing related work remain.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds a one-swap local-optimum definition and a brief convergence proof sketch, absent from v1. Section 5.2 also revises the mathematical definition of PR through length normalization. The original optimization objective and generation equations remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's small-sample empirical foundation through larger evaluations, additional attribution comparators and three-seed uncertainty reporting. The 70B and reasoning tests further support applicability. Missing Captum results in the larger-sample evaluation, briefly documented new protocols, the informal convergence argument, and reporting inconsistencies limit some additions, but the evidence supporting the central method is substantially broader and better assessed.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same joint prompt attribution work, renamed from XPrompt to JoPA. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable matching of retained, revised and added material.

after.justification: V2 retains the original experiments and adds original larger-sample, repeated-seed, larger-model, reasoning, jailbreak-detection and attribution-comparison results.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A.3 report original faithfulness, runtime, convergence and ablation results using LLaMA-2 (7B-Chat) and Vicuna (7B).

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT demonstrate significant potential in the medical domain and are often evaluated using multiple-choice questions (MCQs) modeled on exams like the USMLE. However, such benchmarks may overestimate true clinical understanding by rewarding pattern recognition and test-taking heuristics. To investigate this, we created a fictional medical benchmark centered on an imaginary organ, the Glianorex, allowing us to separate memorized knowledge from reasoning ability. We generated textbooks and MCQs in English and French using leading LLMs, then evaluated proprietary, open-source, and domain-specific models in a zero-shot setting. Despite the fictional content, models achieved an average score of 64%, while physicians scored only 27%. Fine-tuned medical models outperformed base models in English but not in French. Ablation and interpretability analyses revealed that models frequently relied on shallow cues, test-taking strategies, and hallucinated reasoning to identify the correct choice. These results suggest that standard MCQ-based evaluations may not effectively measure clinical reasoning and highlight the need for more robust, clinically meaningful assessment methods for LLMs.
arxiv_record.authors: Maxime Griot, Jean Vanderdonckt, Demet Yuksel, Coralie Hemptinne
arxiv_record.title: Pattern Recognition or Medical Knowledge? The Problem with Multiple-Choice Questions in Medicine

C1.justification: V1 centers its claims on similarly high model performance despite fictional content. V2 adds the central claim that models outperform physicians on this benchmark and explicitly attributes successful answers to shallow cues, test-taking strategies and hallucinated reasoning. Its conclusion also qualifies the earlier claim of isolating reasoning from memorization as only partial isolation.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of answers-only performance and MedQA correlation, and questions whether medical fine-tuning improves knowledge or familiarity with evaluation formats. It introduces clinician-workload concerns about reviewing reasoning traces and acknowledges bias from a single clinician's grounding material. The coherence limitation is revised following partial audits, while v1's explicit sample-size and model-selection limitations are removed.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds archival code identifiers, a standalone dataset identifier and human-annotation instructions, and reports that Glianorex tasks are available in the evaluation harness's main branch. V2 also documents vLLM, eight H200 GPUs and greedy decoding for DeepSeek, and updates the main evaluation runtime from four to ten hours. Existing generation defaults and the core evaluation command are retained.

E1.justification: V2 extends evaluation beyond full-question fictional MCQs to answers-only inputs and adds a cross-benchmark analysis using MedQA-USMLE scores, which v1 only discussed as background. It also evaluates Claude-generated Glianorex questions alongside GPT-generated questions. The fictional medical domain and English/French language coverage remain.

E2.justification: The original 14-model quantitative panel is retained, including Internist.ai and Meerkat under shortened names. V2 adds two physicians as an explicitly evaluated human reference on 100 English questions (Figure 2), substantially broadening the central comparison from differences among models to differences between models and medical experts.

E3.justification: V2 adds 224 Claude-generated questions per language to the 264-question GPT subsets. New protocols include physician testing without textbook exposure, randomized question order and seven-point language-quality ratings, plus four DeepSeek conditions crossing full-question versus answers-only input with direct answering versus chain-of-thought prompting (Sections 3.1.4 and 3.3; Appendix A.4).

E4.justification: V2 adds generator-dependence checks, physician audits of coherence and question quality, prompting/input ablations, an answer-length analysis, MedQA correlation analysis, and qualitative examinations of hallucinations and test-taking strategies. Conversely, v1's per-question correct-answer distribution analysis and Figure 2 are removed.

E5.justification: V1 already reports normal-approximation confidence intervals, binomial chance tests, significance comparisons and Cohen's d. V2 additionally specifies two-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD, regression inference with 95% prediction bands, and Cohen's kappa agreement analysis. It also specifies one prediction per item and ablation setting; this expands statistical reporting without establishing increased repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: The reported overall average changes from about 67% to 63.8% over an expanded question pool, so this is not a same-setting performance decline. V2 adds generator-specific scores (Table 6), physician scores of 27% each, a MedQA association with R-squared 0.5952, and DeepSeek accuracies of 70.1% for full-question zero-shot and 46.5% for answers-only zero-shot evaluation (Table 3). Effect-size and significance results are also revised.

M1.justification: The fictional-textbook-to-MCQ-and-translation approach is retained. V2 extends benchmark construction with a Claude 3.5 Sonnet generation branch and physician review checkpoints before downstream generation (Section 3.1 and Figure 1). These are bounded extensions of the existing construction procedure.

P1.justification: The title changes, Related Work becomes a standalone section, and Methods and Results gain extensive hierarchical subsections. Discussion is reorganized into evaluation implications, medical implications, recommendations and alternatives; Conclusion moves before Limitations. Substantial rewriting also clarifies and shortens retained arguments.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout and adds a generation-pipeline diagram, regression plot, annotation-interface screenshot, ablation table and generator-specific results table. The accuracy figure gains a human reference, significance displays are split, and the original response-distribution figure disappears. The generation prompt and retained question examples are relocated or renumbered rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around benchmark fragility, including MedFuzz, drug-name perturbations and medical metacognition. It connects its interpretations to work on answers-only strategies, medical adaptation and knowledge extraction, and adds literature on clinician workload and alternative clinical assessments. These additions reshape the argument beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical propositions, proofs or a formal model of the phenomenon. V2's additional standard statistical analyses do not introduce new mathematical definitions or theoretical derivations.

improvement.justification: V1's interpretation relied mainly on high scores without reported human validation or direct input ablations. V2 adds language/coherence audits, a human reference, a second question generator and answers-only controls that substantially strengthen the evidence behind its central argument. The two-physician sample, single-model ablations and removal of explicit sample-size/model-selection caveats limit the gains, but do not outweigh the improvement in empirical support and interpretability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Glianorex fictional-medical benchmark, with matching authors, core methodology, model panel and question examples. All 18 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including Appendices A and B, support comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports expanded model evaluations, physician answers and quality ratings, comparisons across question generators, and original DeepSeek prompting and interpretability analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations of 14 language models on 264 fictional medical questions per language, including accuracy, statistical comparisons and per-question response distributions.

arxiv_record.abstract: Topic models are useful tools for discovering latent semantic structures in large textual corpora. Recent efforts have been oriented at incorporating contextual representations in topic modeling and have been shown to outperform classical topic models. These approaches are typically slow, volatile, and require heavy preprocessing for optimal results. We present Semantic Signal Separation ($S^3$), a theory-driven topic modeling approach in neural embedding spaces. $S^3$ conceptualizes topics as independent axes of semantic space and uncovers these by decomposing contextualized document embeddings using Independent Component Analysis. Our approach provides diverse and highly coherent topics, requires no preprocessing, and is demonstrated to be the fastest contextual topic model, being, on average, 4.5x faster than the runner-up BERTopic. We offer an implementation of $S^3$, and all contextual baselines, in the Turftopic Python package.

C1.justification: v3 removes v1's headline claim to be the first exclusively contextual model supporting multiple topics per document and its claim of state-of-the-art topic diversity. It instead claims near-perfect diversity and competitive coherence, while retaining the efficiency contribution and quantifying a median 4.5x advantage over BERTopic. These materially narrow the novelty and performance claims.

C2.justification: v1 flags possible repeated terms from its importance rule; v3 explains the salience/specificity tradeoff and recommends combined scoring. It adds a dimensionality-based explanation for FASTopic's behavior and substantive limitations concerning single-seed testing, untuned baselines, preprocessing evidence from one corpus, and unevaluated document-topic representations.

D1.justification: v3 supplies FASTopic and ECRTM hyperparameters and training settings, updates hardware information, explicitly states that timings exclude embedding computation, and explains whitening dimensionality reduction and unseen-document inference. The timing exclusion is newly documented, not an established change from v1. Existing core hyperparameters, code access, and MIT licensing remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on 75,000 StackExchange entries and 6,861 medical Wikipedia articles, broadening the represented document populations and domains. The original 20 Newsgroups, BBC News, and ArXiv ML corpora remain, as does the raw-versus-preprocessed 20 Newsgroups comparison.

E2.justification: FASTopic and ECRTM become evaluated comparators in quantitative, runtime, and qualitative comparisons, including v3 Tables 4–5 and Appendix I. All six earlier baselines remain. CombinedTM and CTMcombined denote the same comparator, rather than an additional method.

E3.justification: v3 introduces geometric-mean coherence and interpretability metrics and restricts encoder-dependent results in Figure 2 and Table 4 to sentence transformers. Runtime summaries use median ratios instead of mean percentage differences, and reported hardware changes from 64 Xeon Gold cores to 20 Xeon Silver cores. The four encoders, 10–50 topic settings, and top-10-word evaluation remain.

E4.justification: v3 Section 5.4 adds a systematic comparison of axial, angular, and combined importance, examining coherence/diversity tradeoffs and overlap between descriptive terms. It also analyzes FASTopic's encoder sensitivity. Existing preprocessing and noise analyses remain, while the five-topic ArXiv demonstration is retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 reports twice-standard-deviation summaries and highest-density intervals. v3's corpus tables omit those SD summaries, while Figure 2 adds bootstrap confidence intervals and Table 3 adds regression standard errors, p-values, and coefficient intervals. Sections 4.3 and 8.4 newly disclose one run per configuration and a single seed; they do not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial results for the new corpora, baselines, and S3 variants, plus regression findings and changed appendix topic outputs. For example, Table 4 reports WikiMedical aggregate interpretability of 0.63 for Top2Vec versus 0.60 for all S3 variants. Revised runtime results have different reported hardware and aggregation, preventing direct same-setting performance comparisons.

M1.justification: v3 Section 3.1 retains the FastICA decomposition and original projection-based scoring, now called axial importance. It adds angular importance, W_jt/||W_j||, and combined importance, (W_jt)^3/||W_j||. These modify descriptive-word selection within the existing method; expanded whitening and inference explanations do not establish additional procedural changes.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, related work, and results undergo substantial rewriting and restructuring. Results are reorganized around preprocessing, stop words, encoders, and importance estimation; NPMI discussion moves into a dedicated appendix. Limitations and appendix organization expand substantially, beyond changes attributable solely to added experiments.

P2.justification: The existing overview schematic moves to the first page with an expanded caption. New figures present performance/speed rankings, scoring geometry, and encoder effects. Dataset and encoder tables are merged, comparison tables are restructured in the appendices, runtime plots switch to logarithmic axes, and nonalphabetical-term results become boxplots.

R1.justification: A new Semantic Axes subsection discusses Yamagiwa et al. (2023) and Musil and Marecek (2024), distinguishing corpus-specific topic discovery from universal semantic dimensions. v3 also positions S3 against ECRTM and FASTopic and expands references supporting its discussions of evaluation limitations and hyperparameter tuning.

T1.justification: v3 adds mathematical definitions for angular and combined importance and for geometric-mean coherence and interpretability in Sections 3.1 and 4.4. The ICA factorization and pseudoinverse relationship remain. These are limited formal extensions; neither version presents theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens v1's limited empirical coverage through FASTopic/ECRTM comparisons, medical and StackExchange corpora, and direct investigation of the previously unresolved term-importance concern. It also clarifies research positioning and narrows headline claims to better reflect the evidence. Single-seed testing limits robustness, and changed timing conditions prevent direct speed comparisons across versions, but the broader evidence and more precise scope provide a substantial overall quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same S3 research work and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Shared content can be matched despite extensive reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v3 reports original empirical results across the retained and additional corpora, including model comparisons, scoring-variant evaluations, runtime measurements, and qualitative outputs.

before.justification: v1 reports original topic-model benchmarks, runtime measurements, preprocessing and noise analyses, and qualitative topic outputs in Sections 4–6 and the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Misinformation is prevalent in various fields such as education, politics, health, etc., causing significant harm to society. However, current methods for cross-domain misinformation detection rely on effort- and resource-intensive fine-tuning and complex model structures. With the outstanding performance of LLMs, many studies have employed them for misinformation detection. Unfortunately, they focus on in-domain tasks and do not incorporate significant sentiment and emotion features (which we jointly call {\em affect}). In this paper, we propose RAEmoLLM, the first retrieval augmented (RAG) LLMs framework to address cross-domain misinformation detection using in-context learning based on affective information. RAEmoLLM includes three modules. (1) In the index construction module, we apply an emotional LLM to obtain affective embeddings from all domains to construct a retrieval database. (2) The retrieval module uses the database to recommend top K examples (text-label pairs) from source domain data for target domain contents. (3) These examples are adopted as few-shot demonstrations for the inference module to process the target domain content. The RAEmoLLM can effectively enhance the general performance of LLMs in cross-domain misinformation detection tasks through affect-based retrieval, without fine-tuning. We evaluate our framework on three misinformation benchmarks. Results show that RAEmoLLM achieves significant improvements compared to the other few-shot methods on three datasets, with the highest increases of 15.64%, 31.18%, and 15.73% respectively. This project is available at https://github.com/lzw108/RAEmoLLM.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhiwei Liu, Kailai Yang, Qianqian Xie, Christine de Kock, Sophia Ananiadou, Eduard Hovy
arxiv_record.title: RAEmoLLM: Retrieval Augmented LLMs for Cross-Domain Misinformation Detection Using In-Context Learning Based on Emotional Information

C1.justification: The headline gains shift from comparisons with zero-shot methods (20.69%, 23.94%, 39.11%) to other few-shot methods (15.64%, 31.18%, 15.73%), with the latter numbers calculated against random few-shot in Section 3.3.1. The central novelty claim of affect-based, fine-tuning-free cross-domain retrieval and inference remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving dataset size and COVID-specific emotional consistency, interprets its timing comparison as greater efficiency, and explicitly notes that rumours include true, false and unverified cases. Existing imbalance and short-text limitations remain, although the named PHEME failure examples narrow to Prince Toronto.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies an A100 80GB GPU, 256 maximum new tokens, do_sample=False, remaining generation defaults and extraction details for the new embedding baselines. It reports stage-level timings and changes the repository statement from planned release to availability. Conversely, v1's PCA construction and best-dimension selection details are omitted.

E1.justification: Both versions use AMTCele's seven domains, PHEME's nine events and the same held-out COCO topics: Fake Virus, Harmful Radiation and Depopulation. Added diagnostic analyses reuse these datasets without expanding benchmark task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds evaluated domain-generalization comparators MDFEND, EDDFN, MOSE, CANMD and MetaAdapt. Table 4 additionally compares retrieval using RoBERTa semantic embeddings and SentiBERT embeddings. These substantially extend v1's comparisons with fine-tuned BERT/RoBERTa and zero-shot/random few-shot methods.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama3.2 1B/3B configurations and protocols for embedding-substitution controls, source-identification probing and stage-level timing. Benchmark partitions, weighted classification metrics and retrieval-count ranges remain unchanged. Newly disclosed generation parameters do not establish that earlier settings differed.

E4.justification: v2 adds embedding-type ablations, a possible data-leakage diagnostic, timing against BERT and categorical-affect association tests. Conversely, v1's PCA dimensionality sensitivity and time-F1 trade-off studies disappear. Retrieval-count sensitivity and special-case analyses are retained with revised results and placement, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix G.2 and Table 12 add chi-squared independence tests and p-values for categorical affect versus misinformation labels across all three datasets. Existing affective means, variances and t-tests are retained. Benchmark seed counts, repeated-run variability and confidence intervals remain unreported.

E6.justification: Main, per-domain, retrieval-count and special-case scores are extensively revised, alongside new comparator and diagnostic results. For example, Mistral-7b Vreg-addexpl F1 changes from 0.7767/0.6935/0.7725 in v1 Table 4 to 0.7717/0.6920/0.7931 in v2 Table 3. These are revised reports, not established same-setting gains: v1 selects results across embedding dimensions, while v2 omits an equivalent selection description.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 removes v1's cosine-score threshold of 0.2, leaving unconditional scoring before top-K selection. This changes the reported retrieval procedure, while the affective encoder, three-module architecture and inference templates remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: related work moves to Appendix A, dataset preprocessing enters Methodology, special cases move to Appendix D, and retrieval-count analysis enters a module-ablation subsection. The abstract and experimental discussion are rewritten, affective explanations are redistributed, and the standalone ethics statement disappears.

P2.justification: v2 adds tables for embedding controls, source identification, runtime and chi-squared tests; splits and relocates existing affect-statistics tables; and expands the main comparison table. Figure 2's bars and axes change, Figure 7's class labels are corrected, and v1 Figures 11 and 12 are removed. Most remaining affect plots are reused.

R1.justification: The expanded related work adds substantial discussion of domain-generalization methods, retrieval-augmented misinformation detection and demonstration selection, including newly cited works by Nan, Silva, Yue, Wang, Xuan and others. This broadens the research positioning beyond v1's shorter treatment. The Marimont and Shapiro dimensionality citation is removed.

T1.justification: No theoretical propositions, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations are added or revised. The affect definitions are retained and relocated; the added significance tests constitute empirical statistical analysis.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct retrieval alternatives and relevant domain-generalization comparators, leaving important gaps in evaluating its central contribution. v2 Tables 3 and 4 substantially strengthen that evaluation, supported by clearer implementation disclosures. Removing the PCA trade-off study reduces supporting analysis, and the source-identification example does not establish training-data leakage, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger comparative validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RAEmoLLM and contain readable main text, algorithms, tables, figures and appendices. Their shared methods and experiments can be matched reliably despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, embedding comparisons, statistical analyses and runtime measurements in its main text and appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on AMTCele, PHEME and COCO, including per-domain results, retrieval sensitivity studies and affective analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) assesses sentiments towards specific aspects within texts, resulting in detailed sentiment tuples. Previous ABSA models often use static templates to predict all of the elements in the tuples, and these models often fail to accurately capture dependencies between elements. Multi-view prompting method improves the performance of ABSA by predicting tuples with various templates and then ensembling the results. However, this method suffers from inefficiencies and out-of-distribution errors. In this paper, we propose a Dynamic Order Template (DOT) method for ABSA, which dynamically generates necessary views for each instance based on instance-level entropy. Ensuring the diverse and relevant view generation, our proposed method improves F1-scores on ASQP and ACOS datasets while significantly reducing inference time.
arxiv_record.authors: Yonghyun Jun, Hwanhee Lee
arxiv_record.title: Dynamic Order Template Prediction for Generative Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contribution: instance-specific DOT templates combine sentiment-extraction accuracy with faster inference and improved transferability relative to static prompting. Expanded benchmark evidence and updated dataset counts do not introduce a new central capability or novelty claim.

C2.justification: v2 changes the explanation for excluding opinions in stage one toward helping stage-two learning. It adds interpretations connecting implicit-term failures to data size, complex-sentence errors to fewer views, and seed variation to error propagation. It also explicitly limits the assumption that necessary views equal tuple count. Some interpretations overreach: the claimed superiority on BART and complex inputs has Rest-dataset exceptions in Tables 7 and 8.

D1.justification: v2 adds a reported public implementation link, literal-null handling, constrained-decoding disclosure, worked input/target examples in Appendix E, dataset statistics, and training durations. These materially expand reproducibility information without establishing newly introduced procedures. The original optimizer, learning rate, batch sizes, training epochs, and hardware remain; the Ethics Statement still describes release as planned.

E1.justification: Section 3.1 and Table 1 expand evaluation from five to nine datasets by adding MEMD Laptop, Books, Clothing, and Hotel. The original MEMD restaurant dataset, MR, is retained as M-Rest. The sentiment-quadruple extraction task remains unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds TAS-BERT, Extract-Classify, One-ASQP (large), SCRAP, and Qwen-2.5-7b. It reports GPT-4o instead of GPT-3.5-turbo and LLaMa-3.1-8b instead of LLaMa-3-8b, although Figure 9 retains older model labels. The principal generative baselines remain.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce T5-small and T5-large configurations, BART backbones, and quarter/half/full M-Rest training-data comparisons. Appendix G also defines a complex-input evaluation using more than three tuples, more than 22 words, or Flesch-Kincaid grade at least nine. These are additional evaluation protocols; the original training settings remain documented.

E4.justification: The ablation study adds stop-word-filtering and combined-component removals, while replacing the original no-resampling condition with random view sampling to test entropy-based selection. New analyses examine model scale, backbone dependence, implicit terms, training-data size, and complex sentences. The original case study and first-stage analysis are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions already report averaging over five seeds. v2 newly provides standard deviations for Paraphrase, MvP, and DOT on the five original benchmarks in Appendix G, Table 10. It does not report an increase in run count, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original five DOT benchmark scores and cross-dataset results are unchanged, but v2 adds extensive benchmark and diagnostic results. SCRAP's newly included R16 score of 62.48 exceeds DOT's retained 61.24. The ablation Full Model entry changes from 53.94 to 54.33, and the no-multi-view entry from 53.31 to 52.31; these revisions do not establish reruns or a same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: Equation 1 revises the stated view-ranking score from conditional generation probability to an entropy expression. The two-stage architecture, template selection framework, opinion exclusion, and training losses remain. The PDFs do not establish whether the revised equation reflects an implementation change.

P1.justification: Section 2 is substantially rewritten to distinguish views, initial/final templates, and inference steps. The results narrative is reorganized around transferability, model scale, and ablations; the main-text case study moves to Appendix B, and the appendix structure expands substantially. These changes go beyond adding experimental paragraphs.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are redrawn, and Table 1 becomes a full-width comparison with nine datasets, averages, and additional methods. v2 adds the model-scale chart, worked-example figure, and Tables 5–10. The original case-study, tuple-distribution, timing, and LLM-prompt displays are retained with relocation or renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 broadens citations and brief positioning to extraction-based and reasoning-based ABSA, newer LLMs, constrained decoding, BART, scaling laws, and readability analysis. The central relationship to static single-view and multi-view prompting remains unchanged. Consolidating the two Hu 2022 references does not represent a new cited work.

T1.justification: Equation 1 replaces a conditional-probability definition with a negative sum of probability-times-log-probability terms. This revises the mathematical definition of the ranking quantity. The training objectives and classification-loss derivation are retained, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of DOT's design through broader comparisons, explicit filtering and entropy-selection controls, backbone tests, and targeted failure analyses. Standard deviations, training costs, and clearer implementation documentation address important transparency gaps in v1. These gains concern evidential support rather than improved scores on retained benchmarks. Overgeneralized interpretations and inconsistent LLM labels remain weaknesses, but they do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental scrutiny and reproducibility information.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DOT research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised, and added content.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds evaluations across more datasets, model backbones, difficult inputs, and training-data sizes.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, cross-dataset evaluations, ablations, first-stage prediction experiments, and inference-time measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language and multimodal models have shown remarkable success on various benchmarks focused on specific skills such as general-purpose programming, math word problem-solving, and visual question answering. However, it is unclear how well these models perform on tasks that require a combination of these skills. In this paper, we curate a novel program synthesis benchmark based on the real-world tasks in the XLogoOnline visual programming environment. Each task requires a combination of different skills such as spatial planning, basic programming, and logical reasoning. Our evaluation shows that current state-of-the-art models like GPT-4V and Llama3-70B struggle to solve these tasks, achieving only 20% and 2.35% success rates, respectively. Next, we develop a fine-tuning pipeline to boost the performance of models by leveraging a large-scale synthetic training dataset with over 80,000 tasks. Moreover, we showcase how emulator-driven feedback can be used to design a curriculum over training data distribution, through which a fine-tuned Llama3-8B drastically outperforms GPT-4V and Llama3-70B models. Finally, we provide an in-depth failure analysis to understand the limitations of different models. We will publicly release the benchmark for future research on program synthesis in visual programming.
arxiv_record.authors: Chao Wen, Jacqueline Staub, Adish Singla
arxiv_record.title: Program Synthesis Benchmark for Visual Programming in XLogoOnline Environment

C1.justification: The benchmark and synthetic-data/emulator fine-tuning contributions remain central. V2 adds failure diagnosis as an explicit contribution and conclusion, extends the named outperformance claim to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, and removes v1's concluding statement that the best evaluated base model achieves only 20%.

C2.justification: V2 qualifies vision's benefits because textual inputs already encode the grid, and emphasizes reasoning capabilities. New interpretations address model-specific failures, selection and distribution-shift effects, limited math transfer, and possible forgetting on general coding tasks. Limitations now explicitly identify missing advanced programming concepts, while retaining the binary-feedback limitation.

D1.justification: Appendices A, B, and D supply details that v1 only promised: generation parameters, sampling procedures, model identifiers, LoRA settings, learning rates, batch sizes, hardware, training and resampling times, beta=1, and full prompts. V2 also supplies a benchmark repository link. These additions substantially improve documentation of the existing pipeline.

E1.justification: V2 adds general Python synthesis evaluations on HumanEval and MBPP, including their enhanced '+' test suites, and evaluates perturbed grid and constraint scenarios. The original REAL and SIM-EVAL datasets are retained under the names BASIC and SIMEVAL.

E2.justification: Figure 6 retains the original comparators and adds o1, two DeepSeek-R1 distilled models, GPT-4o, and models from the LLaVA, InternVL2, Qwen2-VL, NVLM-D, and Molmo families. A fine-tuned LLaVA comparator is also added, substantially broadening the evaluated comparison set.

E3.justification: New protocols include three-shot/CoT prompting, NL-versus-ASCII representations, training on approximately 72k samples with math tasks excluded, manual quality scoring, and cross-domain pass@1 evaluation. Reasoning models introduce distinct sampling and token budgets; o1's SIMEVAL score excludes 25 unanswered tasks and uses 975 tasks. Original benchmark splits and primary metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds explanation-based failure attribution, constraint and spatial perturbations of ten selected tasks, dataset-quality assessment, prompting and representation sensitivity, withheld-math transfer, and general-programming retention tests. The original epoch analysis moves to Figure 16a; new SIMEVAL learning curves and a perturbed-code case study supplement it.

E5.justification: Retained fine-tuning results continue to report means and standard errors across five random seeds. V2 repeats this practice for additional comparisons without documenting an increased original run count or introducing new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: The original Figure 6 result entries are preserved, but substantial new results appear. These include o1's 76.47% BASIC success rate and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B's 44.71% BASIC and 32.90% SIMEVAL rates. New transfer experiments report fine-tuning deficits of 3.1-5.8 percentage points on general Python benchmarks, alongside numerous failure, quality, and ablation results.

M1.justification: The proposed synthetic-data generation, supervised LoRA training, cross-entropy objective, and emulator-driven reweighting procedure remain unchanged, including Equation 1. V2 expands their documentation and tests additional models and input representations without introducing a new core algorithmic component.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the exposition: generation and fine-tuning details move into appendices, the experimental narrative is rewritten around vision, reasoning, and fine-tuning, and comparative and failure analyses receive separate subsections. Epoch analysis moves to Appendix C.3, limitations become standalone, and dataset terminology is standardized.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, expands and regroups Figure 6, and redraws the skill radars with additional models and linear axes replacing Figure 7's logarithmic presentation. It adds failure, quality, and transfer displays, platform screenshots, and full prompt figures; the original epoch plot becomes part of the two-panel Figure 16.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces the dedicated spatial-planning/navigation discussion with multimodal-benchmark positioning, including MM-Vet and Vibe-Eval, and emphasizes educational applicability. References also expand substantially to cover reasoning and vision models, curriculum learning, prompting, SMT solving, inference infrastructure, and enhanced code evaluation.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 introduces an overall-quality score defined as the minimum of three component ratings: visual appeal, grid-element utility, and code quality. This is a limited new mathematical score definition; the task formalization, DSL, synthesis objective, and resampling equation remain unchanged, with no new proofs or theorems.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical validation and supplies reproducibility details that v1 only promised. Failure, perturbation, and transfer tests clarify what fine-tuning achieves and where it fails, while broader model comparisons improve the benchmark's usefulness. Conflicting o1 identifiers in Figures 6 and 13 and its different SIMEVAL denominator limit that comparison, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe XLOGOMINIPROG, with matching original datasets, methods, and results. Text, equations, figures, and tables support reliable comparison. V1 ends after its references; v2 includes readable Appendices A-D.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices A-C retain the original experiments and add model evaluations, dataset-quality annotations, failure analyses, and transfer experiments.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original model evaluations, fine-tuning results, skill analyses, and training curves on 85 real-world and 1,000 synthetic evaluation tasks.

arxiv_record.abstract:
This study investigates the integration of diverse patient data sources into
multimodal language models for automated chest X-ray (CXR) report generation.
Traditionally, CXR report generation relies solely on CXR images and limited
radiology data, overlooking valuable information from patient health records,
particularly from emergency departments. Utilising the MIMIC-CXR and
MIMIC-IV-ED datasets, we incorporate detailed patient information such as vital
signs, medicines, and clinical history to enhance diagnostic accuracy. We
introduce a novel approach to transform these heterogeneous data sources into
embeddings that prompt a multimodal language model; this significantly enhances
the diagnostic accuracy of generated radiology reports. Our comprehensive
evaluation demonstrates the benefits of using a broader set of patient data,
underscoring the potential for enhanced diagnostic capabilities and better
patient outcomes through the integration of multimodal data in CXR report
generation.
arxiv_record.authors: Aaron Nicolson, Shengyao Zhuang, Jason Dowling, and Bevan Koopman
arxiv_record.title:
The Impact of Auxiliary Patient Data on Automated Chest X-Ray Report
  Generation and How to Incorporate It

metadata.abstract: This study investigates the integration of diverse patient data sources into multimodal language models for automated chest X-ray (CXR) report generation. Traditionally, CXR report generation relies solely on data from a patient’s CXR exam, overlooking valuable information from patient electronic health records. Utilising the MIMIC-CXR and MIMIC-IV-ED datasets, we investigate the use of patient data from emergency department (ED) records — such as vital signs measured and medicines reconciled during an ED stay — for CXR report generation, with the aim of enhancing diagnostic accuracy. We also investigate conditioning CXR report generation on the clinical history section of radiology reports, which has been overlooked in the literature. We introduce a novel approach to transform these heterogeneous data sources into patient data embeddings that prompt a multimodal language model (CXRMate-ED). Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that using a broader set of patient data significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy. The model, training code, and dataset are publicly available.

We introduce a novel approach to transform these heterogeneous data sources into patient data embeddings that prompt a multimodal language model (CXRMate-ED). Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that using a broader set of patient data significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy. The model, training code, and dataset are publicly available.

E2.justification: The ten external benchmark methods and Table 3's embedding comparators are retained. Table 2 expands its internal comparisons from one 'Ours' row to the teacher-forced effective-source model and successive reinforcement-learning reward configurations.

New reward and subgroup experiments extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing ablations, successful case and CheXbert breakdown, v2 adds reward ablations, impression-specific analysis, a vital-sign availability subset, and extensive error analysis using differences in GREEN scores and eight positive/negative cases. E5.justification: Ten-run Table 1 evaluation and the significance-testing procedures remain. v2 removes Table 3's explicit four-run disclosure. New Table E.1 inconsistently states 1,916 evaluations as 958 × 3 runs, while Figure E.2 retains three RL runs. This changes reporting clarity without establishing an actual run-count change.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 contain extensively revised scores; for example, EMNLI's RadGraph-F1 changes from 32.8 to 29.1. The administered-medicine subset's significant benefit in v1 Table 4 becomes nonsignificant in v2 Table F.2. New reward, GREEN, ARN and error-analysis results are added. Table 3's values remain unchanged after matching columns. Changed settings limit direct performance comparisons.

P2.justification: Main tables change metric columns and comparison structure, Figure 4 is replaced, and v2 adds impression/subgroup tables, eight detailed case tables and the GREEN analysis plot. The existing CheXbert chart is revised as Figure E.2, while method diagrams and the attention mask are retained and relocated. Table G.8's caption incorrectly describes pleural effusion rather than its pneumonia example.

R1.justification: v2 adds clinical/EHR motivation references, additional temporal-imaging work, medical-note evaluation work and GREEN. CIDEr and METEOR references disappear with those metrics. arxiv_record.abstract: Despite rising global usage of large language models (LLMs), their ability to generate long-form answers to culturally specific questions remains unexplored in many languages. To fill this gap, we perform the first study of textual multilingual long-form QA by creating CaLMQA, a dataset of 51.7K culturally specific questions across 23 different languages. We define culturally specific questions as those that refer to concepts unique to one or a few cultures, or have different answers depending on the cultural or regional context. We obtain these questions by crawling naturally-occurring questions from community web forums in high-resource languages, and by hiring native speakers to write questions in under-resourced, rarely-studied languages such as Fijian and Kirundi. Our data collection methodologies are translation-free, enabling the collection of culturally unique questions like "Kuber iki umwami wa mbere w'uburundi yitwa Ntare?" (Kirundi; English translation: "Why was the first king of Burundi called Ntare (Lion)?"). We evaluate factuality, relevance and surface-level quality of LLM-generated long-form answers, finding that (1) for many languages, even the best models make critical surface-level errors (e.g., answering in the wrong language, repetition), especially for low-resource languages; and (2) answers to culturally specific questions contain more factual errors than answers to culturally agnostic questions -- questions that have consistent meaning and answer across many cultures. We release CaLMQA to facilitate future research in cultural and multilingual long-form QA.

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds a 2.6K-question mixed dataset and novel CALMSCORE; v3 foregrounds a 51.7K culturally specific resource and multi-aspect answer evaluation. Novelty is qualified as textual multilingual LFQA, and automatic factuality findings become central. The new introductory claim of lower relevance on culturally specific questions is not supported by Table 2 and Figure 11.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning topic balance, translation quality, claim extraction, and online evidence availability. It interprets automatically collected questions as an effective proxy for human-collected questions despite detected distribution differences. Conversely, v1's explicit warning about reliability with one human annotator per language is removed.

D1.justification: v3 supplies filtering and translation prompts, the relevance-judging prompt, claim-verification model details, retrieval settings, and additional costs and hardware/runtime information (Tables 5–8, Figure 15, Appendix C.1). The front-page license statement changes from MIT to CC BY 4.0. Expanded descriptions of retained manual procedures are additional disclosures, not evidence of reruns.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate culturally specific and culturally agnostic long-form QA across the same 23 languages. The additional 50,227 questions expand samples from existing high-resource community sources; they do not introduce a distinct language, domain, or QA task.

E2.justification: The automatic comparison replaces Aya-13B, checkpoint aya-101, with Aya-Expanse-32B; the other six models remain unchanged (v1 Table 10; v3 Table 15). The human comparison retains Claude-3-Opus, GPT-4-Turbo, and Mixtral-8x22B.

E3.justification: v3 adds 100 automatically collected evaluation questions per language for ten languages, bringing evaluation to 3,644 questions. It introduces factuality, relevance, and composite scoring, reports micro-averaged metrics instead of the language-averaged CALMSCORE summary, and additionally excludes Kirundi from aggregation. The zero-shot generation settings and human-evaluation design remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds cross-language topic-distribution similarity analysis, claim-count and response-length analyses, and comparisons between human-collected and automatically collected questions (Figure 6, Figure 8, Figure 12, Tables 14 and 17). The extensive human annotation and error analyses from v1 are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 adds two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests comparing score distributions across collection sources, with reported p-values. The human-evaluation mixed models, standard errors, and adjusted post-hoc tests remain unchanged (v1 Tables 12–17; v3 Tables 18–23).

E6.justification: v3 reports new factuality, relevance, composite-score, and collection-source results, alongside results for Aya-Expanse-32B. For example, Table 2 reports GPT-4o factual precision of 69.6% for agnostic questions and 52.2% for specific questions; v1 has no automatic factuality scores. These are new or differently evaluated results, not comparable performance gains over v1. Human-evaluation results are retained.

M1.justification: v3 adds automated question extraction and two GPT-4o-mini filtering passes to the manual collection pipeline. It also extends surface checking with English translation, claim extraction and evidence verification, and relevance judging. These are substantive new procedure components, described in Sections 2.2 and 3.1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, automatic and human evaluation become separate main sections, and cultural specificity receives a dedicated subsection. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, restructures dataset and performance tables, and adds multi-metric heatmaps, a verification-pipeline diagram, comment examples, and collection-source displays. Existing human-evaluation figures are largely relocated or resized; v1 Figures 7–16 correspond to v3 Figures 17–26.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from a broad survey of multilingual QA datasets toward cultural NLP, multilingual visual QA, and long-form answer evaluation. Added discussion includes VeriScore, Multi-FAct, and Vayani et al.'s multilingual visual QA work, which motivates the revised textual-novelty qualification.

T1.justification: v3 defines the composite instance score S = Ssurf * Sfact * Srel, including zero factuality credit when no verifiable claims are extracted. This extends v1's surface-pass-rate definition of CALMSCORE. The mathematical change is limited to scoring definitions; neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's acknowledged inability to assess answer content automatically by adding factuality and relevance evaluation, collection-source checks, and documented pipelines while retaining the human evidence. These additions materially strengthen evidence about answer quality and reproducibility. Translation and retrieval dependence remain, and the unsupported relevance claim and removed warning about one annotator per language are weaknesses, but they do not outweigh the substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CaLMQA and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. The retained data collection and human evaluation can be matched reliably despite substantial revision.

after.justification: v3 retains the original human evaluation and reports additional factuality, relevance, collection-source comparison, and dataset-analysis results.

before.justification: v1 reports original automatic evaluations of seven LLMs and a 100-question human evaluation across five languages, with detailed results in Appendices C–D.

arxiv_record.abstract: Bilevel optimization has shown its utility across various machine learning settings, yet most algorithms in practice require second-order information, making it challenging to scale them up. Only recently, a paradigm of first-order algorithms has emerged in the theoretical literature, capable of effectively addressing bilevel optimization problems. Nevertheless, the practical efficiency of this paradigm remains unverified, particularly in the context of large language models (LLMs). This paper introduces the first scalable instantiation of this paradigm called ScaleBiO, focusing on bilevel optimization for large-scale LLM data reweighting. By combining with a recently proposed memory-efficient training technique called LISA, our novel algorithm allows the paradigm to scale to $\sim$30B-sized LLMs on $8\times$H100 GPUs, marking the first successful application of bilevel optimization under practical scenarios for large-sized LLMs. Empirically, extensive experiments on data reweighting verify the effectiveness of ScaleBiO for different-scaled models, including Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2-7B, and Qwen-2.5-32B, where bilevel optimization succeeds in instruction-following and math reasoning tasks, outperforming several popular baselines, including uniform sampling, influence-aware data filtering, and reference-model-based sampling methods. Theoretically, ScaleBiO ensures the optimality of the learned data weights, along with a convergence guarantee matching the conventional first-order bilevel optimization paradigm on smooth and strongly convex objectives.

program_record.Abstract:
Bilevel optimization has shown its utility across various machine learning settings, yet most algorithms in practice require second-order information, making it challenging to scale them up. Only recently, a paradigm of first-order algorithms has emerged in the theoretical literature, capable of effectively addressing bilevel optimization problems. Nevertheless, the practical efficiency of this paradigm remains unverified, particularly in the context of large language models (LLMs). This paper introduces the first scalable instantiation of this paradigm called _ScaleBiO_, focusing on bilevel optimization for large-scale LLM data reweighting. By combining with a recently proposed memory-efficient training technique called LISA, our novel algorithm allows the paradigm to scale to $\sim$30B-sized LLMs on $8\times$
H100 GPUs, marking the first successful application of bilevel optimization under practical scenarios for large-sized LLMs. Empirically, extensive experiments on data reweighting verify the effectiveness of ScaleBiO for different-scaled models, including Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B, Qwen-2-7B, and Qwen-2.5-32B, where bilevel optimization succeeds in instruction-following and math reasoning tasks, outperforming several popular baselines, including uniform sampling, influence-aware data filtering, and reference-model-based sampling methods. Theoretically, ScaleBiO ensures the optimality of the learned data weights, along with a convergence guarantee matching the conventional first-order bilevel optimization paradigm on smooth and strongly convex objectives.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statements expand from demonstrating filtering and instruction-tuning benefits to claiming superiority over named strong baselines in instruction following and mathematical reasoning. The headline scalability claim changes from 34B parameters on eight A40 GPUs to approximately 30B on eight H100 GPUs. The central first-order optimization and conditional convergence claims remain.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes broadly shared preferred sources and concentration of over 80% of weight in three sources. v2's Discussion instead emphasizes model-family-dependent preferences, conjecturally linked to pretraining distributions, and argues against universal optimal mixtures for small datasets. Appendix A.2 also attributes the reduced cons@64 advantage to limited data diversity. The existing pretraining and safety limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2 adds baseline optimizer and LoRA settings, reference-model details, tuning information, FSDP, approximately 6K GPU hours, and mathematical-data access and licensing information. Hardware reporting changes to H100, replacing v1's A100 implementation statement and A40 abstract claim. Conversely, v1's explicit ScaleBiO code link disappears, and the new uniform-sampling calculation incorrectly states 10,000/18 as approximately 5556.

E1.justification: v2 adds dedicated mathematical-reasoning training using a ten-source mixture, evaluation on GSM8K and MATH, and AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and AIMO 2025 experiments using DeepSeek-R1-generated reasoning data. The earlier GPT-2 scenarios and 18-source instruction-following coverage remain.

E2.justification: The MT-Bench comparison expands from uniform sampling to LESS, RHO-LOSS, and attempted SOBA comparisons reported as out of memory in v2 Table 2. LESS and RHO-LOSS also participate in the new mathematical-reasoning comparisons; their earlier citations alone did not constitute evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The reported model learning-rate setting changes from a fixed 10^-5 to a search over eight values. New protocols include Qwen and Gemma backbones, 20K-sample mathematical fine-tuning, validation/tuning splits, and 4K-sample DeepSeek distillation evaluated with pass@1 and cons@64. These do not establish that retained MT-Bench results were rerun.

E4.justification: The source-weight analysis expands to Qwen and Gemma and adds mathematical-reasoning weight profiles in v2 Tables 7–8, examining preferences across model families and tasks. The Yi-34B weight trajectory in v1 Figure 4 is removed. The GPT-2 demonstrations and 8B-to-70B transfer analysis remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training-run summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new cons@64 evaluation is a performance metric, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial MT-Bench and mathematical-reasoning results. For example, Table 5 reports Qwen-2.5-32B accuracies of 87.1/59.8 on GSM8K/MATH versus uniform sampling's 78.1/54.0. The earlier Llama-3-8B MT-Bench scores of 6.11 versus 7.12 and 70B transfer scores of 7.85 versus 8.05 remain unchanged. v1's category-level MT-Bench results are removed.

M1.justification: The softmax source weights, penalty-based minimax objective, auxiliary model, and single-loop randomized block updates remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 gains explanatory comments and an iteration-index typo correction, without introducing a different procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanations, and application narrative receive substantial rewriting. Large-scale experiments are reorganized by task, implementation details move into Appendix B.2, and a dedicated Discussion section replaces parts of the earlier interpretation. Author and affiliation information also changes.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. v2 introduces several comparison and dataset tables, expands and relocates the source-weight table to Appendix A.1, and separates retained MT-Bench results across displays. Figures 1–3 are retained and resized, while v1 Figure 4 and its category-level MT-Bench table are removed.

R1.justification: The related-work framework remains largely intact, but Table 1 adds SAMA and (FG)2U, and the stated previous scalability ceiling changes from over 1B to over 3B parameters. The introduction adds data-quality, fairness, and robustness literature, with further references supporting the new experiments.

T1.justification: v2 removes the explicit implicit-function derivation in v1 Equation 3 and makes sampling independence explicit in Appendix D. The main theorem, convergence rate, and proof argument remain intact. Appendix C also rewrites Lemma 6's threshold using undefined symbols, introducing a localized formal-reporting defect rather than a new guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited downstream evidence, which mainly compared against uniform sampling on MT-Bench.
