arxiv_record.abstract: Pretrained language models have significantly advanced performance across various natural language processing tasks. However, adversarial attacks continue to pose a critical challenge to systems built using these models, as they can be exploited with carefully crafted adversarial texts. Inspired by the ability of diffusion models to predict and reduce noise in computer vision, we propose a novel and flexible adversarial defense method for language classification tasks, DiffuseDef, which incorporates a diffusion layer as a denoiser between the encoder and the classifier. The diffusion layer is trained on top of the existing classifier, ensuring seamless integration with any model in a plug-and-play manner. During inference, the adversarial hidden state is first combined with sampled noise, then denoised iteratively and finally ensembled to produce a robust text representation. By integrating adversarial training, denoising, and ensembling techniques, we show that DiffuseDef improves over existing adversarial defense methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance against common black-box and white-box adversarial attacks.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhenhao Li, Huichi Zhou, Marek Rei, Lucia Specia
arxiv_record.title: DiffuseDef: Improved Robustness to Adversarial Attacks via Iterative Denoising

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the central robustness claim to explicitly cover both black-box and white-box attacks. V1 evaluated three black-box attacks and explicitly left white-box robustness unresolved. Flexible integration with existing defense methods was already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: V2 removes the explicit white-box uncertainty and missing-comparisons limitations while retaining the computational-cost limitation. It newly interprets denoising and ensembling as more consequential than adversarial training, discusses training-time tradeoffs and identifies RSMI's incompatibility with SemAttack.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies 10 epochs for base encoder/classifier fine-tuning and supplies comparative training-time information. The diffusion hyperparameters, RTX A6000 hardware, absolute diffusion-training times, data preparation and code URL are retained. The PDFs do not establish a change to the underlying base-training budget.

E1.justification: AGNews, IMDB and QNLI already appear in v1. The substantial expansion is evaluation against gradient-access white-box attacks, T-PGD and SemAttack, on AGNews and IMDB. QNLI evaluation also expands beyond its original TextFooler-only analysis.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds RMLM on AGNews and IMDB and ATINTER on all three BERT datasets. The QNLI comparison gains InfoBERT and EarlyRobust, while Figure 2 introduces an adversarial-augmentation comparator. These materially expand the evaluated defense comparisons; the original RoBERTa comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: V2 introduces white-box testing, TextFooler-generated training augmentation, RoBERTa evaluation on QNLI and training-time comparisons. It replaces the incremental QNLI/TextFooler ablation with component-removal controls on AGNews under three attacks. Existing dataset splits, 1,000-example attack samples and black-box constraints remain unchanged; the newly stated 10-epoch base training is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: V1 Table 2 incrementally adds diffusion and ensembling on QNLI. V2 Table 3 instead removes ensembling, denoising and adversarial training separately on AGNews, and Figure 2 tests compatibility with adversarial augmentation. Token-length and denoising-step analyses, appendix examples and confusion matrices remain, with some relocated.

E5.justification: Both versions report evaluation metrics averaged over five random seeds and use seed 42 for dataset splitting. Neither adds confidence intervals, significance tests, error bars or a revised repeated-run reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds white-box, expanded QNLI, additional-baseline, augmentation, ablation and training-time results, while the old diffusion-only QNLI rows disappear. For example, new Table 3 reports TextFooler AUA of 84.5 for full DiffuseDef versus 64.2 without ensembling. Matched AGNews/IMDB black-box scores, latent distances and appendix examples/confusion matrices remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 and Algorithm 1 retain the same architecture, diffusion loss, two-stage training, one-step noising, iterative denoising and ensemble averaging. The augmentation experiment applies the existing procedure to another base-training approach rather than introducing a new DiffuseDef component.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method by addressing v1's explicit lack of white-box evidence, adding relevant denoising baselines and testing component necessity more directly. Broader QNLI comparisons also improve support for generality. Reporting problems remain, including SemAttack's 0.03 in the prose versus 3.4 in Table 2, but these localized issues do not outweigh the stronger empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DiffuseDef. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite the expanded title and reorganized results.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds white-box evaluations, additional defense comparisons, revised ablations, augmentation experiments and training-time measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract: This study addresses a critical gap in safety tuning practices for Large Language Models (LLMs) by identifying and tackling a refusal position bias within safety tuning data, which compromises the models' ability to appropriately refuse generating unsafe content. We introduce a novel approach, Decoupled Refusal Training (DeRTa), designed to empower LLMs to refuse compliance to harmful prompts at any response position, significantly enhancing their safety capabilities. DeRTa incorporates two novel components: (1) Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) with Harmful Response Prefix, which trains models to recognize and avoid unsafe content by appending a segment of harmful response to the beginning of a safe response, and (2) Reinforced Transition Optimization (RTO), which equips models with the ability to transition from potential harm to safety refusal consistently throughout the harmful response sequence. Our empirical evaluation, conducted using LLaMA3 and Mistral model families across six attack scenarios, demonstrates that our method not only improves model safety without compromising performance but also surpasses baseline methods in defending against attacks.

arxiv_record.abstract: Anonymizing text that contains sensitive information is crucial for a wide range of applications. Existing techniques face the emerging challenges of the re-identification ability of large language models (LLMs), which have shown advanced capability in memorizing detailed information and reasoning over dispersed pieces of patterns to draw conclusions. When defending against LLM-based re-identification, anonymization could jeopardize the utility of the resulting anonymized data in downstream tasks. In general, the interaction between anonymization and data utility requires a deeper understanding within the context of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a framework composed of three key LLM-based components: a privacy evaluator, a utility evaluator, and an optimization component, which work collaboratively to perform anonymization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing baselines, showing robustness in reducing the risk of re-identification while preserving greater data utility in downstream tasks. We provide detailed studies on these core modules. To consider large-scale and real-time applications, we investigate the distillation of the anonymization capabilities into lightweight models. All of our code and datasets will be made publicly available at https://github.com/UKPLab/acl2025-rupta.
arxiv_record.authors: Tianyu Yang and Xiaodan Zhu and Iryna Gurevych
arxiv_record.title: Robust Utility-Preserving Text Anonymization Based on Large Language Models

arxiv_record.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders (MSEs) are commonly obtained by training multilingual language models to map sentences from different languages into a shared semantic space. As such, they are subject to curse of multilinguality, a loss of monolingual representational accuracy due to parameter sharing. Another limitation of MSEs is the trade-off between different task performance: cross-lingual alignment training distorts the optimal monolingual structure of semantic spaces of individual languages, harming the utility of sentence embeddings in monolingual tasks; cross-lingual tasks, such as cross-lingual semantic similarity and zero-shot transfer for sentence classification, may also require conflicting cross-lingual alignment strategies. In this work, we address both issues by means of modular training of sentence encoders. We first train language-specific monolingual modules to mitigate negative interference between languages (i.e., the curse). We then align all non-English sentence embeddings to the English by training cross-lingual alignment adapters, preventing interference with monolingual specialization from the first step. We train the cross-lingual adapters with two different types of data to resolve the conflicting requirements of different cross-lingual tasks. Monolingual and cross-lingual results on semantic text similarity and relatedness, bitext mining and sentence classification show that our modular solution achieves better and more balanced performance across all the tasks compared to full-parameter training of monolithic multilingual sentence encoders, especially benefiting low-resource languages.
arxiv_record.authors: Yongxin Huang, Kexin Wang, Goran Glava\v{s}, Iryna Gurevych
arxiv_record.title: Modular Sentence Encoders: Separating Language Specialization from Cross-Lingual Alignment

metadata.abstract: Multilingual sentence encoders (MSEs) are commonly obtained by training multilingual language models to map sentences from different languages into a shared semantic space. As such, they are subject to curse of multilinguality, a loss of monolingual representational accuracy due to parameter sharing. Another limitation of MSEs is the trade-off between different task performance: cross-lingual alignment training distorts the optimal monolingual structure of semantic spaces of individual languages, harming the utility of sentence embeddings in monolingual tasks; cross-lingual tasks, such as cross-lingual semantic similarity and zero-shot transfer for sentence classification, may also require conflicting cross-lingual alignment strategies. In this work, we address both issues by means of modular training of sentence encoders. We first train language-specific monolingual modules to mitigate negative interference between languages (i.e., the curse). We then align all non-English sentence embeddings to the English by training cross-lingual alignment adapters, preventing interference with monolingual specialization from the first step. We train the cross-lingual adapters with two different types of data to resolve the conflicting requirements of different cross-lingual tasks. Monolingual and cross-lingual results on semantic text similarity and relatedness, bitext mining and sentence classification show that our modular solution achieves better and more balanced performance across all the tasks compared to full-parameter training of monolithic multilingual sentence encoders, especially benefiting low-resource languages.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion expand the contribution from separating monolingual specialization and cross-lingual alignment to also addressing conflicting requirements among cross-lingual tasks. V2 claims balanced performance through joint paraphrase/parallel training, supported by mining and classification evaluations, and explicitly emphasizes improvements over full-parameter training rather than pursuing state-of-the-art performance.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting classification performance with isomorphism and lexical cues, and explains the differing effects of paraphrase and parallel alignment. Its efficiency discussion replaces v1's proposed future use of parameter-efficient specialization with remaining module and vocabulary costs. The limitations newly state that encoder-decoder MSEs require adaptations before the approach can be applied.

D1.justification: The reproduction recipe is substantially revised: v2 documents separate LoRA placements, rank 8, alpha 16, dropout 0.1 and training precision, and adds per-module parameter sizes and timings in Table 4. The model-access inventory and first-page code pointer change. Conversely, v1's explicit MLM sequence length and training-script link are no longer supplied.

E1.justification: V2 retains the 23-language pool and five core paraphrase-training corpora, but removes STS22 news-article similarity and Belebele MCQA. It adds multilingual SICK relatedness, FLORES/Tatoeba bitext mining and SIB-200 classification, and expands cross-lingual STS pairs. K-STS is retained under STSB, with additional Korean cross-language pairs; it is not simply deleted.

E2.justification: The evaluated SONAR, Glot500 and mE5-large comparisons in v1 disappear. V2 retains LaBSE and mE5-base and adds English-only Full_en and Mod_en controls (Tables 1–2). The earlier Single_m, Single_c and Single_mc baselines correspond to Full_m, Full_c and Full_mc; their renaming alone is not a comparator addition.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes LaBSE baseline training from one to three epochs, language adaptation from 100K to 200K steps, and the tokenizer-training cap from 5M to 10M sentences. CLA batch size changes from 128 to 256 and learning rate from 1e-4 to 2e-5. New evaluation procedures include frozen-encoder logistic regression, bitext xsim scores, pooled multilingual language-bias evaluation and RSIM.

E4.justification: V2 adds explicit removal ablations for language adaptation and monolingual SE training, comparisons of paraphrase-only, parallel-only and joint alignment, and language-bias/RSIM analyses. The English-pivot versus all-pair experiment is retained but redesigned for seven STSB languages and both alignment objectives. V1's larger-English-data experiment and independently initialized BERT/BERTbek alignment check are removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests for its experiments. Both present point estimates and averages across languages rather than statistical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive classification, mining, SICK, diagnostic and ablation results, while removing STS22, Belebele, SONAR and Glot500 result blocks. For example, its new trained-mE5 comparison reports cross-lingual STSB correlations of 73.8 for Mod_mc-jt and 66.7 for Full_mc (Tables 2 and 10). LaBSE results are also revised, but changed training and language-pair coverage prevent treating them as clean same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: V1 fully tunes monolingual encoders and trains CLA adapters only on paraphrases. V2 uses language-specific embeddings and separate LoRA language and sentence-encoding adapters with frozen earlier components. Its joint CLA training alternates paraphrase batches using MNRL with parallel batches using cosine-similarity loss (Section 3 and Appendix B). These substantially change the architecture and training procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method and results discussion are extensively rewritten. V2 introduces numbered method/setup subsections, separates Results from Discussion, consolidates detailed evaluation reporting in Appendix D, and changes Single/Multi terminology to Full/Mod. These constitute substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to show individual LoRA modules, trainable components and alternating alignment batches; v1's Belebele bar chart is removed. Main results are reorganized into broad task-and-diagnostic summary Tables 1–2, with extensive language-level tables in Appendix D. V2 also adds the module-size/training-time table, substantially changing the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V1 primarily positions the work around monolingual specialization, fine-grained semantics and differences from LASER3. V2 substantially expands discussion of language-disentanglement and lightweight multilingual-adapter research, including Mao et al., Liu et al. and Yano et al., and claims novelty in jointly addressing conflicting MSE requirements. This changes research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical results or proofs. V2's descriptions of adopted language-bias and RSIM measures specify empirical evaluation procedures; they do not add substantive mathematical theory or derivations.

improvement.justification: V1 leaves parameter-efficient monolingual specialization as future work and lacks direct ablations separating language adaptation from SE training. V2 implements that specialization and adds those ablations on LaBSE and mE5, alongside direct alignment diagnostics, substantially strengthening the central methodological argument. Removing STS22/Belebele and initialization/data ablations narrows some evidence, and v2's mE5 Mod_m SICK mean is inconsistent between Table 2 (75.4) and Table 12 (76.3). These drawbacks do not outweigh the stronger component validation and clearer account of task trade-offs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same modular sentence-encoder research. Their main text, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support matching retained content despite substantial revisions to the method and experiments.

after.justification: V2 reports original LaBSE and mE5 experiments on similarity, relatedness, classification and bitext mining, plus alignment diagnostics and component ablations. Appendix D supplies detailed results.

before.justification: V1 reports original STS/STR and Belebele question-answering experiments, including detailed LaBSE and Glot500 results and alignment ablations in the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) present significant risks when used to generate
non-factual content and spread disinformation at scale. Detecting such
LLM-generated content is crucial, yet current detectors often struggle to
generalize in open-world contexts. We introduce Learning2Rewrite, a novel
framework for detecting AI-generated text with exceptional generalization to
unseen domains. Our method leverages the insight that LLMs inherently modify
AI-generated content less than human-written text when tasked with rewriting.
By training LLMs to minimize alterations on AI-generated inputs, we amplify
this disparity, yielding a more distinguishable and generalizable edit distance
across diverse text distributions. Extensive experiments on data from 21
independent domains and four major LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Gemini, and Llama-3)
demonstrate that our detector outperforms state-of-the-art detection methods by
up to 23.04% in AUROC for in-distribution tests, 37.26% for out-of-distribution
tests, and 48.66% under adversarial attacks. Our unique training objective
ensures better generalizability compared to directly training for
classification, when leveraging the same amount of parameters. Our findings
suggest that reinforcing LLMs' inherent rewriting tendencies offers a robust
and scalable solution for detecting AI-generated text.
arxiv_record.authors: Ran Li, Wei Hao, Weiliang Zhao, Junfeng Yang, Chengzhi Mao
arxiv_record.title: Learning to Rewrite: Generalized LLM-Generated Text Detection

metadata.abstract: Detecting text generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial, yet current detectors often struggle to generalize in open-world settings. We introduce Learning2Rewrite, a novel framework to detect LLM-generated text with exceptional generalization to unseen domains. Capitalized on the finding that LLMs inherently modify LLM-generated content less than human-written text when rewriting, we train an LLM to amplify this disparity, yielding a more distinguishable and generalizable edit distance across diverse text distributions. Extensive experiments on data from 21 independent domains and four major LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Gemini, and Llama-3) demonstrate that our detector outperforms state-of-the-art detection methods by up to 23.04% in AUROC for in-distribution tests, 35.10% for out-of-distribution tests, and 48.66% under adversarial attacks. Our unique training objective ensures better generalizability compared to directly training for classification, even when leveraging the same amount of tunable parameters. Our findings suggest that reinforcing LLMs’ inherent rewriting tendencies offers a robust and scalable solution for detecting LLM-generated text.

C1.justification: v2 makes adversarial robustness and better generalization than equally parameterized direct classification central abstract and contribution claims. It explicitly separates in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance claims, while dropping v1's claim to the world's most diverse dataset. The underlying learned-rewriting contribution remains.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the capacity sweep as an accuracy–generalization tradeoff, attributes advantages over Llama Logits to the rewriting objective, and explains attack resistance through remaining separation between human and AI rewrite distributions. It also interprets the MAGE comparison as evidence for training-data quality. The slow-inference limitation is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds batch size, weight decay, decoding settings, training and per-text inference times, preprocessing instructions, dataset licenses, and four LoRA configurations with parameter counts. It also specifies baseline implementations and matching procedures. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to previously unstated settings. The future release promise now includes data.

E1.justification: v2 retains the original 21 domains, adds GPT-3.5-Turbo as a fourth generator, evaluates M4 with five nonoverlapping English domains and additional generators, and uses MAGE for a training-data comparison. It also evaluates adversarially modified test texts, substantially expanding coverage beyond v1's constructed dataset.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates GPT-2 Detector, Fast-DetectGPT, and RAIDAR with Gemini or Llama rewriting. v2 removes GPT-2 Detector and adds evaluated Ghostbusters and directly fine-tuned Llama Logits baselines, while retaining Fast-DetectGPT and the rewriting comparators. Tables 3–4 also compare reduced-parameter classifier configurations.

E3.justification: v1 Table 1 describes separately trained per-domain comparisons; v2 Table 1 specifies one classifier trained across all domains. Rewriting and ablation reporting switches from accuracy/F1 to AUROC. New protocols include M4 transfer, training on clean data and testing attacked data, matched MAGE training, four LoRA configurations, and controlled length/decoding variations. The default 70/30 split remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds distribution-shift and adversarial robustness tests, a LoRA-capacity sweep, an objective-versus-direct-classification control, a MAGE training-data comparison, and text-length/decoding ablations in Appendix A.6. The existing prompt-diversity and calibration studies are retained in Appendices A.3 and A.5, with revised reporting.

E5.justification: v2 Section 5.1 first explicitly states that experimental results use a single run, citing temperature-zero rewriting. v1 does not specify run counts. Both report standard deviations across domains; neither adds confidence intervals or significance tests. This is added disclosure, not evidence that the actual run count changed.

E6.justification: v1's accuracy/F1 results are replaced by AUROC reporting: its Table 1 gives L2R 0.8313 accuracy and 0.8334 F1, while v2 Table 1 reports 0.9009 AUROC. New results include M4 AUROC of 0.6561/0.7398 for full/reduced L2R and attack scores of 0.8746/0.8927. Dataset-training and generation-variation results are also added. Changed coverage, metrics, and protocols preclude treating these as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The intended L2R procedure remains Llama-3-8B rewriting, signed cross-entropy training, threshold-based loss calibration, and classification using rewrite similarity. The added pseudocode and LoRA-capacity experiments do not establish a new core algorithm. Formal calibration-description changes are assessed under T1.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, with an explicit contribution list. Dataset discussion becomes collection, prompt-diversity, and cleaning subsections; evaluation is reorganized around generalization and robustness. Existing ablations move into an expanded appendix, and conclusion and limitations exchange order.

P2.justification: v2 combines the earlier histograms and calibration schematic in Figure 1, adds edit counts and domain illustrations to Figure 2, and replaces the earlier comparison displays with expanded AUROC tables. It adds a capacity plot and several experimental tables. The calibration curve is redrawn, and the existing rewrite examples move to the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of GLTR, PECOLA, generalization studies, and DPO, and acknowledges RAID, RuTAD, and MAGE when positioning its dataset. Dataset novelty is qualified through comparison with existing diverse datasets. The central relationship to RAIDAR and supervised versus zero-shot detection remains; publication metadata updates are not new cited works.

T1.justification: The signed-loss expression is rewritten equivalently. arxiv_record.abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has revolutionized role-playing, enabling the development of general role-playing models. However, current role-playing training has two significant issues: (I) Using a predefined role profile to prompt dialogue training for specific scenarios usually leads to inconsistencies and even conflicts between the dialogue and the profile, resulting in training biases. (II) The model learns to imitate the role based solely on the profile, neglecting profile-dialogue alignment at the sentence level. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective framework called BEYOND DIALOGUE, designed to overcome these hurdles. This framework innovatively introduces "beyond dialogue" tasks to align dialogue with profile traits based on each specific scenario, thereby eliminating biases during training. Furthermore, by adopting an innovative prompting mechanism that generates reasoning outcomes for training, the framework allows the model to achieve fine-grained alignment between profile and dialogue at the sentence level. The aforementioned methods are fully automated and low-cost. Additionally, the integration of automated dialogue and objective evaluation methods forms a comprehensive framework, paving the way for general role-playing. Experimental results demonstrate that our model excels in adhering to and reflecting various dimensions of role profiles, outperforming most proprietary general and specialized role-playing baselines. All code and datasets are available at https://github.com/yuyouyu32/BeyondDialogue.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain identifying profile-dialogue bias, introducing sentence-level alignment training, and providing automated objective evaluation. Claims of improved profile adherence and superiority to most general and specialized baselines retain their scope. The self-evaluation discussion remains in the alignment-results section.

C2.justification: V6 explicitly discusses limitations involving evolving profiles, autonomous adaptation of global profiles, multi-party dialogue, and inherited safety constraints. It adds an interpretation of judge differences as possible self-preference. Ablation emphasis shifts from Character/Style to Character/Personality when interpreted through Qualification Rate.

D1.justification: V6 adds annotation recruitment and pilot-timing information plus explicit Apache 2.0 and CC BY-NC 4.0 licensing terms. It removes v1's GPU, memory, and operating-system disclosure. Training and inference hyperparameters, substantive prompt templates, and the repository link remain available.

E1.justification: Both use the same Chinese-English coverage: 123 novels/scripts, 311 roles, 3,552 dialogues, and 23,247 turns, alongside NaturalConv and DailyDialog. Added human and judge-validation experiments assess the existing role-playing and profile-alignment tasks.

E2.justification: The role-playing, alignment, and extraction baseline sets are retained. V6 Appendix B.1 adds subjective scoring and objective scoring without chain-of-thought as comparison methods for evaluating the proposed assessment approach.

E3.justification: V6 replaces average CSERP summaries in role-playing and ablation results with Qualification Rate, requiring scores above 60 in every dimension. It adds majority-vote human preferences against GPT-4o, Claude-3-Opus judging, and a 50-instance evaluation-format experiment. Appendix D retains the original seen/unseen-role split; the main text's 'all new roles' wording is inconsistent and does not establish a changed split.

E4.justification: V6 adds controlled subjective/objective and reasoning-prompt comparisons (Appendix B.1), validation across judges (B.2), and dataset profile-misalignment analysis (A.3). The original five task-removal ablations and alignment cases remain; merged dialogue figures largely redisplay existing cases.

E5.justification: Both already report SEMs and t-tests. V6 adds three repeated evaluations per condition in the 50-instance experiment, Krippendorff's alpha, and additional human-agreement statistics including Cohen's kappa. Conversely, Table 12 removes the uncertainty estimates previously accompanying validity and cosine similarity in v1 Table 9. These additions concern evaluation reliability, not additional training seeds.

E6.justification: The original main-table component scores, alignment results, and per-dimension ablation results are unchanged. V6 adds Qualification Rates, human win rates of 71.00% for fully trained Qwen2 and 69.33% for fully trained Mistral against GPT-4o, Claude evaluations, and agreement results. HPD reporting replaces separate character/style bias percentages with an 83.2% any-dimension statistic, rather than a comparable performance change.

M1.justification: The extraction, CSERP alignment, profile adjustment, and supervised training procedures remain substantively unchanged, including the objective and 1:5:4 data mixture. The coarse/refined terminology and expanded reasoning explanation clarify existing components; the appendix prompt templates are substantively identical.

P1.justification: V6 substantially edits and reorganizes the exposition, introduces numbered sections and appendices, repairs missing section references, and separates coarse construction from profile refinement. It rewrites several methodological and results passages and condenses the lengthy cost discussion.

P2.justification: The framework diagrams are reordered and revised; result tables gain Qualification Rate, human preferences, and color shading; Figure 4 changes its aggregate-score panel. V6 adds evaluation and cost tables, expands the human-verification table, merges model-specific dialogue figures, and compacts the prompt layouts.

R1.justification: V6 adds ERAbaL and OpenCharacter, explicitly contrasts sentence-level alignment with loosely profile-guided generation, and adds references supporting the additional judge. The main related-work taxonomy and novelty positioning remain stable; publication and citation-format updates are largely bibliographic.

T1.justification: V6 adds an explicit mathematical definition of the joint unaligned ratio in Appendix A.3 and defines the threshold-based Qualification Rate. The training objective is unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1's central model comparisons relied on GPT-4o judging, while the claimed stability advantage of objective evaluation lacked a controlled comparison. V6 adds human preferences, a second judge, and repeated evaluation-format controls (Tables 2, 8–9, and 11), substantially strengthening evidence for the models and evaluation pipeline. Explicit limitations and repaired organization also improve interpretability. Lost hardware details, removed uncertainty estimates, and inconsistent role-split wording are drawbacks, but the added validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BEYOND DIALOGUE, with matching methods, datasets, and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

after.justification: V6 retains these empirical results and adds human preference comparisons, evaluation-format experiments, and results from a second LLM judge.

before.justification: V1 reports original role-playing evaluations, alignment experiments, ablations, dialogue-extraction measurements, and human verification results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) with extended context windows have significantly improved tasks such as information extraction, question answering, and complex planning scenarios. In order to achieve success in long context tasks, a large amount of work has been done to enhance the long context capabilities of the model through synthetic data. Existing methods typically utilize the Self-Instruct framework to generate instruction tuning data for better long context capability improvement. However, our preliminary experiments indicate that less than 35% of generated samples are multi-hop, and more than 40% exhibit poor quality, limiting comprehensive understanding and further research. To improve the quality of synthetic data, we propose the Multi-agent Interactive Multi-hop Generation (MIMG) framework, incorporating a Quality Verification Agent, a Single-hop Question Generation Agent, a Multiple Question Sampling Strategy, and a Multi-hop Question Merger Agent. This framework improves the data quality, with the proportion of high-quality, multi-hop, and diverse data exceeding 85%. Furthermore, we systematically investigate strategies for document selection, question merging, and validation techniques through extensive experiments across various models. Our findings show that our synthetic high-quality long-context instruction data significantly enhances model performance, even surpassing models trained on larger amounts of human-annotated data. Our code is available at: https://github.com/WowCZ/LongMIT.

metadata.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) with extended context windows have significantly improved various tasks. To improve long-context capabilities, much work focuses on augmenting LLM’s capabilities with synthetic data. Existing methods often leverage the Self-Instruct framework to generate long-context instruction-tuning data. However, our preliminary experiments show that fewer than 35% of samples generated by Qwen-2-72B are multi-hop, and over 40% exhibit poor quality, limiting comprehensive understanding and further research. To address this, we propose the Multi-agent Interactive Multi-hop Generation (MIMG) framework, which integrates a quality verification agent, a single-hop question generation agent, a multiple question sampling strategy, and a multi-hop question merger agent. This framework significantly improves data quality, with high-quality, multi-hop, and diverse data. Furthermore, we conduct a thorough analysis of document selection, question merging, and validation techniques through extensive experiments across various models. Our results demonstrate that synthetic high-quality long-context instruction data can enhance model performance, surpassing even models trained on larger amounts of human-annotated data.

C1.justification: The abstract now explicitly qualifies the preliminary low-multi-hop and poor-quality findings as applying to Qwen2-72B-generated samples. The principal claims about MIMG, LongMIT, improved data quality, and outperforming larger human-annotated datasets remain; the over-85% and 7.54% claims are retained in the introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting quality, diversity, and multi-hop content to different downstream capabilities, a hypothesis explaining long-input classification bias, and explanations of component contributions. It also discusses instruction-following preservation and newly acknowledges limitations from small manual samples, random sampling, and difficulty holding generated questions fixed.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset sample/token counts, manual-annotation procedures, and an explanation that the existing 8.5 threshold was selected using a 200-item verification set. It also supplies the code-extension prompt and revises sequence-length reporting. The hardware, optimizer, retrieval recipe, and main generation prompts were already documented in v1.

E1.justification: v2 adds RULER evaluation across context lengths from 4K to 128K, short-context instruction-following evaluation on IFEval and ArenaHard, and exploratory code-question generation using torch.nn documentation. The original bilingual corpus domains and eight LongBench tasks remain.

E2.justification: The original LongBench comparators—ChatQA2, LongAlign, LongAlpaca, and NQ—are retained. The new comparisons introduce base-model controls: InterLM-2.5-7B-Enhance in Table 4 and Llama-3-8B-ProLong in Tables 6 and 8. This is a limited extension of the comparator set.

E3.justification: The stated maximum training sequence length changes from 32K in v1 Appendix C.1 to 4K–128K in v2 Appendix E.1. Added protocols include RULER testing at five lengths, strict/loose instruction- and prompt-level IFEval metrics, and a 100-sample backbone-quality assessment. The PDFs do not establish whether the unchanged LongBench results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds direct removal ablations for all four MIMG components, measuring quality, diversity, and multi-hop content in Table 5. It also adds cross-backbone human assessments, checks for instruction-following degradation, and a code-generation case study. The earlier strategy sweeps, scaling analyses, and reasoning examples are retained.

E5.justification: v2 Tables 2 and 5 explicitly average three independent manual evaluations, and Table 8 reports 95% confidence intervals for ArenaHard. These add statistical reporting absent from v1; they do not establish additional training runs for the retained experiments.

E6.justification: All 135 numerical cells in v1 Figure 12 match v2 Table 1. Substantial new results appear elsewhere, including RULER averages of 47.56 for the base model and 70.27 with LongMIT at 128K, component-ablation scores, and instruction-following results. ArenaHard reports LongMIT at 6.7, versus 7.2 for the base model and 4.4 for ChatQA2.

M1.justification: The core four-component MIMG pipeline and its principal generation prompts remain unchanged. Appendix G adds a limited code-generation extension: an additional prompt transforms merged code question-answer pairs into programming challenges and solutions.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and much of the main exposition are extensively rewritten and condensed, with standardized component abbreviations. Dataset-construction material moves into the expanded appendices, which are reorganized from A–D into A–G. Limitations, ethical considerations, and additional explanatory sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. Pipeline diagrams are revised, several strategy plots are consolidated into multipanel figures, and the main results display becomes Table 1. New tables and a context-length distribution panel are added, while retained case studies are relocated and their captions corrected.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on LLM-based evaluation, agents, and newer reasoning research. Appendix C.1 additionally positions MIMG as encompassing Self-Instruct and LLM-rechecking procedures. The main long-context research positioning and identification of Quest as the closest work remain substantially intact.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain the same mathematical content, with notation changes such as Score/Class becoming FS/FC. Neither version contains theoretical proofs. The added metric descriptions explain evaluation practices without introducing substantive mathematical results.

improvement.justification: The component-removal ablations directly address v1's limited evidence for individual components' contributions. Dataset-quality comparisons, RULER testing through 128K, and instruction-following checks substantially strengthen validation of the central claims. Annotation details and explicit limitations improve transparency while the original LongBench results are preserved. The broader training-length description remains insufficiently tied to individual experiments, and the code extension is weakly validated, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIMG framework and LongMIT dataset. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite extensive reformatting.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds component ablations, dataset-quality comparisons, RULER, IFEval, ArenaHard, and exploratory code-generation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation-strategy experiments, human quality assessments, LongBench fine-tuning results, scaling analyses, and qualitative cases.

arxiv_record.abstract: Critical text assessment is at the core of many expert activities, such as fact-checking, peer review, and essay grading. Yet, existing work treats critical text assessment as a black box problem, limiting interpretability and human-AI collaboration. To close this gap, we introduce Structured Reasoning In Critical Text Assessment (STRICTA), a novel specification framework to model text assessment as an explicit, step-wise reasoning process. STRICTA breaks down the assessment into a graph of interconnected reasoning steps drawing on causality theory (Pearl, 1995). This graph is populated based on expert interaction data and used to study the assessment process and facilitate human-AI collaboration. We formally define STRICTA and apply it in a study on biomedical paper assessment, resulting in a dataset of over 4000 reasoning steps from roughly 40 biomedical experts on more than 20 papers. We use this dataset to empirically study expert reasoning in critical text assessment, and investigate if LLMs are able to imitate and support experts within these workflows. The resulting tools and datasets pave the way for studying collaborative expert-AI reasoning in text assessment, in peer review and beyond.
arxiv_record.authors: Nils Dycke and Matej Ze\v{c}evi\'c and Ilia Kuznetsov and Beatrix Suess and Kristian Kersting and Iryna Gurevych
arxiv_record.title: STRICTA: Structured Reasoning in Critical Text Assessment for Peer Review and Beyond

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from modeling natural-language diagnostic abduction to specifying a broader family of structured critical-text-assessment problems, with abduction as one experimental setting. The biomedical dataset and principal claims about prior knowledge, writing style, error propagation and human oversight remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the rationale for fixed causal workflows and verdict-conditioned assistance, and interprets metric suitability separately for extraction and explanation alignment. It adds explicit limits on comparing annotator groups, using unvalidated NLP-transfer annotations, and generalizing small user-study findings to real human–AI collaboration.

D1.justification: v1 promises code and data upon acceptance; v2 reports public availability and supplies a repository address. v2 also provides complete feedback/refinement prompts in Tables 12–13, graph-encoding details and instructions for populating prompt inputs. Existing model versions, generation settings and hardware disclosures remain.

E1.justification: v2 extends actual coverage beyond biomedical assessment: Appendix A.5 reports 33 NLP researchers assessing six NLP papers, and A.2 analyzes 30 NLPEER reviews. It also tests live human–LLM assistance. The original 22-paper biomedical dataset remains; essay scoring is only a proposed application.

E2.justification: The four LLM backbones and human/majority baselines remain. v1's graph-free GPT4o§ comparison corresponds to the unrefined GPT4oγ in v2 Table 14. v2 additionally evaluates a self-refined graph-free GPT-4o comparator, now labeled GPT4o§.

E3.justification: Main-table program F1 changes from majority-vote references to individual annotator references; v2 Table 14 reports both. v2 also adds paper-referenced SummaC and a human-evaluation protocol covering eight workflow steps on three papers, with fact-matching and explanation-alignment judgments. The original 20/2-paper test/development split remains.

E4.justification: v2 adds explicit refinement ablations, leave-one-paper-out stability analysis, paper-grounded factual-alignment analysis and human validation of automatic metrics. The original variability-propagation and graph-removal error analyses are retained, including material relocated to Appendices A.6 and A.7.2.

E5.justification: Targeted statistical additions include leave-one-paper-out t-tests with Bonferroni correction and p-values, plus human–metric correlations. Existing standard deviations across steps and papers remain; additional repeated runs are not documented. The correlation procedure is ambiguously identified as Pearson in A.7.3 and Spearman in Table 16.

E6.justification: Table 14 retains v1's unrefined results and adds refined results, individual-reference F1 and paper-referenced SummaC. Tables 15–16 add human-evaluation outcomes and metric correlations; transfer and assistance studies add survey findings. Main-table numerical differences partly reflect changed procedures and scoring references, so they do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 5 adds verdict-conditioned feedback and refinement after the forward LLM workflow, using previous answers and the encoded graph. v1 uses forward execution without this stage. This substantially changes inference and its inputs; the original biomedical workflow and Gaussian-process SCM fitting remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial portions of Sections 3–5 are rewritten around STRICTA. Formal causal background and error-propagation discussion move to appendices, a transfer section precedes the conclusion, and the appendix is reorganized with expanded positioning and design discussions.

P2.justification: Figures 1–2 are redrawn, v1 Figures 3–4 become the two panels of v2 Figure 3, and a new Figure 4 illustrates diagnosis across domains. Tables 12–16 add prompt displays, expanded experimental comparisons and human-evaluation results. Original workflow graphs and specification tables are retained.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially expanded and repositioned around document-quality assessment, review generation, fact-checking, essay grading and clinical diagnostic assistance. Section 2 and Appendix A.1 add substantive comparisons with these approaches. Much of v1's abductive-reasoning and explainability discussion is retained in the appendix.

T1.justification: v2 Definition 1 generalizes v1 Definition 2: inference can concern hidden components or verdicts given partially observed workflow variables, rather than all components given inputs and verdicts. It also explicitly requires input-to-step connectivity. The existing SCM, intervention, counterfactual and ACE mathematics is retained, partly in Appendix A.2.1.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens experimental relevance and validation: it explicitly implements verdict-conditioned reasoning, preserves unrefined controls, and supplements automatic and simulated evaluation with human metric assessment, live assistance and domain-transfer evidence. Fuller procedural documentation and reported resource release improve reproducibility. These address important gaps in v1, although small pilot samples, unvalidated transfer annotations and the Pearson/Spearman inconsistency limit the strength of the new conclusions.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and framing, both PDFs describe the same SCM-based assessment framework and biomedical dataset. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds refinement experiments, human evaluation, an NLP-domain transfer study and a live-assistance pilot.

before.justification: v1 reports original human annotations, analyses of assessment variability and causal effects, and experiments with four LLMs.

arxiv_record.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoEs) have been adopted for reducing inference costs by sparsely activating experts in Large language models (LLMs). Despite this reduction, the massive number of experts in MoEs still makes them expensive to serve. In this paper, we study how to address this, by pruning MoEs. Among pruning methodologies, unstructured pruning has been known to achieve the highest performance for a given pruning ratio, compared to structured pruning, since the latter imposes constraints on the sparsification structure. This is intuitive, as the solution space of unstructured pruning subsumes that of structured pruning. However, our counterintuitive finding reveals that expert pruning, a form of structured pruning, can actually precede unstructured pruning to outperform unstructured-only pruning. As existing expert pruning, requiring $O(\frac{k^n}{\sqrt{n}})$ forward passes for $n$ experts, cannot scale for recent MoEs, we propose a scalable alternative with $O(1)$ complexity, yet outperforming the more expensive methods. The key idea is leveraging a latent structure between experts, based on behavior similarity, such that the greedy decision of whether to prune closely captures the joint pruning effect. Ours is highly effective -- for Snowflake Arctic, a 480B-sized MoE with 128 experts, our method needs only one H100 and two hours to achieve nearly no loss in performance with 40% sparsity, even in generative tasks such as GSM8K, where state-of-the-art unstructured pruning fails to. The code will be made publicly available.
arxiv_record.authors: Jaeseong Lee, seung-won hwang, Aurick Qiao, Daniel F Campos, Zhewei Yao, Yuxiong He
arxiv_record.title: STUN: Structured-Then-Unstructured Pruning for Scalable MoE Pruning

metadata.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoEs) have been adopted for reducing inference costs by sparsely activating experts in large language models (LLMs). Despite these reductions, the massive number of parameters in MoEs still makes them expensive to serve. Conventionally, unstructured or structured pruning has been considered to reduce number of parameters. Our key contribution is exploring the interpolation between structured and unstructured pruning, to propose a novel structured-then-unstructured (STUN) approach outperforming both of structured or unstructured pruning, especially for MoEs. In the first stage, we show a scalable expert pruning with O(1) forward pass, unlike existing work requiring O(\frac{k^n}{\sqrt{n}}) forward passes for n experts that cannot scale for recent MoEs with hundreds of experts. We then show our expert-pruned MoEs are robust to unstructured pruning to follow. Experiments on Snowflake Arctic and Mixtral shows that our proposal is highly effective– For Snowflake Arctic, a 480B-sized MoE with 128 experts, our method needs only one H100 and two hours to achieve nearly no loss in performance with 40% sparsity, even in generative tasks such as GSM8K, where state-of-the-art structured or unstructured pruning methods fail. The code is publicly available.

program_record.Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoEs) have been adopted for reducing inference costs by sparsely activating experts in large language models (LLMs). Despite these reductions, the massive number of parameters in MoEs still makes them expensive to serve. Conventionally, unstructured or structured pruning has been considered to reduce number of parameters. Our key contribution is exploring the interpolation between structured and unstructured pruning, to propose a novel structured-then-unstructured (STUN) approach outperforming both of structured or unstructured pruning, especially for MoEs. In the first stage, we show a scalable expert pruning with O(1) forward pass, unlike existing work requiring $O(\frac{k^n}{\sqrt{n}})$ forward passes for $n$ experts that cannot scale for recent MoEs with hundreds of experts. We then show our expert-pruned MoEs are robust to unstructured pruning to follow. Experiments on Snowflake Arctic and Mixtral shows that our proposal is highly effective-- For Snowflake Arctic, a 480B-sized MoE with 128 experts, our method needs only one H100 and two hours to achieve nearly no loss in performance with 40% sparsity, even in generative tasks such as GSM8K, where state-of-the-art structured or unstructured pruning methods fail. The code is publicly available.

C1.justification: v2 explicitly makes outperforming both structured-only and unstructured-only pruning a headline contribution, whereas v1 primarily emphasizes outperforming unstructured-only pruning. The central O(1) scalability and Arctic performance-at-40%-sparsity claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 removes the targeted-dropout explanation for inherent robustness to expert pruning while retaining the kurtosis-based argument for subsequent unstructured pruning. Appendix F adds a generation-versus-multiple-choice explanation for GSM8K difficulty. The limitations newly identify highly imbalanced or skewed data distributions as unevaluated.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the promised code release with stated public availability and an access link. It adds CPU-time information and method-specific GPU pruning times in Table 7. Existing C4 sample counts, sequence lengths, quantization, hardware, and reconstruction settings are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions retain C4 calibration data, GSM8K, and the same eight NLU benchmarks. OLMoE-7B adds a model configuration, without a documented new dataset or task. Evaluation under skewed data distributions is proposed only as future work.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated comparisons with LLM-Pruner in Figure 1 and Table 2, and SEER-MoE, Expert Drop, and Layer Drop in Table 4. These substantially expand the structured and efficient pruning alternatives beyond v1's comparisons with OWL, Wanda, and Lu et al.

E3.justification: v2 adds a fixed-50%-sparsity interpolation comparison, OLMoE-7B evaluations, and higher-sparsity points for Arctic and Mixtral-8x22B. Table 4 explicitly uses different metrics following He et al., although their specification is limited. Existing calibration, quantization, and hyperparameter search grids are retained.

E4.justification: The original clustering and reconstruction ablations survive as Tables 8–10. v2 adds an O(n)-versus-O(1) comparison, reports sensitivity to similarity weights and expert sparsity, provides expert-only results, and introduces a dedicated cost analysis. These substantially broaden evidence about approximation quality, tuning, and efficiency.

E5.justification: Both implementation appendices state that evaluation is performed once because no randomness is introduced. v2 adds no repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Original main-table and clustering/reconstruction ablation scores are retained. New results include Table 5's GSM8K scores of 53.22 for STUN's expert pruning versus 48.52 for Lu et al. at 25% sparsity, additional comparator and OLMoE results, and cost and kurtosis measurements. Some low-sparsity Arctic points from v1 Figure 1 are no longer reported.

M1.justification: The clustering, representative selection, selective reconstruction, and subsequent OWL/Wanda pruning procedures remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–2 move from the appendix into the main text; the additional probability definition supports the derivation without changing the implemented procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around inter- and intra-expert sparsity. Detailed derivations move into Appendix A, algorithms move into the main text, the original ablation discussion moves into Appendix D, and a dedicated Cost Analysis section is introduced.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the introductory plot, adds a method schematic and comparison taxonomy, and expands the MoE figure from three to four panels with revised axis ranges. It condenses the main expert-comparison table while retaining its detailed counterpart in the appendix, and adds multiple comparison and analysis tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds efficient expert-pruning references, including Liu, Zhang, Muzio, and He, and GPU sparsity references such as Mishra and Zhao. It removes the targeted-dropout and regularization discussion and associated citations. The broader positioning as combined structured and unstructured pruning remains.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix A.1, Equation 10, explicitly defines joint pruning probability through normalized inverse reconstruction loss, supporting an equivalence previously asserted without that definition. Most derivations are relocated unchanged. v1 Section 5's targeted-dropout formulation and its connection to MoE training are removed.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central design: additional structured and efficient pruning comparisons address v1's limited comparator coverage, while the O(n)-versus-O(1), sensitivity, and cost analyses directly support approximation and scalability choices. Reorganization and code-access information improve usability. New reporting weaknesses temper these gains: Table 4's unpruned average is 71.5 despite the displayed scores averaging about 73.6, and OLMoE evaluation details are sparse. These localized issues do not outweigh the stronger overall support for the contributions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe STUN and contain readable methods, equations, results, figures, and appendices. Relocated and renumbered material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and reports additional comparator results, approximation comparisons, sensitivity analyses, and cost measurements.

before.justification: v1 reports original pruning experiments on Arctic, Mixtral, and Llama-2, including benchmark results and clustering/reconstruction ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems have advanced significantly with
models like Whisper, Conformer, and self-supervised frameworks such as Wav2vec
2.0 and HuBERT. However, developing robust ASR models for young children's
speech remains challenging due to differences in pronunciation, tone, and pace
compared to adult speech. In this paper, we introduce a new Mandarin speech
dataset focused on children aged 3 to 5, addressing the scarcity of resources
in this area. The dataset comprises 41.25 hours of speech with carefully
crafted manual transcriptions, collected from 397 speakers across various
provinces in China, with balanced gender representation. We provide a
comprehensive analysis of speaker demographics, speech duration distribution
and geographic coverage. Additionally, we evaluate ASR performance on models
trained from scratch, such as Conformer, as well as fine-tuned pre-trained
models like HuBERT and Whisper, where fine-tuning demonstrates significant
performance improvements. Furthermore, we assess speaker verification (SV) on
our dataset, showing that, despite the challenges posed by the unique vocal
characteristics of young children, the dataset effectively supports both ASR
and SV tasks. This dataset is a valuable contribution to Mandarin child speech
research. The dataset is now open-source and freely available for all academic
purposes on https://github.com/flageval-baai/ChildMandarin.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the Mandarin dataset for children aged 3–5, its demographic coverage, and its demonstrated utility for ASR and speaker verification. Fine-tuning benefits and proposed applications remain the same. The added analyses support these existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: Section 4.1.5 adds interpretations involving age, gender, possible pitch/articulation variability, and targeted adaptation. Appendix B discusses residual difficulty with longer or complex utterances. Existing limitations remain unchanged. The new statement that CER decreases with age overgeneralizes Figure 5/Table 8, where four-year-olds outperform five-year-olds within each gender.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies previously absent model-specific batch sizes, learning rates, warmup settings, epoch counts, SV learning-rate schedules, hardware, and approximate runtime. v3 also provides a dataset access link, specifies character-level annotation, and documents parental consent, compensation, anonymization, and access restrictions. These substantially expand reproducibility and collection documentation without establishing changed experiments.

E1.justification: Both evaluate ASR and speaker verification on the same 41.25-hour Mandarin corpus from 397 children aged 3–5. The new age/gender breakdowns and utterance examples analyze existing coverage rather than introducing another dataset, population, or task.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator sets remain unchanged: Transformer, Conformer, Paraformer, Wav2vec 2.0, HuBERT, CW, and Whisper for ASR, and x-vector, ECAPA-TDNN, and ResNet-TDNN for speaker verification. v1's speaker-verification Table 8 becomes Table 9 in v3 without comparator changes.

E3.justification: Table 5 revises Wav2vec 2.0 base/large parameter counts from 368M/1,215M to 97M/318M and HuBERT counts from 369M/1,216M to 97M/319M. These are reported model-size revisions, without evidence of checkpoint substitution or rerunning. v3 also adds groupwise CER and error-component evaluation. Dataset splits, decoding beam size, and SV trial design remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds a substantial diagnostic layer absent from v1: Section 4.1.5 compares CW performance across six age/gender groups and decomposes errors into substitutions, deletions, and insertions. Appendix B adds five transcription comparisons illustrating corrections and residual errors after fine-tuning.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added subgroup results and Figure 5 continue reporting point estimates without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Table 7 changes CW's zero-shot/fine-tuned CER from 19.36%/14.39% to 18.05%/13.66%, without explaining the revision. v3 additionally reports subgroup error profiles and five utterance-level outcomes. The other aggregate ASR scores and all speaker-verification scores remain unchanged, preserving the principal model rankings.

M1.justification: The same ASR and speaker-verification architectures, training approaches, and decoding procedures remain. Shortened baseline descriptions, revised parameter-count reporting, and newly disclosed hyperparameters do not establish an algorithm or architecture change.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the statistics discussion, condenses baseline explanations, updates authors and affiliations, and adds an analysis subsection, Ethics Statement, and appendices. Most existing prose and section order remain intact. Section 4.1.2 introduces an incorrect reference to Table 8 for scratch-training results, which remain in Table 4.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands visual reporting with paired demographic CER bars, an error-type comparison table, three configuration tables, and color-highlighted transcription comparisons in Figure B.1. Table 2 is compacted and relocated, and existing figures and tables are reflowed. The original demographic plots and benchmark-table designs are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: The Dong and Xu (2020) CIF citation and reference are removed when the Paraformer description is shortened. The remaining related-work coverage and positioning around scarce Mandarin resources for young children are substantively unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces original theoretical results or proofs. v3 removes the standard CER formula and its explanation without changing the metric; the EER and DCF definitions remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important documentation omissions for a dataset paper: it provides an explicit access reference, model-specific training configurations, and consent, compensation, and anonymization information absent from v1. These substantially improve reproducibility and scrutiny of data collection, while the new diagnostics make recognition errors easier to inspect. The overstated age trend, unexplained CW score revisions, and incorrect table reference temper but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ChildMandarin dataset and benchmark study. Their text, tables, figures, and equations support comparison. All 11 pages of v1 and 13 pages of v3 were inspected; v3 adds Appendices A and B, while v1 ends with references.

after.justification: v3 retains original ASR and speaker-verification experiments and adds demographic performance breakdowns, error-type results, and utterance-level comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset statistics, ASR experiments in Tables 4, 6, and 7, and speaker-verification results in Table 8.

arxiv_record.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved significant success in Speech-to-Text Translation (S2TT) tasks. While most existing research has focused on English-centric translation directions, the exploration of many-to-many translation is still limited by the scarcity of parallel data. To address this, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning strategy that leverages the machine translation capabilities of large language models and adapts them to S2TT tasks, enabling effective learning in low-resource settings. We trained MLLMs with varying parameter sizes (3B, 7B, and 32B) and evaluated the proposed strategy using the FLEURS and CoVoST-2 datasets. C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from activating multimodal chain-of-thought and achieving selected CoVoST-2/MuST-C improvements to transferring LLM translation capabilities into low-resource, many-to-many S2TT. V2 adds claims of state-of-the-art average performance across 210 directions and the first supporting MLLM at 32B scale.

C2.justification: The inherited MT-capability explanation gains new interpretations involving English-data scarcity, MT/S2TT score correspondence and language mixing. V1's hardware limitation to models up to 8B is replaced by a substantive applicability boundary: performance and language coverage depend on the underlying LLM's translation capabilities.

D1.justification: V2 adds metric signatures and appendix settings covering Common Voice 19 training hours, stage-specific steps and learning rates, query dimensions, LoRA configurations and trainable parameter counts. It reports A100 training hardware and runtimes and changes the release information to a dedicated code-and-model repository. V1's CPU/RAM and software-version details are omitted.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates English-to-German/Japanese/Chinese translation on CoVoST-2 and MuST-C. V2 removes MuST-C, adds FLEURS evaluations covering 6×12 and 15×14 directions, and reports multilingual Common Voice ASR training. CoVoST-2 coverage is retained, with additional evaluation of FLEURS-trained models.

E2.justification: The corresponding CoVoST-2 comparison drops SALMONN, BLSP-KD, GenTranslate variants and several Seamless configurations, while adding Qwen2.5-based cascades and direct instruction-tuning baselines. FLEURS comparisons additionally evaluate LoRA-adapted SeamlessM4T-V2. SALMONN and BLSP-KD remaining in related work does not preserve their experimental participation.

E3.justification: New FLEURS protocols introduce 52/129-hour S2TT training budgets, Qwen2.5 configurations at 3B/7B/32B, and LoRA controls. V2 adds COMET and Japanese char-versus-ja-mecab evaluation. The retained inference-speed table also changes its stated precision from bf16 to FP16; this does not establish that timings were rerun.

E4.justification: Curriculum ablations expand from en-zh to all three CoVoST-2 target languages. V2 adds MT-versus-S2TT comparisons, model/data scaling analyses and language-mixing error analysis, while replacing the original case studies and encoder/LLM combination analysis. The original MuST-C zero-shot investigation is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. V2's additional averages, COMET scores and score-trend plot remain point-estimate reporting rather than uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive FLEURS results, including 20.6/21.4/24.6 average BLEU for its 3B/7B/32B models in Table 3 and COMET results in Table 15. CoVoST-2 and ablation values are revised, and MuST-C results disappear. Changed models and settings prevent interpreting these replacements as same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: The three-stage curriculum and encoder-adapter-LLM design remain. However, the intermediate task changes from generating transcription plus translation to generating translation alone, and instructions now identify both source and target languages (Table 1 in both versions). These are limited procedural adaptations beyond renaming.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, methodological explanation and conclusion are extensively rewritten. CoT-ST/SLM/MMT terminology becomes LLM-SRT/MLLM/SMT, problem formulation is integrated into methodology, and experimental discussion is reorganized with a new appendix.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are substantially redrawn, and Figure 3 adds an MT/S2TT score comparison. Benchmark, multitask, ablation and case-study tables are restructured or replaced, with new appendix tables for languages, training settings and detailed results. The inference-time table is largely retained.

R1.justification: V2 removes the standalone CoT discussion and associated foundational citations, repositioning the contribution around low-resource transfer learning with Pham et al. and Mueller et al. It also updates the multimodal-model discussion with Li et al. and Qwen2.5-Omni. This changes the research positioning substantially.

T1.justification: The formal intermediate-task definition changes from producing both Y and Z in v1 Section 2 to producing only Z in v2 Section 2.1. Additional adapter equations and dimensional specifications mainly document implementation; neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical grounding and reproducibility through matched instruction-tuning baselines, MT/S2TT comparisons across 210 directions, and detailed training, LoRA and metric specifications absent from v1. These improve support for the curriculum and its transfer-learning interpretation. MuST-C evidence is lost, and some claims overreach: the 32B 'all directions' statement conflicts with Table 3's English-source scores of 32.5 versus SeamlessM4T-V2's 33.1. Nevertheless, the stronger validation and transparency provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same underlying three-stage speech-translation framework, despite substantial renaming and revision. Their text, equations, figures and tables are readable, including v2's appendix; v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: V2 reports original FLEURS and CoVoST-2 experiments, scaling and ablation results, case studies, and appendix BLEU/COMET results.

before.justification: V1 reports original CoVoST-2 and MuST-C translation results, ASR measurements, architecture comparisons, curriculum ablations and inference timings.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have shown significant progress, approaching human perception levels. In this work, we demonstrate that despite these advances, LLMs still struggle to reason using molecular structural information. This gap is critical because many molecular properties, including functional groups, depend heavily on such structural details. To address this limitation, we propose an approach that sketches molecular structures for reasoning. Specifically, we introduce Molecular Structural Reasoning (MSR) framework to enhance the understanding of LLMs by explicitly incorporating the key structural features. We present two frameworks for scenarios where the target molecule is known or unknown. We verify that our MSR improves molecular understanding through extensive experiments.
arxiv_record.authors: Yunhui Jang, Jaehyung Kim, Sungsoo Ahn
arxiv_record.title: Structural Reasoning Improves Molecular Understanding of LLM

C1.justification: The central contribution remains explicit structural reasoning to improve molecular understanding. v2's introduction and conclusion extend the claimed empirical effectiveness from captioning and molecule generation to three tasks, including retrosynthesis; the principal methodological claims remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly discusses dependence on accurate molecular inputs and vulnerability to noisy or incomplete representations. It qualifies ChemCrow's suitability as a comparator, argues that structural metrics matter more than BLEU for retrosynthesis, and interprets new ablations as supporting k=5 and the sufficiency of the selected descriptors.

D1.justification: v2 adds rouge-score and nltk versions, replaces anonymous code-access information with a named GitHub repository, and newly states that trained models are released. Existing hardware and hyperparameter tables remain. However, v1's explicit explanation of shared reasoning/answering weights for MolT5-large is omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds L+M for captioning and text-to-molecule generation, Mol-Instructions for captioning, and Mol-Instructions product-to-reactant retrosynthesis while retaining ChEBI-20. Sections 4.1–4.3 therefore broaden both dataset coverage and task requirements.

E2.justification: New evaluated comparators include Meditron-7B, Mol2Lang-VLM, BioT5+, Lang2Mol-Diff, and the Mol-Instructions model. Conversely, RNN and Transformer disappear from the corresponding ChEBI-20 comparisons. ChemCrow comparisons remain in Appendix B.4 rather than being removed.

E3.justification: Added settings include L+M validation evaluation with MolT5-small/base/large, additional exclusion of chain-length and chirality descriptors for L+M, and MSR-enriched prompting for Mol-Instructions. The new ablations vary sampling counts and descriptor inputs. Original ChEBI-20 hyperparameter tables and metric definitions are retained.

E4.justification: v2 extends the rejection-sampling comparison to k=1, 2, and 5, adds individual-versus-combined structural-component tests, and evaluates Morgan fingerprints, TPSA, and molar refractivity as alternative/additional descriptors (Figures 7–9). Appendix B.2 also adds retrosynthesis examples. These substantially expand analysis beyond v1's sampling and ChemCrow comparisons.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix A newly states that experiments are based on a single run; v1 does not disclose a run count. Neither version reports variability estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is a reporting addition, not evidence that the number of runs changed.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial L+M, Mol-Instructions, retrosynthesis, and ablation results while retaining corresponding ChEBI-20 and ChemCrow scores. For example, its new retrosynthesis comparison reports Exact 0.009 without MSR versus 0.016 with MSR, but BLEU 0.705 versus 0.502 and unchanged validity of 1.000 (Table 5). These are newly reported comparisons, not gains over v1 under identical settings.

M1.justification: The described core procedure remains: structural descriptors, tool-based extraction when molecules are available, a fine-tuned reasoner otherwise, reliability filtering, and beam-candidate selection by structural agreement. MSR and analytic/synthetic reasoning reframe the existing method. Dataset-specific component selection applies the previously described filtering rule.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and method narrative are extensively rewritten around MSR and analytic/synthetic reasoning. Related work moves after experiments, structural analysis moves earlier, and new limitations, broader-impact, and artifact sections change the document's organization substantially.

P2.justification: v2 switches to two-column layout, converts descriptor explanations into Table 1 and prompt tables into boxed figures, and redesigns result tables without delta columns. It replaces the opening failure example with a new composite illustration, adds ablation and retrosynthesis figures, and relocates retained examples and ChemCrow comparisons.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for L+M and new comparison models, Ganeeva et al.'s structural-understanding work, and Kant's analysis/synthesis distinction.
