arxiv_record.abstract: Retrieval augmented generation (RAG), while effectively integrating external knowledge to address the inherent limitations of large language models (LLMs), can be hindered by imperfect retrieval that contain irrelevant, misleading, or even malicious information. Previous studies have rarely connected the behavior of RAG through joint analysis, particularly regarding error propagation coming from imperfect retrieval and potential conflicts between LLMs' internal knowledge and external sources. Through comprehensive and controlled analyses under realistic conditions, we find that imperfect retrieval augmentation is inevitable, common, and harmful. We identify the knowledge conflicts between LLM-internal and external knowledge from retrieval as a bottleneck to overcome imperfect retrieval in the post-retrieval stage of RAG. To address this, we propose Astute RAG, a novel RAG approach designed to be resilient to imperfect retrieval augmentation. It adaptively elicits essential information from LLMs' internal knowledge, iteratively consolidates internal and external knowledge with source-awareness, and finalizes the answer according to information reliability. C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for reduced conflicts at zero retrieval precision, benefits of source information and consolidation over filtering/refinement, and CompAct's failures. It interprets results as supporting smaller-model applicability and reduced ordering sensitivity. The longer-output limitation becomes a longer-input limitation, while earlier Gemini iteration interpretations and context-type/multimodal future directions are removed.

D1.justification: v2 supplies an intermediate-step judging prompt, added model versions and sizes, and a more specific RGB subset description. Existing method prompts and retrieval instructions remain. v1's explicit USC sampling temperature of 0.7 is omitted; this establishes a disclosure loss, not an actual temperature change.

E1.justification: v2 adds long-form question answering on ASQA (Section 5.2, Figure 5), extending beyond v1's short-form evaluation. NQ, TriviaQA, BioASQ, PopQA, and the negative-passage RGB scenario remain.

E2.justification: The original main-table comparators remain. Appendices C–E add evaluated Answer Refinement, retrieved-only Context Filtering, generated-and-retrieved Context Filtering, and CompAct baselines (Tables 4–7), substantially expanding comparisons with alternative correction and context-processing strategies.

E3.justification: v2 adds Mistral-Large and Mistral-Nemo model configurations, LLM judging of intermediate outputs, source-removal controls, passage-order experiments, and a maximum-generated-passages sweep. The retained short-form benchmark still contains 1,042 questions with ten passages each, and default Astute RAG settings remain one generated passage maximum and one consolidation iteration.

E4.justification: New analyses examine retrieval precision versus conflict rate, source-awareness, adaptive passage counts, intermediate-step correctness, token costs, filtering versus consolidation, and passage-order robustness. Earlier conflict-subset and qualitative analyses remain. Claude's iteration experiment is redisplayed, while the Gemini iteration analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added intermediate-step confidence-assignment evaluation does not introduce experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds ASQA results, Mistral overall accuracies of 59.9 and 51.3, and numerous ablation and comparator results. Retained Claude/Gemini default scores match apart from rounding. Figure 7 swaps the InstructRAG/Self-Route curve labels relative to v1 Figure 4a, aligning their aggregate ordering with the main table. Gemini's two- and three-iteration result rows disappear.

M1.justification: v1 Section 3 and v2 Section 4 retain the same adaptive passage generation, iterative source-aware consolidation, and answer finalization. Algorithm 1 and the three method prompts in Appendix A are substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction and pitfall discussion are substantially rewritten. Related work moves from Section 5 to Section 2, problem formulation merges into the method overview, experimental discussion is reorganized, limitations receive a separate heading, and appendices expand from A–B to A–F.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, combines the original main tables, separates v1 Figure 4 into individual plots, and adds multiple figures and tables. Iteration and API-call results are redisplayed graphically, legends are revised, and several displays—including the retained qualitative examples—move after the references.

R1.justification: v2 more explicitly acknowledges prior observations and adds references for practical knowledge conflicts, ASQA, CompAct, and passage ordering. T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, source indicators, and generation/consolidation equations remain equivalent. improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method. arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) struggle with maintaining accurate knowledge due to conflicting/outdated parametric memories. While locate-and-edit methods address this, their reliance on models' internal representations leads to robustness failures in long-context reasoning and paraphrased queries. We identify a fundamental limitation of locate-and-edit methods: existing semantic keys (for memory localization) cannot simultaneously satisfy robustness (context-invariant activation) and specificity (precise knowledge discrimination). Through theoretical error-bound analysis, we establish formal criteria for effective editing. Our solution introduces \textit{Robust Edit Pathway (REP)}, a plug-and-play module that: (1) disentangles editing keys from native model representations; (2) dynamically adjusts keys via contrastive learning to achieve robustness-specificity balance. Extensive experiments across various editing methods (ROME/MEMIT/R-ROME/EMMET), existing LLMs (LLaMA2, QWen, Mistral), and datasets (CounterFact, ZsRE) show that REP improves success rate over robustness tests by up-to 66.4\% while maintaining the success rate unaffected. Our code can be found at https://github.com/ElliottYan/RobustKeyEdit .
arxiv_record.authors: Jianhao Yan, Futing Wang, Yun Luo, Yafu Li, Yue Zhang
arxiv_record.title: Keys to Robust Edits: from Theoretical Insights to Practical Advances

C1.justification: The central claim about unreliable internal keys and REP's robustness remains. V2 strengthens v1's acknowledged success-rate tradeoffs into claims of unaffected or preserved success, adds quantified robustness and fluency-preservation claims, and stops advertising the group-discussion analogy as a principal contribution.

C2.justification: V2 introduces target-key drift as motivation for the consistency loss and explicitly identifies training overhead and inapplicability to other editing families as limitations in Section 8. The single-fact boundary and interpretations concerning key collisions and large edited values were already present in v1.

D1.justification: Most training details already appear in v1 Appendix B.2. V2 adds the consistency-loss weight, but Section 6.1 specifies 5e4 while Appendix D specifies 1e5. It also changes the stated code-repository location and removes v1's Algorithm 1, despite still referring readers to an appendix algorithm.

E1.justification: V2 adds ZsRE alongside CounterFact, with extensive editing and robustness results in Table 3. Both versions retain single-fact editing and the existing subject-rephrasing, token-shuffling, and long-context scenarios.

E2.justification: V1 Table 1 evaluates only ROME and ROME+REP, despite mentioning MEMIT elsewhere. V2 Tables 1-3 actually evaluate MEMIT, R-ROME, and EMMET, each with and without REP, substantially expanding the comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 adds Qwen2-7B, changes the stated long-context length from 300 to 512 tokens, and adds paraphrase, fluency, and reversion metrics. Figure 3 also changes to normalized key similarities. The 100-validation/400-test split and equal in-domain/out-of-domain query split were already present in v1.

E4.justification: V2 adds a consistency-loss-weight sensitivity study in Figure 6, updates the gate-threshold study, and expands the quantitative key-similarity diagnostic to compare three perturbations. The Slovenia PCA case and value-norm analysis are retained in Appendices E-F rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 reports point estimates without specifying repeated runs or uncertainty. V2 explicitly reports three-seed averages and supplies standard deviations throughout Tables 2-3. This is substantial new uncertainty reporting; v1's underlying run count remains unspecified.

E6.justification: The original results are extensively replaced and supplemented. For example, v1 reports LLaMA2/CounterFact success of 84.5 for ROME and 81.0 for ROME+REP; v2 Table 2 reports 100.0 ± 0.0 for both. Additional editor, model, dataset, and metric results greatly expand the evidence. These revised reports do not establish a same-setting performance gain between versions.

M1.justification: V2 Section 6 adds an MSE target-consistency loss to the existing key-aggregation objective to control target-key drift. The projection module, token gate, and thresholded inference remain, making this a bounded training-objective refinement.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten; explicit contribution bullets and an expanded architectural explanation replace portions of the earlier narrative. V2 removes the group-discussion exposition, adds a limitations section, and reorganizes substantial existing material into appendices.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column layout, combines v1 Figures 2 and 6 into its Figure 2, replaces the similarity histogram, and relocates the PCA and value-norm plots to appendix Figures 7-8. It also restructures the main results table and adds extensive appendix tables and a loss-weight plot.

R1.justification: V2 removes the broad taxonomy of parameter-preserving and meta-learning approaches and several associated citations. It adds references including Rebuilding ROME, Yoon et al.'s editing study, and the Qwen technical report. The central positioning against existing locate-and-edit methods remains.

T1.justification: V2 adds Lemma 4.8 with explicit lower and upper whitened-similarity bounds. It replaces v1 Appendix A.3's unfinished proof placeholder with separate robustness and specificity derivations in A.3-A.4, and reformulates Definition 3.1 using predictions over a prompt set.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical support for REP by testing transfer across four editors, three models, and two datasets with three-seed uncertainty reporting. It also supplies previously missing derivations and a new sensitivity analysis. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including conflicting consistency-loss weights and overstated preservation claims: Table 2 shows Qwen2/EMMET locality falling from 92.5 to 76.4 despite the introduction's claim of a drop below 1.6 points. The expanded evidence materially improves assessment of both effectiveness and tradeoffs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REP research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive rewriting and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments across four editing methods, three models, and two datasets, including three-seed results and parameter-sensitivity analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original key-representation analyses, ROME versus ROME+REP experiments on CounterFact, and a gate-threshold study.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Some statements have one well-defined continuation (e.g., "the Eiffel Tower
is in [Paris]"), whereas others have a natural distribution over multiple
options (e.g., "the weighted coin flip was [Heads/Tails].") We argue that
language model (LM) outputs should capture these natural distributions. Our
work specifically tests whether LM output probabilities are calibrated to
numeric information within their textual contexts. For example, if the context
(the prompt) concerns two equally likely options (e.g., heads or tails for a
fair coin), the LM output probabilities should also be equal. Likewise, in a
context with nonuniformly likely events (e.g., rolling a pair with two dice) an
LM should output proportionate probabilities. However, we find that even in
simple settings, the best LMs (1) are poorly calibrated and (2) have systematic
biases: artifacts like word identity, word order, and word frequency all impact
calibration. For example, gpt-4o-mini often picks the first of two options
presented in the prompt regardless of the options' implied likelihoods, whereas
Llama-3.1-8B picks the second. Models do not allocate probability mass among
valid options in a calibrated manner.

Charles Lovering, Michael Krumdick, Viet Dac Lai, Seth Ebner, Nilesh
  Kumar, Varshini Reddy, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Chris Tanner

C1.justification: The central claims of poor calibration, mode collapse and option-order bias remain. However, v2 elevates training-data number-frequency effects from speculation in v1's discussion to an explicit contribution and an abstract/conclusion finding, substantially extending the paper's explanatory claims.

C2.justification: v1 reports little shared structure between color hierarchies and no obvious explanation; v2 identifies correlated hierarchies and suggests a training-data explanation. It also interprets differing frequency associations across Base and Chat models, acknowledges occasional successful calibration, and adds specific limitations concerning corpus proxies, synthetic templates and restricted numeric coverage.

D1.justification: v2 specifies the SciPy Wasserstein implementation, number-frequency query details, approximately 48 hours on eight A100 GPUs, and an MIT license. It points to a different data/experiment release folder. Both versions still describe release prospectively, so actual availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: v2 adds 33.6K Wordproblems covering scenarios such as tree species and occupations, and uses Dolma number-frequency data for original corpus analysis. These broaden the represented contexts and data sources. Probabilities is renamed Colors, while Distributions and the human study remain.

E2.justification: The evaluated LM panel and principal heuristic baselines remain. However, v2 Tables 4 and 11 report Pick First/Second for Distributions, where v1's corresponding tables reported random baselines. Several Random-temperature and Pick Higher-weight comparisons from v1's aggregate baseline sweeps are omitted.

E3.justification: Relative entropy changes from an entropy ratio to an entropy difference. v2 also introduces compatibility-rate summaries, a WD < 0.05 success criterion and experiments with 500 introductions and 500 additional templates. The stated numeric scales change from numbers under 10/100/1000 to 1–10/10–100/100–999; this establishes revised protocol reporting, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds template-robustness tests, analyses of when models achieve good calibration, correlations between models' color hierarchies, and number-frequency analyses (Appendices D–H). Conversely, v1's detailed per-digit distribution heatmaps and numerical unprompted-versus-prompted human-study comparison are no longer fully reported.

E5.justification: v1's main model tables report point estimates, although its human study already includes randomness tests. v2 adds option-pair-clustered uncertainty estimates, 95% confidence intervals, paired Chat–Base intervals and correlation significance reporting. These substantially change statistical reporting; they do not establish additional seeds or repeated runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds Wordproblems results, template-test outcomes, successful-calibration counts and frequency/hierarchy correlations. Retained benchmark estimates also change: GPT-4o's Probabilities/Colors WD is 0.42 in v1 Table 2 and 0.40 in v2 Table 4. Given revised setting descriptions, this is an updated result rather than an established same-setting gain. Prompted human-study scores remain, but unprompted columns are removed.

M1.justification: The fixed language models, calibration prompts, aggregation of tokenization probabilities and human-study n-gram opponent are retained. The revisions concern evaluation and diagnostic analysis, without introducing a new model, training objective or calibration procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. Results are reorganized from dataset-based sections into metric-based sections, followed by dedicated bias analyses. The human study moves to Appendix I, and the appendices are rebuilt into explanatory sections followed by corresponding figure sections.

P2.justification: The main text switches to two columns, combined result tables are split by metric, and numerous statistical and frequency displays are added. Per-model heatmaps are consolidated into overview grids with revised legends and separate compatibility/distance views. Detailed digit-distribution plots are removed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around linguistic and pragmatic calibration, mathematical capabilities and training-frequency effects. New references include Mielke et al., Tsvilodub et al., McCoy et al., and the Dolma/infini-gram work. Several earlier general training and GAN references disappear; publication updates to retained works are not new citations.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 changes RE from H(Π)/H(P) to H(Π)−H(P), moving the calibrated reference from one to zero. v2 also defines the frequency-gap quantity used in its new analysis. These are limited mathematical-definition changes; neither version supplies a substantial theorem or proof development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence that the findings extend beyond v1's narrow color templates through Wordproblems and the additional-template tests, while clustered confidence intervals improve assessment of model differences. Frequency analyses also turn earlier speculation into measured associations. These gains outweigh remaining reporting problems, including Tables 2 and 10 retaining an ideal RE of one despite the new zero-reference definition; the frequency evidence also remains correlational.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same contextual-calibration study and contain readable main text and appendices. Matching models, prompts, experiments and retained results establish continuity despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original model and human results and adds Wordproblems evaluations, template-robustness experiments and corpus-frequency analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on Distributions and Probabilities, plus a Matching Pennies comparison with human participants (Tables 1–3).

arxiv_record.abstract: Ensuring awareness of fairness and privacy in Large Language Models (LLMs) is critical. Interestingly, we discover a counter-intuitive trade-off phenomenon that enhancing an LLM's privacy awareness through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) methods significantly decreases its fairness awareness with thousands of samples. To address this issue, inspired by the information theory, we introduce a training-free method to \textbf{S}uppress the \textbf{P}rivacy and fa\textbf{I}rness coupled \textbf{N}eurons (\textbf{SPIN}), which theoretically and empirically decrease the mutual information between fairness and privacy awareness. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that SPIN eliminates the trade-off phenomenon and significantly improves LLMs' fairness and privacy awareness simultaneously without compromising general capabilities, \eg improving Qwen-2-7B-Instruct's fairness awareness by 12.2\% and privacy awareness by 14.0\%. More crucially, SPIN remains robust and effective with limited annotated data or even when only malicious fine-tuning data is available, whereas SFT methods may fail to perform properly in such scenarios. Furthermore, we show that SPIN could generalize to other potential trade-off dimensions. We hope this study provides valuable insights into concurrently addressing fairness and privacy concerns in LLMs and can be integrated into comprehensive frameworks to develop more ethical and responsible AI systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/SPIN.
arxiv_record.authors: Chen Qian, Dongrui Liu, Jie Zhang, Yong Liu, Jing Shao
arxiv_record.title: The Tug of War Within: Mitigating the Fairness-Privacy Conflicts in Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add the claim that SPIN can generalize beyond fairness–privacy trade-offs, supported by the safety extension. The central claims about simultaneous awareness improvements, general-capability preservation and robustness to limited or malicious data remain, including the same headline improvement percentages.

C2.justification: Section 2, Appendix H and the new Limitations section substantially clarify scope. They distinguish appropriate responses from sensitivity and deeper understanding, distinguish privacy awareness from training-time privacy preservation, discuss localization and capability-preservation mechanisms, and acknowledge unresolved intervention during training and coarse module-level analysis.

D1.justification: Appendix F newly documents filtering keywords, safe-answer selection, three-annotator intersection and sampling for the existing datasets, plus Figure 2's sigma value. v2 also supplies evaluation frameworks, localization formulas and runtime information, and changes the code pointer to SPIN. These disclosures do not establish changed original experiments; v1's blanket default evaluation-harness statement is omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds a privacy–safety scenario using safety-related BeaverTails data and SALAD-bench's Toxic Content subset. Coverage also expands to AG News, IMDB, SummEval, QAGS, FaithEval's unanswerable/inconsistent settings, TruthfulQA and HaluEval-QA, substantially broadening the evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: The FFT, LoRA, DoRA and ReFT baselines remain. Figure 4 adds Random, Wanda and SparseGPT as alternative neuron-locating methods within the suppression framework across four model families. This introduces substantive direct controls for the localization component beyond the original fine-tuning comparisons.

E3.justification: The added evaluations introduce UniEval relevance scoring, FaithEval accuracy, and hallucination assessment through lm-evaluation-harness and HaluEval. Appendix F adds HSIC evaluations at sigma values 100, 200, 300 and 400. Existing training budgets and extraction settings remain unchanged; the newly specified sigma=50 for Figure 2 is additional disclosure.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of the neuron-localization choice, HSIC kernel-width sensitivity, and paired model-response case studies in Appendix I. These extend scrutiny of the mechanism and its outputs. The earlier malicious-data, dataset-size, extraction-ratio/module and word-frequency analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental run/seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. The additional results retain this reporting practice.

E6.justification: New results cover localization controls, runtime, safety–privacy behavior, additional capabilities and HSIC sensitivity. For example, v2 Table 7 reports Qwen2 privacy/safety scores of 0.8158/0.7190 versus the original model's 0.7412/0.6720 in the new setting. Matched original fairness/privacy, model-size, general-capability and privacy-only fine-tuning table values are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 and Algorithm 1 retain the same gradient-based importance scores, intersection of task-related neuron sets, exclusion of general-capability neurons and zeroing of selected weights. DEAN-to-SPIN renaming and alternative localization experiments do not change the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper and renames the method, replaces the main related-work section with a problem statement, and relocates related work, the algorithm and model-size discussion to appendices. A contents page and reorganized experimental and discussion sections substantially change the document's structure.

P2.justification: The single-column preprint becomes a predominantly two-column document. v2 expands the general-capability table, adds localization and HSIC-sensitivity figures, introduces several experimental tables and boxed QA examples, and relocates existing displays such as the model-size table and word-frequency figure.

R1.justification: The core PEFT and neuron-localization positioning remains. Added citations cover pruning, privacy-preserving training, over-refusal and the new evaluations. Appendices A/H refine the distinction from traditional fairness/differential-privacy research and explicitly claim that prior work had not explored the LLM awareness trade-off.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 replaces the shared-Z non-strict inequality with distinct Z1/Z2 variables and a strict inequality assuming I[Z1;Z2|X,Y]>0; Appendix B supplies a revised proof. Proposition 1 replaces averaged representations with layer-specific original/modified-model representations and asserts strict reduction under an explicit coupling assumption.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps through direct localization controls, HSIC sensitivity tests and broader checks of generation quality (Figures 4/8 and Table 8). The revised conditional argument, fuller data-curation documentation and explicit scope limitations also improve assessability. Mixed new capability scores and absent uncertainty reporting still limit blanket preservation claims, but the stronger controls and transparency substantially improve the paper's evidential support.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds neuron-localization comparisons, safety–privacy experiments, runtime measurements and further capability evaluations.

arxiv_record.abstract:
AI holds promise for transforming scientific processes, including hypothesis
generation. Prior work on hypothesis generation can be broadly categorized into
theory-driven and data-driven approaches. While both have proven effective in
generating novel and plausible hypotheses, it remains an open question whether
they can complement each other. To address this, we develop the first method
that combines literature-based insights with data to perform LLM-powered
hypothesis generation. We apply our method on five different datasets and
demonstrate that integrating literature and data outperforms other baselines
(8.97\% over few-shot, 15.75\% over literature-based alone, and 3.37\% over
data-driven alone). Additionally, we conduct the first human evaluation to
assess the utility of LLM-generated hypotheses in assisting human
decision-making on two challenging tasks: deception detection and AI generated
content detection. Our results show that human accuracy improves significantly
by 7.44\% and 14.19\% on these tasks, respectively. These findings suggest that
integrating literature-based and data-driven approaches provides a
comprehensive and nuanced framework for hypothesis generation and could open
new avenues for scientific inquiry.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: combining literature and data improves hypothesis utility, and generated hypotheses assist human decisions. The headline automatic and human accuracy improvements remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V3 interprets the added experiments as evidence of robustness and applicability to smaller models, and discusses a novelty–plausibility tradeoff for NOTEBOOKLM. It also explains paper summarization through context-length and distracting-detail concerns. Existing AIGC failure explanations and Section 7's limitations are retained.

D1.justification: V3 makes initialization and hypothesis-bank bookkeeping more explicit, revises the documented proposal count, and supplies rating criteria, participant qualifications, and manual hypothesis-selection details (Appendices B–C). The original prompt appendix, hardware and cost disclosures, and code/data access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The five benchmark datasets and four classification tasks remain unchanged. V3 adds a distinct human hypothesis-rating task involving participants with graduate-level social-science degrees, assessing deception-detection hypotheses for clarity, novelty, and plausibility (Section 3.1).

E2.justification: The automatic benchmark baseline roster is retained. V3 additionally compares HYPOREFINE against NOTEBOOKLM and HYPERWRITE in the new human-rating study (Table 4), whereas v1 compared them only automatically. SciMON's added example is explicitly borrowed from prior work, not a newly run benchmark baseline.

E3.justification: V3 adds Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct evaluations, three prompt variations, hypothesis-bank limits of 10 and 30 alongside 20, and a 30-participant, five-point rating study. Appendix B.6 also changes the stated proposals per update from 1 to 10. This is an explicit setting revision, but the PDFs do not establish whether the retained benchmark experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing OOD, cross-model, and qualitative analyses, v3 adds systematic sensitivity tests for generation/inference prompts and hypothesis-bank size across both models and IND/OOD settings (Appendix D, Tables 11–14). Appendix E.1 also adds an illustrative comparison distinguishing SciMON research ideas from explanatory hypotheses.

E5.justification: V3 adds paired t-tests against few-shot inference to the automatic results, with p < 0.05 indicated in Table 1, and mean-plus/minus entries and significance markers for human ratings in Table 4. The five inference seeds and original human-utility t-tests are retained. The meaning of Table 4's plus/minus quantities is not specified.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial results in Tables 4 and 10–14, including clarity ratings of 4.22, 3.71, and 3.08 for HYPOREFINE, NOTEBOOKLM, and HYPERWRITE. The original within-model benchmark values are retained. The cross-model table revises IND row attribution and recalculates relative differences (v1 Table 2; v3 Table 3), without establishing new same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The HYPOGENIC backbone, alternating literature/data refinement, specificity booster, and union/redundancy mechanisms are retained. V3 formalizes their description without introducing a new component. The revised proposal count per update is an experimental hyperparameter change, assessed under E3.

P1.justification: Section 2 receives substantial localized clarification and more consistent notation, while related-work wording and experimental transitions are revised. Human studies are renumbered, and a new additional-experiments appendix precedes the relocated qualitative appendix. The overall narrative structure and much of the original prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the displays with human-rating results and criteria, smaller-model and sensitivity tables, a SciMON comparison table, and two survey screenshots. Figure 1 is simplified, the cross-model table is reorganized, and benchmark boldface gains a significance interpretation. Existing survey images and qualitative tables are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: The bibliography retains the same works. Section 5 now distinguishes literature-based research ideation from hypotheses explaining observed phenomena, replacing the earlier broader theory-driven framing. Appendix E.1 illustrates this distinction using an attributed SciMON example and an existing deception-detection finding.

T1.justification: V3's expanded agent, dataset, and hypothesis-bank notation formalizes existing descriptions. Equation 1 restates the existing accuracy-plus-UCB reward, and the alternating refinement recurrence is equivalent. Neither version presents additional theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses important validation gaps through direct human quality comparisons and systematic prompt and bank-size sensitivity tests, while adding smaller-model evidence and statistical assessment of retained results (Tables 4 and 10–14). These substantially strengthen the paper beyond its unchanged headline scores. The gains require qualification: rating hypotheses were manually selected, and Table 11 contains large individual prompt-related drops despite reassuring averages.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, research questions, and core framework. The main texts and complete appendices, including equations, tables, and image-based survey materials, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains these empirical results and adds human quality ratings, smaller-model results, and prompt and hyperparameter sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification accuracy and F1 results across five datasets, cross-model evaluations, and human studies of decision-making utility and hypothesis novelty.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Full-duplex spoken dialogue systems significantly surpass traditional
turn-based dialogue systems, as they allow simultaneous bidirectional
communication, closely mirroring human-human interactions. However, achieving
low latency and natural interactions in full-duplex dialogue systems remains a
significant challenge, especially considering human conversation dynamics such
as interruptions, backchannels, and overlapping speech. In this paper, we
introduce a novel End-to-End GPT-based model OmniFlatten for full-duplex
conversation, capable of effectively modeling the complex behaviors inherent to
natural conversations with low latency. To achieve full-duplex conversation
capabilities, we propose a multi-stage post-training scheme that progressively
adapts a text large language model (LLM) backbone into a speech-text dialogue
LLM, capable of generating text and speech in real time, without modifying the
architecture of the backbone LLM. The training process comprises three stages:
modality alignment, half-duplex dialogue learning, and full-duplex dialogue
learning. In all training stages, we standardize the data using a flattening
operation, which enables unifying the training methods and the GPT backbone
across different modalities and tasks. Our approach offers a simple modeling
technique and a promising research direction for developing efficient and
natural end-to-end full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. Audio samples of
dialogues generated by OmniFlatten can be found at this web site
(https://omniflatten.github.io/).

V1's detailed semantic-context and chunk-size explanations are removed; backchannel limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies the 15% high-quality WenetSpeech training subset, random user versus fixed assistant timbres, and Chinese ASR scoring resources. It removes the NanoGPT implementation pointer and the normal-distribution pause-sampling detail. These documentation changes do not establish corresponding changes to the underlying implementation.

E1.justification: TTS evaluation switches from Librispeech/WenetSpeech to LibriTTS/AIShell-3, including replacing Mandarin meeting speech with a multi-speaker TTS corpus. The core English/Chinese ASR, TTS, and simulated voice-dialogue coverage remains.

E2.justification: V2 adds Whisper-small and reported VITA scores to ASR comparisons, retaining Whisper-Large-V3. TTS gains ChatTTS and CosyVoice comparators. Dialogue evaluation adds LLaMA-Omni, Moshi, GLM-Voice, and two Qwen2-Instruct sizes; turn-taking evaluation adds Moshi. V1's dialogue comparisons primarily involved internal ablations and ground-truth responses.

E3.justification: V2 changes English evaluation from CER to WER, uses Paraformer-zh for Chinese speech scoring, and adds WenetSpeech test-net. Chat evaluation explicitly focuses on single turns and adds ASR-transcribed speech scoring; turn-taking introduces a 1.5-second failure threshold. Reported dialogue sessions change from 360K to 390K and noise SNR from 15–25 to 15–30 dB.

E4.justification: V2 retains the modality-alignment and half-duplex-stage ablations, adds evaluation of the final two-stream model, and examines speech-versus-text outputs and comparisons with text-only models. The chunk-size-5 versus chunk-size-10 sensitivity analysis in v1 Table 3 is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests. Both present point estimates; additional rows and changed numerical precision do not alter uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: The result tables are substantially replaced and expanded. V2 Table 3 newly reports two-stream speech scores of 2.19 for English and 3.06 for Chinese, below the corresponding three-stream scores of 3.92 and 5.15. Test-set CE losses disappear. Reported assistant/user response times change from 160/805 ms for v1's chunk-size-10 model to 193/287 ms, but revised data and evaluation rules prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: Both versions retain Qwen2-0.5B, CosyVoice tokenization, the modality-alignment and four-/three-/two-stream training progression, and the same dialogue loss masking and chunking procedure. Revised explanations and additional evaluations do not establish an algorithmic or architectural change.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially condensed, related-work and evaluation narratives are rewritten, and method explanations are tightened. V2 adds a dedicated Limitations section and updates the author list and Appendix A heading. The appendix's evaluation prompt itself is unchanged.

P2.justification: V1 Figures 1–4 are consolidated into four panels of v2 Figure 1, and a new data-simulation diagram becomes Figure 2. The combined ASR/TTS table is split, dialogue tables gain language/modality groups and model sizes, and turn-taking rows change from chunk sizes to model comparisons.

R1.justification: V2 adds references and positioning around Mini-Omni2, GLM-4-Voice, LSLM, and dGSLM, plus the FunASR reference supporting Chinese recognition. The main contrasts with Moshi's parallel streams and SyncLM's deduplication remain.

T1.justification: The token-sequence specifications and verbal Acc@k definitions retain their mathematical substance. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions, proofs, or new derivations; the new response deadline is an experimental protocol rule.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses a central evidence gap: v1 evaluated three-stream textual responses while leaving the final speech-only model unscored. V2 adds external comparisons and ASR-transcribed speech evaluation, exposing two-stream weaknesses, and provides a Moshi turn-taking comparison and specific limitations. These substantially strengthen empirical assessment. Single-turn scoring narrows dialogue evaluation, the chunk-size analysis is lost, and the leakage attribution is unsupported, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the improved scrutiny of the proposed system.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OmniFlatten and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and Appendix A. The retained method and reorganized material can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: Section 4 and Tables 1–4 report original OmniFlatten results, including bilingual text and speech evaluations and results for the two-stream model.

before.justification: Section 4 and Tables 1–3 report original ASR, TTS, dialogue-quality, training-ablation, and turn-taking results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Improving the mathematical reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) is critical for advancing artificial intelligence. However, access to extensive, diverse, and high-quality reasoning datasets remains a significant challenge, particularly for the open-source community. In this paper, we propose ScaleQuest, a novel, scalable, and cost-effective data synthesis method that enables the generation of large-scale mathematical reasoning datasets using lightweight 7B-scale models. ScaleQuest introduces a two-stage question-tuning process comprising Question Fine-Tuning (QFT) and Question Preference Optimization (QPO) to unlock the question generation capabilities of problem-solving models. By generating diverse questions from scratch -- without relying on powerful proprietary models or seed data -- we produce a dataset of 1 million problem-solution pairs. Our experiments demonstrate that models trained on our data outperform existing open-source datasets in both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations. Furthermore, our approach shows continued performance improvement as the volume of training data increases, highlighting its potential for ongoing data scaling. The extensive improvements observed in code reasoning tasks demonstrate the generalization capabilities of our proposed method. Our work provides the open-source community with a practical solution to enhance the mathematical reasoning abilities of LLMs.

C1.justification: The central low-cost, scalable synthesis contribution remains, but v2 adds demonstrated code generalization to the abstract and long-CoT applicability to the introduction. It also removes the abstract/conclusion claims of surpassing GPT-4-Turbo, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, and all competitors in the 7B–70B range, substantially narrowing those headline comparisons.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds substantive model-selection guidance distinguishing domain-specific generators from general-purpose preference-data optimizers. The human evaluation introduces a qualified comparison with human-curated questions, and Section 3.2 acknowledges unmatched training volumes. The limitations now emphasize uncertain effectiveness with larger models and insufficient generation quality, replacing much of v1's expansion and self-improvement agenda.

D1.justification: v2 documents model choices, sampling amounts, and the code evaluation script for the extensions; most original hyperparameters simply move to Appendix A. It omits the explicit difficulty-head specification and v1's explanation of reevaluating released comparators or retraining unavailable ones. The access pointer changes from a direct repository link to a project page, without establishing a change in actual resource availability.

E1.justification: v2 extends the mathematics-only experiments to CodeFeedback-derived training data and HumanEval, MBPP, and BigCodeBench evaluation. It also adds GSM-Hard numerical shifts, MathChat follow-up questions and error correction, and long-CoT evaluation including AIME24 and AMC25, as labeled in Table 8.

E2.justification: New comparisons include CodeFeedback-Filtered and its response-enhanced CFB-Aug variant in Table 9, and Llama3.1-70B-Instruct as a question optimizer in Figure 4. Conversely, v1 Figure 1's model-ranking comparison, including Claude-3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro, disappears. Table 1's mathematics comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: New protocols include human ratings of 40 examples per dataset on 1–5 scales, approximately 400K-example controlled comparisons, and QPO training-volume experiments spanning 5K–40K examples. For the retained component ablation, v1 specifies GPT-4o-mini as judge, whereas v2 refers to the GPT-4o evaluation in Section 2.3; this is a reported setting revision, without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a 13-gram contamination analysis, human assessment of question quality, QPO data-volume sensitivity, and evaluation of a simplified pipeline. It also tests numerical and conversational robustness and extends the controlled question-quality comparison to three additional backbones. The original component and generator-mixture ablations remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeat counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added evaluations continue to report point estimates; the human-study sample count does not establish repeated-run or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 is unchanged, but Figure 5 revises raw-model GSM8K/MATH/College Math/OlympiadBench scores from 70.9/43.0/35.2/12.3 to 75.9/47.7/38.2/14.6. Substantial new results include teacher versus fine-tuned long-CoT averages of 75.0 versus 81.8, and code averages of 64.0/69.3/69.9 for CFB/CFB-Aug/ScaleQuest. Human, contamination, robustness, and controlled-comparison results are also added.

M1.justification: The core QFT, QPO, question-filtering, and reward-selection pipeline remains unchanged. Appendix D adds ScaleQuest-Simple, using Qwen2-Math-7B-Instruct across stages previously assigned to several models; Appendix C.2 also reports adapting the QPO prompts for code reasoning.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, method and baseline descriptions are condensed, and the related-work discussion and conclusion are substantially shortened. Hyperparameters move into a dedicated appendix, limitations become a separate section, and the appendix structure expands from two sections to six. These are substantial editorial and organizational changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: The paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. Figure 1 drops its model-ranking panel and redesigns the scaling display; Figure 4 gains an optimizer comparison, and several tables are compacted. New evaluation tables and a sensitivity plot are added, while retained prompts and examples receive new typography, colors, and placement.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting code reasoning, DeepSeek-R1, MathChat, RewardBench, and contamination checking, while removing the cited works on reformatted alignment and scaling mathematical reasoning. The central positioning against question-driven and knowledge-driven synthesis remains intact.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1 Equation 3's explicit definition of the linear difficulty-score head, its MSE expression, and variable explanations, retaining only a prose description of the scorer and MSE training. The instruction-tuning and QPO equations remain unchanged, and no new theorem or proof appears.

improvement.justification: The contamination check, additional controlled comparisons, and code-transfer experiments materially strengthen evidence for question quality and generalization, while narrower headline claims improve calibration. Reporting weaknesses remain: human-evaluation prose claims better reasonableness despite Table 5's tie, and Table 12 reports a Mistral OlympiadBench score inconsistent with Table 1. These issues and the continued absence of uncertainty estimates temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial evidential improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ScaleQuest and contain readable main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained content can be matched despite substantial reformatting and appendix expansion.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds human evaluation, contamination analysis, code reasoning, long-chain-of-thought experiments, and further controlled comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training evaluations, component ablations, scaling experiments, and synthetic-data analyses, including Table 1 and Figure 5.

arxiv_record.abstract: Speech translation for Indian languages remains a challenging task due to the scarcity of large-scale, publicly available datasets that capture the linguistic diversity and domain coverage essential for real-world applications. Existing datasets cover a fraction of Indian languages and lack the breadth needed to train robust models that generalize beyond curated benchmarks. To bridge this gap, we introduce BhasaAnuvaad, the largest speech translation dataset for Indian languages, spanning over 44 thousand hours of audio and 17 million aligned text segments across 14 Indian languages and English. Our dataset is built through a threefold methodology: (a) aggregating high-quality existing sources, (b) large-scale web crawling to ensure linguistic and domain diversity, and (c) creating synthetic data to model real-world speech disfluencies. Leveraging BhasaAnuvaad, we train IndicSeamless, a state-of-the-art speech translation model for Indian languages that performs better than existing models. Our experiments demonstrate improvements in the translation quality, setting a new standard for Indian language speech translation. We will release all the code, data and model weights in the open-source, with permissive licenses to promote accessibility and collaboration.

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on the dataset, spontaneous-speech benchmark, and shortcomings of existing systems. v3 elevates ST-Aligner and the trained IndicSeamless model to main contributions and claims state-of-the-art performance and competitiveness with strong cascaded systems. The approximately 44,000-hour dataset claim remains substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: Interpretation shifts from cascaded-system advantages and spontaneous-speech failures toward the benefits of fine-tuned direct models. Section 7 adds concrete missing-domain limitations, while Appendix D discusses SONAR's low-resource weaknesses and recommends language-specific filtering thresholds. v1's explicit synthetic-benchmark bias and pending human-verification caveats disappear with that benchmark.

D1.justification: v3 documents training hardware, batch size, optimizer, learning rate, warmup, and early stopping, and supplies punctuation and translation prompt templates in Appendices B–C. It also expands the promised releases to model weights and permissive licensing. These substantially extend v1's implementation and reproducibility information.

E1.justification: FLEURS evaluation is retained, but the dedicated IndicVoices-dev/Svarah spontaneous-speech benchmark is replaced by a holdout sampled from BhasaAnuvaad's collected sources. This changes the represented evaluation scenarios. v3 also incorporates FLEURS training data and uses the assembled corpus for model training.

E2.justification: v3 adds Azure to the reported AST comparisons and removes direct Whisper, IndicWhisper+IndicTrans2, and IndicConformer+Seamless from the main chrF++ comparison. The earlier S+IT2 cascade remains under the SC+IT2 label. New qualitative checks also compare Llama with IndicTrans2 and indic-punct.

E3.justification: v3 introduces training/holdout construction using mining scores of at least 0.6 and alignment scores of at least 0.8, a 430,000-step fine-tuning experiment, and additional BLEU and COMET-family evaluation. The exact holdout size is inconsistent: Section 4.1.1 specifies approximately 20 minutes per language and direction, whereas Appendix A and Table A3 report 26.22 and 28.18 hours in total.

E4.justification: v3 adds comparisons of mining-score distributions against SeamlessAlign, extensive language-specific analyses, human checks of synthetic translations, and a punctuation-restoration comparison (Sections 3.2–3.4; Figures 3 and A4–A8). The earlier dedicated read-versus-spontaneous evaluation and accent-related error analysis are not retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new human-rating mean and mining-score histograms do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds IndicSeamless, Azure, BLEU, and COMET-family results and replaces the earlier spontaneous-benchmark results. On retained FLEURS evaluation, IndicSeamless scores 54.36 chrF++ for Indic-to-English and 49.46 for English-to-Indic, versus retained Seamless baselines of 47.20 and 48.10 (Tables 1–2). BhasaAnuvaad-Test scores cannot be interpreted as gains over v1's different spontaneous benchmark.

M1.justification: v3 introduces IndicSeamless, obtained by fine-tuning SeamlessM4T-v2-large on filtered BhasaAnuvaad data; v1 deferred corpus-trained modeling to future work. Punctuation restoration also changes from DeepMultilingualPunctuation to Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct. The ST-Aligner name largely rebrands the existing alignment pipeline rather than establishing an entirely new procedure.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around dataset construction and a trained model. Dataset construction moves ahead of experiments, related work is condensed, and dedicated limitations, ethics, and appendix sections are introduced. This materially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the construction pipeline, removes the aggregate radar chart, updates and relocates directional radar plots, and splits the main results into colored heatmap tables. Corpus tables move into the appendix, which also adds metric tables, prompt figures, and extensive mining-score histograms.

R1.justification: The core cascaded/end-to-end and low-resource literature framing is retained. v3 adds references concerning speech foundation models, GigaST, indic-punct, IndicMT evaluation, and XCOMET, while removing the IWSLT discussion and references associated with the former spontaneous benchmark.

T1.justification: Neither version presents substantive formal theory, theorems, or proofs. Cosine similarity and Levenshtein-based scoring already appear in v1; v3's filtering thresholds are operational settings rather than new mathematical results.

improvement.justification: v3 closes an important gap explicitly deferred in v1: testing the corpus's value for training a translation model. Results on retained FLEURS evaluation, together with new data-quality checks and training/prompt documentation, substantially strengthen the empirical support and reproducibility. Material weaknesses remain: the dedicated spontaneous benchmark is lost, holdout-duration descriptions conflict, and the claimed FLEURS gain of over seven points overgeneralizes the much smaller English-to-Indic gain. These qualify, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BhasaAnuvaad and share substantial corpus-construction content. The text, tables, figures, and v3 Appendices A–D support comparison; v1 has no separate appendix. Internal reporting inconsistencies qualify specific judgments but do not prevent comparison.

after.justification: Sections 3–5 and the appendix report original fine-tuning results, baseline evaluations, human translation-quality assessments, and mining-score analyses.

before.justification: Section 4 and Table 2 report original evaluations of speech-translation systems on FLEURS and Indic-Spontaneous-Synth.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Generating long sequences of tokens given a long-context input is a very
compute-intensive inference scenario for large language models (LLMs). One
prominent inference speed-up approach is to construct a smaller key-value (KV)
cache, relieving LLMs from computing attention over a long sequence of tokens.
While such methods work well to generate short sequences, their performance
degrades rapidly for long-form generation. Most KV compression happens once,
prematurely removing tokens that can be useful later in the generation. We
propose a new inference method, RefreshKV, that flexibly alternates between
full context attention and attention over a subset of input tokens during
generation. After each full attention step, we update the smaller KV cache
based on the attention pattern over the entire input. Applying our method to
off-the-shelf LLMs achieves comparable speedup to eviction-based methods while
improving performance for various long-form generation tasks. Lastly, we show
that continued pretraining with our inference setting brings further gains in
performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Fangyuan Xu, Tanya Goyal, Eunsol Choi
arxiv_record.title: RefreshKV: Updating Small KV Cache During Long-form Generation

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes broad RULER improvements, including a headline twofold performance claim over earlier baselines. v2 makes identifying eviction failures during long-form generation an explicit contribution, distinguishes short- and long-output behavior, and introduces chain-of-key as a new task. The central cache-refreshing idea remains, but the claimed contribution scope is substantially revised.

C2.justification: The earlier suggestion that refreshing matters is sharpened into the claim that occasional full-cache attention itself contributes little, supported by v2 Table 4. v2 replaces attention-recovery/locality explanations with generation-length and layer-adaptation interpretations and adds discussion of transfer from shorter training contexts. Limitations newly address small-scale, single-domain pretraining and uniform cache sizes, while v1's explicit minimal-speedup warning for very short outputs is dropped.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents SnapKV's observation window, the pooling kernel, threshold-selection grid, dataset statistics, and chain-of-key generation/scoring examples (Appendices A.1, A.4, A.6; Table 6). These substantially expand reproducibility information. Most FlashAttention and training implementation details are retained and relocated; code release remains promised under a renamed repository.

E1.justification: v2 adds QMSum, GovReport, NovelSumm, HTML-to-TSV, the new chain-of-key task, and four additional LongProc tasks in Appendix A.7. RedPajama and RULER remain, while PG19 is removed. Coverage expands substantially into summarization, procedural generation, and retrieval conditioned on earlier outputs.

E2.justification: SnapKV newly participates in the retained language-modeling and RULER comparisons, while StreamingLLM++ disappears from those comparisons. Continued-pretraining comparisons also add H2O and SnapKV and remove StreamingLLM++ (v1 Table 6; v2 Table 5), substantially revising the comparator set.

E3.justification: Main results switch from fixed scheduling to dynamic QC strides of 5/10. The earlier dynamic experiment's Llama threshold changes from 0.8 to 0.85, with 0.95 used for Qwen following held-out tuning. v2 also removes 64K RULER evaluation, adds 16K continued-pretraining evaluation and 70B/72B chain-of-key models, and introduces ROUGE-L, row-level F1, and chain-validity evaluation protocols.

E4.justification: v2 adds complementary controls without cache refreshing or without full-cache attention, perplexity-versus-generation-position analysis, threshold sensitivity, and per-layer effective-stride analysis. Existing dynamic-scheduling and GQA aggregation ablations are expanded. v1's attention-recovery plots, local-versus-distant token analysis, and cache-size/stride trade-off sweeps are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report point-estimate tables and shaded diagnostic plots without specifying how the bands are estimated. Neither specifies repeated-run or seed counts, confidence levels, or significance tests. Different sample counts for the replaced diagnostics do not establish a change in statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: Results are extensively added and replaced. Llama's 32K RULER accuracy changes from 63 with v1's fixed stride 50 to 86/80 with v2's QC strides 5/10; pooling and scheduling differ, so this is not a same-setting gain. v2 Table 2 newly reports HTML-to-TSV F1 of 17/10 for RefreshKV QC=5 on Llama/Qwen versus 0/0 for SnapKV and H2O. PG19 and 64K RULER result entries disappear.

M1.justification: v2 adds neighborhood max pooling before top-K token selection, whereas v1 selects directly from attention scores (v1 Figure 3; v2 Figure 2). This is a limited algorithm refinement: the two-cache procedure, query-similarity scheduler, and continued-pretraining objective already existed in v1.

P1.justification: The title, terminology, abstract, introduction, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Dynamic scheduling moves from further improvements into the method description, continued pretraining becomes a separate section, and memory, FlashAttention, and detailed RULER material move to appendices.

P2.justification: The document changes from one-column to two-column layout, with a redrawn overview Figure 1, new generation-position and effective-stride plots, and substantially restructured tables. Memory-comparison and detailed RULER tables move to appendices, while the earlier attention-recovery and cache/stride trade-off figures are removed.

R1.justification: v2 substantively positions the method against query-aware eviction through SnapKV and NACL, adds Quest and PyramidKV, and removes TOVA and speculative-decoding discussion. Its relationship to prior work now explicitly centers on refreshing a SnapKV-like cache during generation. New benchmark and summarization references support the revised research scope.

T1.justification: v2 introduces mathematical validity constraints and a normalized valid-chain-length score for chain-of-key evaluation (Section 3 and Appendix A.6). This is a limited definition-level addition. The existing cache-size and computation-cost expressions are retained in Appendix A.2; neither version contains theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 motivates long-form generation but mainly evaluates short RULER answers and next-token perplexity. v2's long-output evaluations, stronger SnapKV comparisons, and complementary cache-refresh ablations substantially improve the relevance and explanatory strength of the evidence. These gains outweigh the removal of PG19 and attention-recovery analyses, although reporting needs correction: Table 3 claims fewer full-attention steps despite showing shorter Qwen dynamic strides.

A1.justification: These are versions of the same work, renamed from Recycled Attention to RefreshKV. Both PDFs provide readable main text, figures, tables, pseudocode, and appendices sufficient for reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original language-modeling, RULER, summarization, HTML-to-TSV, chain-of-key, additional LongProc, ablation, and continued-pretraining results.

before.justification: v1 reports original RULER accuracies, RedPajama and PG19 perplexities, inference timings, ablations, and continued-pretraining results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Developing robust automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems for Arabic requires effective strategies to manage its diversity. Existing ASR systems mainly cover the modern standard Arabic (MSA) variety and few high-resource dialects, but fall short in coverage and generalization across the multitude of spoken variants. Code-switching with English and French is also common in different regions of the Arab world, which challenges the performance of monolingual Arabic models. In this work, we introduce a suite of ASR models optimized to effectively recognize multiple variants of spoken Arabic, including MSA, various dialects, and code-switching. We provide open-source pre-trained models that cover data from 17 Arabic-speaking countries, and fine-tuned MSA and dialectal ASR models that include at least 11 variants, as well as multi-lingual ASR models covering embedded languages in code-switched utterances. We evaluate ASR performance across these spoken varieties and demonstrate both coverage and performance gains compared to prior models.
arxiv_record.authors: Amirbek Djanibekov, Hawau Olamide Toyin, Raghad Alshalan, Abdullah Alitr, Hanan Aldarmaki
arxiv_record.title: Dialectal Coverage And Generalization in Arabic Speech Recognition

program_record.Abstract: Developing robust automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems for Arabic requires effective strategies to manage its diversity. Existing ASR systems mainly cover the modern standard Arabic (MSA) variety and few high-resource dialects, but fall short in coverage and generalization across the multitude of spoken variants. Code-switching with English and French is also common in different regions of the Arab world, which challenges the performance of monolingual Arabic models. In this work, we introduce a suite of ASR models optimized to effectively recognize multiple variants of spoken Arabic, including MSA, various dialects, and code-switching. We provide open-source pre-trained models that cover data from 17 Arabic-speaking countries, and fine-tuned MSA and dialectal ASR models that include at least 11 variants, as well as multi-lingual ASR models covering embedded languages in code-switched utterances. We evaluate ASR performance across these spoken varieties and demonstrate both coverage and performance gains compared to prior models.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes dialectal pretraining, joint versus individual fine-tuning, and unseen-dialect generalization. v3 expands the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to claim multilingual code-switching capability, improved code-switching recognition, and a corresponding cost to monolingual performance. The contribution now explicitly includes dialectal and multilingual model releases.

C2.justification: v1 identifies limited code-switching recognition and unexplored multilingual/multidialectal training as limitations. v3 replaces that open question with an interpretation of measured tradeoffs: code-switching benefits, modest MSA degradation, and 4–16 percentage-point WER increases for some dialects, attributed to language interference. Existing limitations concerning coarse dialect labels and transcription variability remain.

D1.justification: v3 supplies multilingual dataset inventories and quantities, estimates approximately 6,000 GPU-hours overall, and reports 14–21 days of pretraining per model instead of the earlier single 21-day description. It also expands the stated checkpoint and reproduction-script availability. Both versions already provide code links, optimizer settings, hardware, and normalization information.

E1.justification: v3 adds deliberate multilingual training using English, French, and Spanish CommonVoice data, and evaluates Egyptian-English ArzEn and Tunisian-French TunSwitch alongside the existing Emirati-English Mixat dataset. Tables 10 and 12 document substantially broader language and code-switching coverage.

E2.justification: v1 Table 6 reports Whisper and MMS comparisons on Mixat; that row disappears from v3 Table 5, while the new Mixat comparison in Table 11 contains ArTST variants. Comparator membership in the retained MGB benchmarks and other dialect comparisons is otherwise unchanged.

E3.justification: The new code-switching experiments compare direct target fine-tuning with initialization from different adapted checkpoints: MGB2 for ArTST v1, joint dialectal training for v2, and joint multilingual training for v3. v3 also adds multilingual-versus-dialectal evaluation on Arabic-only data. These are substantial additional experimental designs; the original splits, normalization, and basic evaluation metrics remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds explicit language-interference analysis on MSA and individual dialects, plus code-switching output comparisons across checkpoints and adaptation strategies. It removes v1 Figures 5–6, which illustrated zero-shot adaptation and held-out-dialect outputs. The original cross-dialect numerical analysis is retained in Appendix C.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates, or statistical significance tests. v3's use of 'significant' for performance differences does not introduce statistical testing.

E6.justification: New Table 11 reports adapted multilingual-model WERs of 27.43%, 36.66%, and 21.66% on ArzEn, TunSwitch, and Mixat. The retained adaptation table also changes values: MGB3 after MGB2 adaptation changes from 29.39 to 25.28, and Mixat after QASR adaptation from 27.73 to 35.21. Joint-dialect and cross-dialect matrices remain numerically unchanged. These are new results and reported revisions, without establishing same-setting rerun gains.

M1.justification: Both retain the SpeechT5/ArTST architecture, self-supervised pretraining, staged fine-tuning, and dialect-ID forcing/inference procedures. The new multilingual ArTST v3 variant is distinguished by its training data; no new architecture, loss, or decoding algorithm is documented.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of related work, methodology, and conclusions are rewritten around broader coverage. Methodology separates dialectal and multilingual fine-tuning, a code-switching section is introduced, and the cross-dialect discussion moves into a reorganized three-part appendix.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn with axes, gridlines, and revised labeling. v3 adds multilingual data/results tables and an interference plot, replaces two earlier qualitative figures with code-switching examples, expands and relocates the pretraining table, and moves the cross-dialect matrix to Appendix C. These substantially revise the exhibit organization.

R1.justification: Related work adds focused context on MSA-dominated research, distilled Arabic models, and code-switching, including Dhouib et al. (2022), Waheed et al. (2024), and Kadaoui et al. (2024), plus new dataset references. The central positioning around Arabic-specialized ArTST versus multilingual speech models remains.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The dialect-prefixed decoding sequence and underlying conceptual framework are retained.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses an important gap explicitly acknowledged in v1: multilingual/code-switching training was unexplored. Section 8, Table 11, Figure 4, and appendix examples provide evidence across three code-switching datasets while exposing the cost to Arabic-only recognition, substantially improving the paper's account of coverage/performance tradeoffs. Reporting remains imperfect: a new sentence in Section 5.1 incorrectly says dialect forcing gives the lowest average WER, contradicting Table 7. arxiv_record.abstract: Podcasts provide highly diverse content to a massive listener base through a unique on-demand modality. However, limited data has prevented large-scale computational analysis of the podcast ecosystem. To fill this gap, we introduce a massive dataset of over 1.1M podcast transcripts that is largely comprehensive of all English language podcasts available through public RSS feeds from May and June of 2020. This data is not limited to text, but rather includes audio features and speaker turns for a subset of 370K episodes, and speaker role inferences and other metadata for all 1.1M episodes. Using this data, we also conduct a foundational investigation into the content, structure, and responsiveness of this ecosystem. Together, our data and analyses open the door to continued computational research of this popular and impactful medium.

arxiv_record.title: Mapping the Podcast Ecosystem with the Structured Podcast Research Corpus

C1.justification: The introduction qualifies the novelty claim from the first large-scale podcast dataset to the first large-scale open dataset providing a nearly comprehensive public snapshot, and presents the analyses as preliminary. The principal corpus contribution and structural and temporal findings remain.

C2.justification: Appendices A–B add substantive explanations of why edited reference transcripts inflate apparent WER, why manual estimates can be optimistic, and why proper names, Spanish speech, and many-speaker episodes cause errors. They also explicitly limit generalization beyond the six sampled shows, substantially expanding v1's general processing caveats.

D1.justification: v2 adds a Hugging Face dataset access link and reproducibility details for validation, including transcript cleanup, spaCy/NLTK alignment, manual adjudication rules, and speaker matching. Existing corpus-processing budgets, hardware, classifier hyperparameters, and release formats remain documented as before.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the May–June 2020 English-podcast corpus, its 370K-episode diarized subset, and the same substantive tasks. The new reference-transcript sample evaluates transcription and diarization within that retained podcast coverage; its sampling and reference annotations change validation design rather than establish a new domain or task.

E2.justification: No evaluated comparison method is added or removed. v2 uses professional transcripts as references and quotes Whisper-paper results, including Whisper Large V2 results on other datasets; these are not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Appendices A–B add automated validation on six episodes from each of six shows, manual checks of the first five content minutes of 18 episodes, and token-level evaluation of unfiltered diarization output. They specify alignment, speaker matching, and error-counting procedures. The reported transcription model also changes from whisper-base to whisper-base.en, without establishing that the corpus was reprocessed.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial error analysis beyond v1's brief manual checks: adjudication of reference-transcript disagreements, analysis of substitution and omission errors, estimates excluding a Spanish-heavy episode, and examination of diarization failures in episodes with many speakers. The pitch analysis is retained and relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: The existing 95% confidence-interval reporting is retained. New Figures 4–6 display episode-level errors and show averages, with vertical bars explicitly denoting means; they introduce no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds transcription WER results, including 3.0% from manual review and 2.4% after excluding the Spanish-heavy episode, plus diarization error of 1.8% excluding This American Life and 2.1% for interviews. These are newly reported validation results, not improvements over comparable v1 measurements. Tables 1–3 and the 0.87/0.88 role-classification accuracies are retained.

M1.justification: The Whisper, openSMILE, pyannote, and RoBERTa pipeline, filtering rules, and topic/network methods are retained. The single-host restriction clarified in v2 was already stated in v1's limitations. The revised Whisper model designation is a reported configuration change, without evidence of a redesigned procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction is substantially rewritten, and Section 4 reorganizes its research questions and consistently distinguishes topical from networked communities. Explanations throughout the methods are revised, and the pitch discussion moves into a dedicated Speech Characteristics appendix. These constitute substantial narrative revision despite retaining the overall main-section sequence.

P2.justification: v2 adds three validation plots, recolors the collective-attention plots and adjusts their legends, and expands the network caption. Existing appendix figures are relocated and renumbered. The principal visualizations, table structures, and two-column layout are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly discusses the Popular Political Podcasts Dataset and positions its network analysis against DeMets and Spiro (2025). It adds several references on podcast definitions, listening, and education while removing some introductory citations. Most research positioning remains intact; the Baldini-to-Bonini correction concerns the same cited work.

T1.justification: The name-probability independence assumption, modularity equation, and binary category partitions are unchanged after appendix renumbering. The added error-scoring procedures concern empirical evaluation; no new theoretical claims, proofs, or mathematical derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: For a corpus paper, transcription and speaker-label reliability are central. v1 supported these components mainly through qualitative inspection; v2 adds quantitative reference-based validation, manual error analysis, and documented failure conditions in Appendices A–B. This substantially strengthens the evidence for using the dataset. The selected six-show sample and acknowledged scoring limitations still prevent treating these estimates as corpus-wide guarantees.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SPORC corpus and podcast analyses. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds reference-based transcription and diarization evaluations and manual transcription-error analysis in Appendices A–B.

before.justification: v1 reports original speaker-role classification results, topic and guest-network analyses, and temporal analysis of discussion following George Floyd's murder.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Speculative decoding (SD) has been demonstrated as an effective technique for
lossless LLM inference acceleration. Retrieval-based SD methods, one kind of
model-free method, have yielded promising speedup, but they often rely on
incomplete retrieval resources, inefficient retrieval methods, and are
constrained to certain domains. This paper presents a novel retrieval-based
speculative decoding method that adapts suffix automaton (SAM) for efficient
and accurate draft generation by utilizing common text corpus and dynamic text
sequence. Unlike existing $n$-gram matching methods, SAM-Decoding finds the
exact longest suffix match, achieving an average time complexity of O(1) per
generation step of SAM update and suffix retrieval. It can also integrate with
existing methods, adaptively selecting a draft generation strategy based on
match length to generalize to broader domains. Extensive experiments on
Spec-Bench show that our method is $18\%+$ faster than other retrieval-based SD
methods. Additionally, when combined with advanced EAGLE-2, it provides an
additional speedup of $3.28\%$ -- $11.13\%$ across various-sized LLM backbones.
Our code is available at our
\href{https://github.com/hyx1999/SAM-Decoding}{repository}.

Yuxuan Hu, Ke Wang, Xiaokang Zhang, Fanjin Zhang, Cuiping Li, Hong
  Chen, Jing Zhang
