program_record.Abstract:
Speculative decoding (SD) has been demonstrated as an effective technique for lossless LLM inference acceleration.
Retrieval-based SD methods, one kind of model-free method, have yielded promising speedup, but they often rely on single retrieval resources, inefficient retrieval methods, and are constrained to certain tasks. This paper presents a novel retrieval-based speculative decoding method that adapts the suffix automaton (SAM) for efficient and accurate draft generation by utilizing the generating text sequence and static text corpus. Unlike existing $n$-gram matching methods, SAM-Decoding finds the exact longest suffix match, achieving an average time complexity of O(1) per generation step of SAM update and suffix retrieval.
It can also integrate with existing methods, adaptively selecting a draft generation strategy based on match length to generalize to broader domains. Extensive experiments on Spec-Bench show that our method is $18$\% faster than other retrieval-based SD methods. Additionally, when combined with advanced EAGLE-2, it provides an additional speedup of $3.28$\% -- $11.13$\% across various-sized LLM backbones.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are known to be vulnerable to backdoor attacks,
where triggers embedded in poisoned samples can maliciously alter LLMs'
behaviors. In this paper, we move beyond attacking LLMs and instead examine
backdoor attacks through the novel lens of natural language explanations.
Specifically, we leverage LLMs' generative capabilities to produce
human-readable explanations for their decisions, enabling direct comparisons
between explanations for clean and poisoned samples. Our results show that
backdoored models produce coherent explanations for clean inputs but diverse
and logically flawed explanations for poisoned data, a pattern consistent
across classification and generation tasks for different backdoor attacks.
Further analysis reveals key insights into the explanation generation process.
At the token level, explanation tokens associated with poisoned samples only
appear in the final few transformer layers. At the sentence level, attention
dynamics indicate that poisoned inputs shift attention away from the original
input context during explanation generation. These findings enhance our
understanding of backdoor mechanisms in LLMs and present a promising framework
for detecting vulnerabilities through explainability.
arxiv_record.authors: Huaizhi Ge, Yiming Li, Qifan Wang, Yongfeng Zhang, Ruixiang Tang

  Model-Generated Explanations

C1.justification: A central headline finding reverses. V1's abstract, introduction, and Section 3.4 claim that poisoned-input explanations are more consistent; v3's abstract, introduction, and Section 4 describe them as more diverse and less consistent. The principal claims about delayed token emergence and reduced attention to input context remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretations of the new controls and transfer studies: trigger presence alone has relatively little effect on clean-model explanations, and detector transfer is attributed to recognizing irrational explanations rather than attack-specific overfitting. Appendix J proposes an explanation for poison-rate effects on clean-input scores. The limitations replace the earlier trigger/model restrictions with a new qualification about excluding self-explaining rationalization techniques.

D1.justification: V3 discloses complete quality-assessment and detector prompts, human-rating criteria, additional training settings, and generation-ASR assessment details. Appendix A.2 adds A100 hardware information and approximate training, explanation-generation, and lens-computation times. These substantially improve documentation, although v1's explicit QLoRA training disclosure is removed and detector training/test splits remain unspecified.

E1.justification: V3 adds syntactic-trigger evaluation on SST-2, sentence-trigger evaluation on Twitter Emotion, and an actual poisoned-input detection task with cross-dataset and cross-trigger transfer tests. V1's flip-token scenario disappears. Sentiment classification and jailbreak generation remain covered; the PDFs do not establish whether renaming the generation dataset from BadNets to AdvBench represents different underlying data.

E2.justification: V3 Table 4 introduces a comparison among GPT-4o, logistic regression, SVM, decision tree, and random-forest detectors. V1 has no corresponding evaluated detector comparison. This adds a substantial set of comparison methods.

E3.justification: The LLaMA 2-13B configuration is removed, and DeepSeek-7B is introduced with its own training settings. V3 changes the token-level metric from MPC to MED and introduces human-rating, five-shot detection, and classifier evaluation protocols. Quality assessment changes from a stated 20-example GPT-4 subset to GPT-4o scoring of generated explanations. The reported generation-training mix also changes from 150 clean/200 poisoned samples to 200 clean/150 poisoned samples.

E4.justification: V3 adds independent human validation of explanation quality, a non-backdoored-model control, a 2% versus 9% poison-rate study, and detector transfer across datasets and triggers (Appendices B, D, J, and K). New aggregate layerwise and tokenwise plots supplement the retained example trajectories and attention analyses. These substantially expand validation and robustness analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions generate five explanation variants per input and report t-tests for clean-versus-poisoned differences. V3 extends this practice to additional results but introduces no new confidence intervals, error bars, significance-testing procedure, training-run counts, or seed reporting. The human assessments do not report inter-rater uncertainty.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive quality, control, human-assessment, robustness, and detector results; Table 4 reports 97.5% accuracy for GPT-4o and 98.8% for logistic regression. It corrects the reported consistency finding to favor clean explanations. Table 1 changes SST-2 word-trigger ASR from 98% to 95%, although v3 Appendix A.1 still states 98%. Generation results are replaced under a changed reported training mix, so they do not establish a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: V1 leaves explanation-based detection as future work. V3 Section 6 introduces operational detection procedures: five-shot GPT-4o classification of explanation texts and supervised classifiers using layerwise maximum-token probabilities. These extend the retained explanation-analysis framework with a substantial new inference component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, explanation analysis, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. V3 organizes the introduction around two research questions, separates explanation analysis into its own section, and presents the internal-generation analysis through four explicit findings. The limitations and appendix organization are also substantially revised.

P2.justification: V3 redraws the workflow in Figure 2, adds quality and aggregate trajectory plots, introduces numerous structured evaluation tables, and displays complete prompts in boxed figures. Table 1 becomes a compact performance table, and explanation examples are reformatted. Several earlier heatmaps and prediction trajectories are retained with changed placement and numbering.

R1.justification: V3 adds literature on natural-language explanation uncertainty and self-rationalization, including Bills et al., Tanneru et al., and Liu et al., plus references for newly named models and data. It removes the mechanistic-circuit discussion and associated references. The central positioning of using LLM-generated explanations to investigate backdoors remains.

T1.justification: Equation 3 changes mathematically: v1's MPC averages token probabilities, whereas v3's MED averages layer-index-weighted probabilities. Appendix A.2 also adds asymptotic computational-cost estimates. The other lens, attention, and similarity definitions remain essentially unchanged; renaming lookback ratio as contextual reliance does not change its formula. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V3 corrects v1's central consistency claim, bringing it into agreement with the earlier similarity plot and stated tests. Human assessments, clean-model controls, syntactic-trigger and poison-rate tests substantially strengthen the explanation-quality evidence, while evaluated detectors replace a speculative application. Full prompts and resource details also improve reproducibility. Important reporting problems remain: attack scores disagree between tables and Appendix A.1, and the new MED formula is not reconciled with Figure 7's plotted scale. These limit confidence in particular quantitative claims, but the gains in validation and clarity constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of backdoored LLMs through model-generated explanations. All 14 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v3, including their appendices, equations, tables, and figures, support comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical analyses and adds human assessments, clean-model controls, poison-rate experiments, and evaluated backdoor detectors.

before.justification: V1 reports original backdoor experiments, explanation-quality scores, similarity tests, and analyses of prediction trajectories and attention.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deliver impressive results but face challenges from increasing model sizes and computational costs. Structured pruning reduces model size and speeds up inference but often causes uneven degradation across domains, leading to biased performance. To address this, we propose DRPruning, a method that dynamically adjusts the data distribution during training to restore balanced performance across heterogeneous and multi-tasking data. Experiments in monolingual and multilingual settings show that DRPruning surpasses similarly sized models in both pruning and continued pretraining over perplexity, downstream tasks, and instruction tuning. Further analysis demonstrates the robustness of DRPruning towards various domains and distribution shifts. Furthermore, DRPruning can determine optimal reference losses and data ratios automatically, suggesting potential for broader applications. Code and scripts are available at https://github.com/hexuandeng/DRPruning.
arxiv_record.authors: Hexuan Deng, Wenxiang Jiao, Xuebo Liu, Jing Li, Min Zhang, Zhaopeng Tu
arxiv_record.title: DRPruning: Efficient Large Language Model Pruning through Distributionally Robust Optimization

Structured pruning reduces model size and speeds up inference but often causes uneven degradation across domains, leading to biased performance. To address this, we propose DRPruning, a method that dynamically adjusts the data distribution during training to restore balanced performance across heterogeneous and multi-tasking data. Experiments in monolingual and multilingual settings show that DRPruning surpasses similarly sized models in both pruning and continued pretraining over perplexity, downstream tasks, and instruction tuning. Further analysis demonstrates the robustness of DRPruning towards various domains and distribution shifts. Furthermore, DRPruning can determine optimal reference losses and data ratios automatically, suggesting potential for broader applications. Code and scripts are available at https://github.com/hexuandeng/DRPruning.

C1.justification: The introduction refocuses its headline superiority claim from Sheared Llama and other LLMs to data-scheduling methods. The principal claims about balanced pruning, distribution robustness, and broader applicability remain, so this is a limited change in claimed comparison scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds a specific failure boundary at 0.5B, interprets finer partitioning as increasing the difficulty of fixed hyperparameter selection, and explains translation distribution collapse through excessive sampling of small domains. It also clarifies the unfavorable comparison with public 2.7B Sheared Llama and updates the remaining applicability limitations.

D1.justification: V2 supplies the five evaluation prompts per task, CPU overhead and parallel-update details, four-A800 hardware information, the 0.5B architecture, MiniLM/k-means domain partitioning, validation/test sample counts, and translation sampling and training settings. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond the retained Appendix A.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original coverage and adds machine-translation instruction tuning using News-Commentary training data and FLORES-200 validation/test sets across 14 directions, including German, Indonesian, and Hindi (B.6). This substantially extends task coverage. The finer CC/C4 partitions in B.5 reuse existing data.

E2.justification: Corresponding retained experiments preserve their comparator sets, including Sheared Llama/ReSheared, Pythia, Constant, naive DRO, and the multilingual reference models. New experiments reuse ReSheared or compare DRPruning variants; they introduce no new baseline algorithm.

E3.justification: V2 adds five-prompt evaluation, a 0.5B target with 24k continued-pretraining steps, 1600-step coarse/fine domain comparisons, and 2k-step translation instruction tuning evaluated with BLEU. These introduce substantial new protocols; the original training budgets and evaluation settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices B.3-B.6 add prompt-sensitivity tests, parallel-update efficiency checks and extreme-compression analysis, coarse-versus-fine domain segmentation experiments, and translation data-allocation analysis. The original mask-similarity and larger-source-model analyses remain. Section 5.4 mainly relocates existing hyperparameter analysis.

E5.justification: Beyond the retained mask-similarity SEM reporting, v2 adds paired t-tests for downstream performance across five prompt variants. Appendix B.3 reports p-values of 0.0458 for 1.3B, 0.0312 for 2.7B, and 0.0032 combined. These concern prompt variation; additional independent training runs are not established.

E6.justification: Matched original result tables retain their numerical entries. New tables add prompt-level scores, runtime measurements, domain cross-entropies, and translation outcomes. For example, Table 19 reports average BLEU of 20.4 for DRPruning versus 18.0 for ReSheared, alongside an EN-HI disadvantage of 1.5 versus 5.6.

M1.justification: The core pruning procedure, DRO objective, scaling-law reference losses, and reference-ratio updates remain unchanged. Appendix B.4 introduces parallel data-ratio computation with a one- to two-step update delay, a limited procedural adaptation.

P1.justification: V2 extensively edits the abstract, introduction, and methodological and experimental exposition. It moves the workflow summary to the start of Section 3, reorganizes existing hyperparameter analysis into Section 5.4, and moves the multilingual data description into Appendix A.2. These changes substantially reshape presentation beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adds multi-prompt comparison tables, a full prompt-template table, and efficiency, domain, and translation tables (13-20). It also redraws the sentence-generation workflow, resizes and relocates retained displays, changes highlighting and captions, and moves the former Figure 5 to Figure 6 without adding a new analysis there.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting the new work, including ParroT, FLORES, WMT23, MiniLM, and DeepSeek-R1, plus several introductory citations. It removes references including Bang et al., Duchi et al., and Levy et al. The central positioning around structured pruning, Sheared Llama, and DRO remains.

T1.justification: Equations 1-6 retain the same pruning constraints, DRO formulation, scaling-law model, distribution constraint, and reference-ratio update. V2 introduces no new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through direct tests of prompt sensitivity, scheduling overhead, domain granularity, and scheduler use during translation instruction tuning (B.3-B.6). It also documents extreme-compression failure and supplies detailed reproduction settings. These address important evidential gaps in v1's robustness, efficiency, and broader-applicability arguments. The original scores remain unchanged, and prompt-based significance tests still do not establish robustness across independent training runs.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DRPruning. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained methods, experiments, equations, and displays can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds prompt-robustness, efficiency, domain-granularity, and translation instruction-tuning experiments in Appendices B.3-B.6.

before.justification: V1 reports original pruning, continued-pretraining, instruction-tuning, multilingual, and domain-level experiments, plus mask-similarity and model-size analyses in Appendix B.

arxiv_record.abstract: Tokenization methods like Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) enhance computational efficiency in large language models (LLMs) but often obscure internal character structures within tokens. This limitation hinders LLMs' ability to predict precise character positions, which is crucial in tasks like Chinese Spelling Correction (CSC) where identifying the positions of misspelled characters accelerates correction processes. We propose Token Internal Position Awareness (TIPA), a method that significantly improves models' ability to capture character positions within tokens by training them on reverse character prediction tasks using the tokenizer's vocabulary. Experiments demonstrate that TIPA enhances position prediction accuracy in LLMs, enabling more precise identification of target characters in original text. Furthermore, when applied to downstream tasks that do not require exact position prediction, TIPA still boosts performance in tasks needing character-level information, validating its versatility and effectiveness.

C1.justification: v4 broadens the headline contributions from CSC improvements to multilingual capabilities, general-model performance preservation and full-parameter training, while emphasizing shorter correction outputs. Its conclusion also attributes a 5.64-point F1 gain to traditional CSC, although that gain belongs to the position-aware experiment in Table 4.

C2.justification: v4 replaces the Chinese-only evaluation limitation with a warning that excessive TIPA mixing can bias generation toward shorter outputs. It adds discussion of MTIPA training cost and possible LoRA task interference, qualifies cross-tokenizer comparisons, and interprets the new evaluations as evidence of broader transfer. The OOV limitation remains.

D1.justification: v4 supplies an explicit TIPA prompt, detailed pruning and dataset-mixing procedures, full-parameter hardware/hyperparameters/runtime, and 1.5B resource figures. It newly documents exclusion of unequal-length model outputs and half-/full-width character normalization; these disclosures do not establish changes to the earlier experiments. Construction details for the new character-task datasets remain limited.

E1.justification: v4 retains Wang271K, CSCD-NS and LEMON, and adds Tulu-3 instruction training plus IFEVAL, GSM8K, MMLU, AExams, KoBEST, HumanEval and TyDi QA evaluation. It also introduces multilingual occurrence-counting, length-prediction and distinct-character tasks, substantially broadening coverage beyond Chinese spelling correction.

E2.justification: v4 Table 4 adds DeepSeek v2.5, GLM-4-Plus and ERNIE-4.0 to the position-aware CSC comparison in v1 Table 1. The new general-model experiments also introduce Llama-3.1-Tulu as the comparator for Tulu-TIPA. The original CSC comparators remain.

E3.justification: v4 adds a Llama-3.1-8B full-parameter training protocol with two epochs and batch size 32, and extends CSC evaluation to 1.5B models. New benchmark protocols include zero-shot IFEVAL, eight-shot GSM8K and five-shot MMLU. The previously reported CSC splits and training budgets are retained.

E4.justification: v4 adds an output-token efficiency comparison between traditional and position-based CSC in Table 3, and extends forward/reverse and output-length analyses to 1.5B models. Earlier position-wise analyses, training curves and qualitative examples remain; the loss analysis moves to Appendix A.7.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates or significance tests. The additional v4 tables continue reporting point estimates; averages across languages or domains do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Matched existing CSC scores are unchanged, but v4 adds substantial results for new comparators, 1.5B models, output-token counts and general-model evaluations. Within the new v4 experiment, TULU/TULU-TIPA achieve TyDi QA averages of 47.85/52.81 and distinct-character scores of 9.29/18.74, while HumanEval falls from 53.05 to 51.83.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 adds full-parameter instruction fine-tuning with TIPA and Tulu-3 data alongside the original LoRA-based CSC training. This extends the parameter-update procedure, while the reverse-position targets, optional pruning and TIPA/MTIPA algorithms remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v4 substantially rewrites the abstract, condenses the introduction and related work, and recasts the contributions and conclusion. The narrative expands from two experiments to three, implementation details gain dedicated subsections, and the loss discussion moves from the main analysis to the appendix.

P2.justification: v4 redraws Figures 1-2, restyles existing plots, expands CSC tables and adds explanatory and general-evaluation tables. v1's token-length Table 11 becomes a logarithmic bar chart in v4 Figure 5, while the retained loss plot moves to the appendix as Figure 6.

R1.justification: Related work adds targeted contrasts with ByT5, CANINE and Itzhak and Levy's explicit-spelling study, alongside citations supporting the new models and benchmarks. Some foundational GPT references are removed. These refine the existing positioning around architecture-preserving character-position training.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 rewrites the PPA numerator from a set of correctly matched prediction pairs to a set of equality expressions. The surrounding prose retains the original intended metric, creating a local formal ambiguity. Equations 1-3 and the reverse-position construction remain unchanged, with no new proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially addresses v1's explicit restriction to Chinese CSC through a second model family, full-parameter training, multilingual QA and direct character-task evaluations, supported by better training documentation. This materially strengthens evidence about generality. The new character datasets remain underdocumented, and the conclusion overstates benchmark preservation and misattributes the 5.64-point gain, but these reporting weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TIPA/MTIPA work. All 14 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v4, including Appendix A, are readable, and the retained methods, experiments, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds comparator evaluations, 1.5B-model experiments, and general and multilingual evaluations of a TIPA-trained Llama model.

before.justification: v1 reports original Chinese spelling-correction experiments, forward/reverse training comparisons, training dynamics and output analyses in the main text and appendix.

arxiv_record.abstract: Current language models (LMs) use a fixed, static subword tokenizer. This default choice typically results in degraded efficiency and language capabilities, especially in languages other than English. To address this issue, we challenge the static design and propose retrofitting LMs with dynamic tokenization: a way to dynamically decide on token boundaries based on the input text via a subword-merging algorithm inspired by byte-pair encoding. We merge frequent subword sequences in a batch, then apply a pre-trained embedding-prediction hypernetwork to compute the token embeddings on-the-fly. For encoder-style models (e.g., XLM-R), this on average reduces token sequence lengths by >20% across 14 languages while degrading performance by less than 2%. The same method applied to pre-filling and scoring in decoder-style models (e.g., Mistral-7B) results in minimal performance degradation at up to 17% reduction in sequence length. Overall, we find that dynamic tokenization can mitigate the limitations of static tokenization by substantially improving inference speed and promoting fairness across languages, enabling more equitable and adaptable LMs.
arxiv_record.authors: Darius Feher, Ivan Vuli\'c, Benjamin Minixhofer
arxiv_record.title: Retrofitting Large Language Models with Dynamic Tokenization

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Current language models (LMs) use a fixed, static subword tokenizer. This default choice typically results in degraded efficiency and language capabilities, especially in languages other than English. To address this issue, we challenge the static design and propose retrofitting LMs with dynamic tokenization: a way to dynamically decide on token boundaries based on the input text via a subword-merging algorithm inspired by byte-pair encoding. We merge frequent subword sequences in a batch, then apply a pre-trained embedding-prediction hypernetwork to compute the token embeddings on-the-fly. For encoder-style models (e.g., XLM-R), this on average reduces token sequence lengths by >20% across 14 languages while degrading performance by less than 2%. The same method applied to pre-filling and scoring in decoder-style models (e.g., Mistral-7B) results in minimal performance degradation at up to 17% reduction in sequence length. Overall, we find that dynamic tokenization can mitigate the limitations of static tokenization by substantially improving inference speed and promoting fairness across languages, enabling more equitable and adaptable LMs.

C1.justification: The central retrofitting, efficiency, and cross-lingual fairness claims persist. Decoder headline claims change from up to 40% reduction relative to word-level compression in v1 to 17% absolute reduction for multilingual MMLU and approximately 6% for English MT-Bench in v3. Large-vocabulary generation remains a contribution but receives less emphasis in the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: v3 newly attributes decoder degradation primarily to output embeddings and discusses key-value-cache compression. It adds near-linear FLOPs interpretations and explicit qualifications concerning hypernetwork accuracy, availability, training cost, and overhead. The requirement to know the input sequence and the bounded, static generation vocabulary were already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: v3 adds extensive LoRA hyperparameters, optimizer settings, precision and sequence limits, decoder generation settings, GPU/CUDA information, ScaNN configuration, and hypernetwork access and training-cost information (Appendices B, C, and F). These substantially expand reproducibility documentation. However, v1's footnote identifying the corrected MT-Bench source is omitted.

E1.justification: Decoder knowledge-scoring coverage expands from English MMLU to Global-MMLU-lite in English, French, German, Spanish, and Portuguese. XNLI, UNER, MT-Bench, and the MADLAD-400 vocabulary-training corpus remain. The encoder language-count correction from 15 to 14 does not represent changed coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Figure 4a adds FVT input embeddings with original output embeddings to the decoder-scoring comparison. v1 evaluates FVT in encoder experiments but compares only original and hypernetwork embeddings for decoders. The other embedding, adapter, and ANN-versus-exhaustive comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: The reported five-shot MMLU template removes the topic preamble and context sentences preceding demonstrations (v1 Appendix C versus v3 Figure 5). The added efficiency evaluation introduces per-sample model and hypernetwork FLOPs across eleven compression levels. Newly disclosed training and index settings do not establish changes to retained experiments.

E4.justification: v3 adds systematic analysis of hypernetwork computational overhead relative to compression savings across five languages (Table 4 and Appendix E). It also extends embedding-control analysis to decoder FVT and tokenizer/vocabulary comparisons to English MMLU (Table 9). The fixed-versus-sampled merge and LRU-cache analyses already exist in v1.

E5.justification: v3 Table 5 newly reports Python, PyTorch, and NumPy random seeds for encoder, MMLU, and MT-Bench experiments. This is new seed documentation, not evidence of additional repeated runs. Neither version reports confidence intervals, multi-seed variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v3 reports new five-language MMLU curves, English MMLU vocabulary-expansion results, and FLOPs estimates. Table 9 reports 55.9% accuracy with 13.6% shorter prompts for the 1M vocabulary. Matched XNLI, UNER, and MT-Bench table rows remain numerically identical. The changed MMLU coverage prevents interpreting its replacement curves as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Batch-level BPE-style merging, pretrained hypernetwork embeddings, fixed or sampled merge-count adapters, and longest-prefix tokenization with ANN retrieval remain unchanged. The vocabulary-expansion method moves from v1 Section 3.3 to v3 Appendix C; expanded training and scoring explanations do not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanations, and results narrative. It separates encoder and decoder experimental subsections, moves the detailed vocabulary-expansion method and discussion into Appendix C, and adds a limitations section and reorganized reproducibility appendices. These changes substantially restructure the presentation.

P2.justification: v3 adds an introductory English/Swahili tokenization table, combines encoder and prefilling diagrams into Figure 1, and relocates the ANN diagram to the appendix. It redraws the decoder comparison, adds computational-cost and implementation tables, regroups encoder displays, and clarifies compression captions. The existing cache plot and MT-Bench results are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds work on tokenizer choice and limitations, including Ali et al., Bostrom and Durrett, and Dagan et al., plus Global-MMLU and softmax-bottleneck references. Some earlier citations, including Sachidananda et al. and Petrov et al., disappear. The central positioning relative to ZeTT and vocabulary expansion remains; publication metadata updates do not constitute new works.

T1.justification: The tokenizer definitions, update-function equations, hypernetwork embedding equation, uniform merge sampling, ANN softmax formulation, and BPE merge-conflict example are retained. The expanded conditional-probability explanation introduces no substantive new derivation, assumption, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v1 through detailed reproducibility settings and quantitative accounting of model and hypernetwork computation. Multilingual decoder evaluation and the FVT control strengthen empirical support, while explicit limitations and absolute compression figures clarify applicability. FLOPs estimates still do not establish end-to-end latency, and the corrected-MT-Bench source note is lost, but the overall gains in experimental grounding, reproducibility, and clarity are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same dynamic-tokenization research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original encoder and decoder experiments and reports additional multilingual MMLU results, vocabulary comparisons, and model/hypernetwork FLOPs estimates.

before.justification: v1 reports original XLM-R experiments on XNLI and UNER, Mistral-7B experiments on MMLU and MT-Bench, and an embedding-cache analysis.

arxiv_record.abstract: With the significant advancement of Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs), concerns about their potential misuse and abuse have grown rapidly. Previous studies have highlighted VLMs' vulnerability to jailbreak attacks, where carefully crafted inputs can lead the model to produce content that violates ethical and legal standards. However, existing methods struggle against state-of-the-art VLMs like GPT-4o, due to the over-exposure of harmful content and lack of stealthy malicious guidance. In this work, we propose a novel jailbreak attack framework: Multi-Modal Linkage (MML) Attack. Drawing inspiration from cryptography, MML utilizes an encryption-decryption process across text and image modalities to mitigate over-exposure of malicious information. To align the model's output with malicious intent covertly, MML employs a technique called "evil alignment", framing the attack within a video game production scenario. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate MML's effectiveness. Specifically, MML jailbreaks GPT-4o with attack success rates of 97.80% on SafeBench, 98.81% on MM-SafeBench and 99.07% on HADES-Dataset. Our code is available at https://github.com/wangyu-ovo/MML.

C1.justification: The central framework and contribution claims remain. The abstract and introduction raise the headline GPT-4o SafeBench success claim from 97.80% to 99.40%, reflecting the new shift-cipher variant, and the introduction updates the corresponding baseline advantage from 64.80 to 66.4 percentage points.

C2.justification: v5 explicitly qualifies encryption-decryption as metaphorical, explains runtime differences through image size and response length, and discusses possible single-evaluator bias. It removes the earlier inability-to-test-o1 limitation. The central safety-alignment interpretation and vulnerability to output detection remain.

D1.justification: v5 supplies the full shift-cipher prompt, three defense-prompt forms, and timing implementation information, including Apple M1 Pro hardware and image sizes. The original code-access information, replacement-word lists, four method prompts, and preprocessing instructions remain, with some details relocated to Appendix D.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate visual jailbreaks using SafeBench, MM-SafeBench, and HADES-Dataset, including defended SafeBench evaluation. The additions concern target models, evaluator-specific subsets, timing measurements, and prompt placement within this existing coverage.

E2.justification: FigStep and QueryRelated remain the comparators on SafeBench and MM-SafeBench, HADES remains the HADES-Dataset comparator, and FigStep remains the defense-experiment baseline. Added comparisons reuse these methods. Llama-Guard is introduced as an evaluator.

E3.justification: v5 adds Llama-Guard-3-8B evaluation using its unsafe-response criterion and subsets of 307, 867, and 687 instructions, respectively. It also adds o1 evaluation, timing protocols for 500 images and 10 fixed queries, and prefix/suffix AdaShield placements alongside the original infix configuration. The original main benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: The component ablations in Table 3 are unchanged. v5 substantially expands analysis through defense-prompt placement sensitivity in Table 6, evaluator cross-validation in Appendix D.7, and encryption/inference efficiency analysis in Section 5.4.

E5.justification: The new timing experiment reports three independent runs, individual measurements, and averages in Table 5. This does not establish additional runs for the original attack-success experiments. Both versions retain five defense attack attempts and omit confidence intervals and seed information for their main ASR results.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results, and v1's defense results reappear as the infix columns of v5 Table 6. Substantial additions include timing results, alternative-evaluator scores, prefix/suffix defense outcomes, MML-SC's 99.40% SafeBench ASR, and o1 results of 64.4% for MML-WR versus 34.8% for FigStep and 15.6% for QueryRelated. These are newly reported configurations, not improvements to unchanged experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models face intrinsic limitations in coding with APIs that are unseen in their training corpora. As libraries continuously evolve, it becomes impractical to exhaustively retrain LLMs with new API knowledge. This limitation hampers LLMs from solving programming problems which require newly introduced or privately maintained libraries. Inspired by exploratory programming paradigm in human behavior, we propose ExploraCoder, a training-free framework that empowers LLMs to invoke multiple unseen APIs in code solution by (1) planning a complex problem into several API invocation subtasks, and (2) experimenting with correct API usage at intermediate steps through a novel chain-of-API-exploration. We conduct evaluation on program synthesizing tasks involving complex API interactions. Experimental results demonstrate that ExploraCoder significantly improves performance for models lacking prior API knowledge, achieving absolute increases of up to 11.99% over retrieval-based approaches and 17.28% over pretraining-based methods in pass@10.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Traditional fixed test sets fall short in evaluating open-ended capabilities of foundation models. To address this, we propose ONEBench(OpeN-Ended Benchmarking), a new testing paradigm that consolidates individual evaluation datasets into a unified, ever-expanding sample pool. ONEBench allows users to generate custom, open-ended evaluation benchmarks from this pool, corresponding to specific capabilities of interest. By aggregating samples across test sets, ONEBench enables the assessment of diverse capabilities beyond those covered by the original test sets, while mitigating overfitting and dataset bias. Most importantly, it frames model evaluation as a collective process of selecting and aggregating sample-level tests.
  The shift from task-specific benchmarks to ONEBench introduces two challenges: (1)heterogeneity and (2)incompleteness. Heterogeneity refers to the aggregation over diverse metrics, while incompleteness describes comparing models evaluated on different data subsets. To address these challenges, we explore algorithms to aggregate sparse measurements into reliable model scores. Our aggregation algorithm ensures identifiability(asymptotically recovering ground-truth scores) and rapid convergence, enabling accurate model ranking with less data. On homogenous datasets, we show our aggregation algorithm provides rankings that highly correlate with those produced by average scores. We also demonstrate robustness to ~95% of measurements missing, reducing evaluation cost by up to 20x with little-to-no change in model rankings. We introduce ONEBench-LLM for language models and ONEBench-LMM for vision-language models, unifying evaluations across these domains. Overall, we present a technique for open-ended evaluation, which can aggregate over incomplete, heterogeneous sample-level measurements to continually grow a benchmark alongside the rapidly developing foundation models.
arxiv_record.authors: Adhiraj Ghosh, Sebastian Dziadzio, Ameya Prabhu, Vishaal Udandarao, Samuel Albanie, Matthias Bethge
arxiv_record.title: ONEBench to Test Them All: Sample-Level Benchmarking Over Open-Ended Capabilities

E2.justification: v1 evaluates aggregation against Elo and LMArena. v2 retains these and adds Borda Count and the Dowdall System across the four real benchmarks in Table 2. Section 4.3 also introduces random retrieval as a comparator for capability-based retrieval, substantially broadening the comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include Gumbel simulations with 100 systems and 1,000 measurements, dispersion and missingness sweeps, equal-half partition tests, retrieval comparisons at 100/1,000/10,000 samples, and top-5/top-10 ranking comparisons. These substantially extend the evaluation design; the original benchmark setup and retrieval thresholds remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's sample-removal and sparsity experiments, v2 adds synthetic sensitivity tests, checks whether consistent subset rankings survive aggregation, controls capability queries against random subsets, and quantifies differences between global and capability-specific top rankings. These additions in Section 4.3 and Appendices D, E and F.2 address substantial new diagnostic questions.

E5.justification: The original three-run mean/variance reporting is retained. v2 adds five random-retrieval repetitions, five partition repetitions with explicit mean/standard-deviation reporting, and Wilcoxon signed-rank statistics and p-values in Table 11. No increase in the original experiments' run count is stated.

E6.justification: Substantial new results appear in Tables 2, 4, 7–9 and 11. For example, Table 2 reports LMMs-Eval correlations of 0.64 for ONEBench, 0.08 for Borda and 0.18 for Dowdall; Table 9 reports 100% separability consistency for both Plackett-Luce and LMArena. Per-concept AP values are retained, while neuroscience and Gothic-architecture qualitative ranking examples are omitted.

M1.justification: Both versions use sample pooling, conversion to ordinal rankings, structured and embedding-based retrieval, and Plackett-Luce aggregation with partial rank breaking. Expanded evaluation and relocated mathematical descriptions do not establish an algorithmic change.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the main text are substantially condensed and rewritten. Detailed ranking definitions, dataset descriptions, extended related work and future directions move into appendices. The main contents list and introductory verse disappear, and dedicated Limitations and Broad Impacts sections are introduced.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, retained summary tables are transposed, and six result tables are added. Dataset displays move to Appendix A. v1 Figure 5 becomes v2 Figure 4 with two concept rows removed, while the additional qualitative Figure 6 is retained.

R1.justification: Most related work is retained in Appendix G. v2 adds positioning around ranking stability and benchmark longevity through Recht et al., Salaudeen and Hardt, and Hardt and Recht, plus Noothigattu et al. on aggregation axioms. Several citations, including those supporting the removed active-aggregation discussion, are dropped without fundamentally changing the research positioning.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1's active-aggregation/PAC property discussion and adds definitions and stated violations of pairwise majority consistency and separability in Section 7. The principal likelihood, identifiability and sample-complexity statements remain, without new proofs. The rewritten model-set definition also introduces an apparent intersection-for-union error.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked known-truth simulations and random-subset controls for its capability-specific rankings. v2 adds both, expands aggregation baselines, and explicitly discusses violated axioms and other limitations. Together these substantially strengthen validation of the aggregation and personalization claims. Minor notation and documentation regressions, and fewer illustrative examples, do not outweigh the gains in evidence and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ONEBench research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison. Material relocated or renumbered in v2 can be matched to v1.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, synthetic simulations, separability experiments, and quantitative analyses of capability-specific rankings.

before.justification: v1 reports original aggregation comparisons, missing-data experiments, retrieval evaluations with human annotations, and capability-specific model rankings.

arxiv_record.abstract: One key characteristic of the Chinese spelling check (CSC) task is that incorrect characters are usually similar to the correct ones in either phonetics or glyph. To accommodate this, previous works usually leverage confusion sets, which suffer from two problems, i.e., difficulty in determining which character pairs to include and lack of probabilities to distinguish items in the set. In this paper, we propose a light-weight plug-and-play DISC (i.e., decoding intervention with similarity of characters) module for CSC models.DISC measures phonetic and glyph similarities between characters and incorporates this similarity information only during the inference phase. This method can be easily integrated into various existing CSC models, such as ReaLiSe, SCOPE, and ReLM, without additional training costs. Experiments on three CSC benchmarks demonstrate that our proposed method significantly improves model performance, approaching and even surpassing the current state-of-the-art models.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: training-free, plug-and-play similarity-based decoding intervention, compatibility with existing CSC models, reduced over-correction and improved benchmark performance. Additional experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies the interpretation of ECSpell performance by attributing high scores despite low seen-edit coverage to train–test leakage (Section 6 and Appendix E). It also interprets DISC's benefits for unfine-tuned BERT and explains larger gains on glyph errors. The existing language and domain limitations remain.

D1.justification: The listed code link changes from an anonymous repository to the authors' GitHub DISC repository. v2 documents bert-base-chinese initialization for the new control and the error-filtering and deduplication procedures. Existing checkpoint, fine-tuning, hardware and prompt details remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds phonetic-only and glyph-only SIGHAN15 test scenarios while retaining the three benchmark families and seven documented LEMON domains, including appendix results. The additional SIG-labeled row in v1 Table 3 disappears; its precise dataset identity is not explained.

E2.justification: v2 adds Zhou et al. (2024)'s prompt-free, training-free Baichuan2-7B comparator on LEMON, distinct from the fine-tuned Baichuan2 already reported on ECSpell. Table 5 also adds vanilla BERT with and without DISC. Existing principal comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces evaluation after removing ECSpell training examples whose correct sentences overlap the test data. Section 6 adds unfine-tuned BERT and error-isolated SIGHAN15 protocols, repairing non-target errors using a similarity threshold of 0.5. The stated basis for ECSpell seen-pair statistics also changes from the synthetic-data confusion set to training-set pairs.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether DISC helps without task-specific fine-tuning, how its effects differ between phonetic and glyph errors, and whether improvements survive ECSpell leakage removal (Tables 5, 7 and 11). Existing component ablations, sensitivity plots, case studies and copy-punishment analyses remain. The decoding-efficiency analysis is relocated, not newly added.

E5.justification: Both Appendix A versions state that experiments are conducted once, and both Table 8 captions report decoding times averaged over three runs. v2 adds no seed information, uncertainty intervals or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for BERT, error types, cleaned ECSpell and the new LLM comparator. Cleaned ECSpell-MED reports ReLM/DISC F1 of 68.8/74.8, versus 90.2/93.9 under the retained original training setting. Table 4 revises ECSpell seen-pair percentages from 82.31/74.44/84.41 to 54.10/47.47/41.58. Table 3 removes the unexplained SIG results and adds seven-domain averages; retained individual-domain scores are unchanged.

M1.justification: The decoding intervention, phonetic and glyph similarity components, and Equations (3)–(10) are unchanged. Appendix C retains the same 0.1 copy punishment. The new experiments apply the existing method.

P1.justification: There are limited grammar and wording edits, added acknowledgements and localized structural changes. Decoding efficiency moves from Appendix D into Section 6, the prompt appendix becomes D, and cleaned-ECSpell experiments occupy Appendix E. Most existing prose and the main narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5, 7 and 11, restructures Table 3 around four displayed LEMON domains plus an overall average, and relocates existing figures and the timing table. Other LEMON domain results remain in Appendix C. Existing diagrams, sensitivity curves and the two-column presentation are largely preserved.

R1.justification: v2 adds Zhou et al. (2024) and positions its training-free, prompt-free LLM approach as a state-of-the-art comparator. The existing related-work coverage and broader novelty positioning are otherwise retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and encoding, classification, scoring and similarity formulas in Equations (1)–(10) match. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: Appendix E identifies substantial ECSpell train–test overlap and evaluates after removing duplicates, addressing an important validity gap in v1. The cleaned MED comparison still favors DISC, from 68.8 to 74.8 F1, while new controls and error analyses strengthen empirical support. These gains outweigh limited reporting problems, including the apparent precision/recall/F1 inconsistency of 66.1/71.0/70.0 in Table 11's new LAW baseline row.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DISC research. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds original unfine-tuned-BERT, error-type and cleaned-ECSpell experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original DISC evaluations on SIGHAN, ECSpell and LEMON, including component ablations, copy-punishment experiments and decoding-time measurements.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Despite recent progress achieved by code large language models (LLMs), their
remarkable abilities are largely dependent on fine-tuning on the high-quality
data, posing challenges for data collection and annotation. To address this,
current methods often design various data flywheels to collect complex code
instructions, enabling models to handle more intricate tasks. However, these
approaches typically rely on off-the-shelf datasets and data augmentation from
a limited set of proprietary LLMs (e.g., Claude, GPT4, and so on), which
restricts the diversity of the constructed data and makes it prone to systemic
biases. In this paper, we propose WarriorCoder, a novel paradigm learns from
expert battles to address these limitations. Specifically, we create an arena
where leading expert code LLMs challenge each other, with evaluations conducted
by impartial judges. This competitive framework generates novel training data
from scratch, leveraging the strengths of all participants. Experimental
results show that WarriorCoder achieves state-of-the-art performance compared
to previous models of the same size, even without relying on proprietary LLMs.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion strengthen the central performance claim from competitive results to state-of-the-art performance among similarly sized models. V2 also broadens its claimed demonstrated capabilities to reasoning and library usage. The central contribution of learning from expert battles without seed datasets or proprietary annotations remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds a specific limitation that battles become time-consuming with many experts. It interprets task composition and expert win rates as support for diverse knowledge transfer, including why the highest-rated expert need not be best on every task. Overlap is reframed as evidence of independence from existing datasets; the difficulty and case-study interpretations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly supplies instruction-mining and pairwise-judging prompts and describes withholding opponent identities. V2 also specifies exact expert models, nine temperature/top-p combinations, alpha=0.7, and a step-based training budget. These materially expand reproducibility information, although benchmark decoding becomes less explicit by referring to previous work instead of directly specifying greedy decoding.

E1.justification: V2 adds CRUXEval input/output reasoning and DS-1000 Python-library tasks to the four retained code-generation benchmarks. These expand evaluated task requirements beyond the HumanEval and MBPP families. The CodeAlpaca and CodeUltraFeedback overlap analyses remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the original comparator membership. The added evaluations substantially expand the comparisons: CRUXEval includes Claude-3-Opus, DeepSeekCoder-Instruct, and additional CodeLlama/WizardCoder sizes, while DS-1000 introduces INCODER and CodeGen-Mono. These are reported comparison rows, rather than citation-only additions.

E3.justification: V2 revises the expert pool, including Llama-3.3 and newly specified Athene, DeepSeek-Coder-V2, and QwQ experts, and changes Elo K from 0.005 to 40. Training is specified as 448 steps instead of two epochs; equivalent budgets cannot be established. CRUXEval adds pass@5 evaluation. Table 1 also relabels CodeLlama-family baselines from 7B to 6.7B while retaining their scores.

E4.justification: V1's Qwen/Mistral/all-teachers ablation is replaced by a 1/2/5-expert study in v2 Table 5. V2 adds training-task composition analysis and an expert win-rate heatmap, and expands difficulty analysis to show individual experts. The overlap analysis remains, and the two existing case studies move to Appendix A.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-training-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests for its experiments. The added pass@5 results extend performance metrics rather than uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces WarriorCoder's HumanEval/HumanEval+/MBPP/MBPP+ scores of 72.1/66.0/70.5/57.8 with 80.5/75.6/76.2/64.8. V2 additionally reports CRUXEval results, DS-1000 overall pass@1 of 38.1, and new ablation and data-analysis results. Expert and training conditions also change, limiting direct interpretation of the higher scores as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The reported final-training procedure changes substantively: v1 Section 3.3 explicitly employs KTO with thresholded chosen/rejected responses alongside SFT, whereas v2 Section 3.4 specifies SFT on the highest-scored response and removes the KTO procedure. Instruction mining, KCenterGreedy compression, and the voting/Elo framework are retained.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introductory explanation and contributions, and results discussion. It introduces a Competitors Setting subsection, reorganizes data analysis, and moves the existing case studies and fairness rules into Appendices A and C. These constitute substantial narrative and structural revisions beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redesigned from a Quicksort battle example into a complete workflow diagram. V2 adds benchmark and task-composition tables, an expert win-rate heatmap, and prompt tables. The pooled difficulty-count histogram becomes an expert-specific percentage plot, while existing plots and tables are reformatted or relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for CRUXEval, DS-1000, BigCodeBench, QwQ, and Su et al. (2025), while removing the KTO, DPO, and Mistral-7B references. The related-work categories and positioning against existing data-generation and arena approaches remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The voting, Elo-update, and combined-score equations retain their mathematical substance. V2's added filtering equation restates v1's existing restriction to difficulty scores of at least six. Neither version contains additional theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited evidence for broader coding capabilities through CRUXEval and DS-1000 evaluations and more informative expert/data analyses. Newly supplied prompts, explicit settings, and the redesigned workflow materially improve reproducibility and clarity, while the scaling limitation qualifies applicability. Evaluation details remain incomplete and simultaneous training changes limit causal attribution of higher scores, but the broader evidence and documentation provide a substantial overall quality gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe WarriorCoder, with matching authors and a shared methodological framework. Text, equations, tables, and figures are readable. V1 ends with references; v2's Appendices A-C are available, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 reports original code-generation, CRUXEval, and DS-1000 results, along with expert-count ablations and training-data analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original WarriorCoder benchmark results, teacher ablations, and analyses of mined instructions in Tables 1-2 and Figures 3-4.

arxiv_record.abstract: As chatbots become integral to daily life, personalizing systems is key for fostering trust, engagement, and inclusivity. This study examines how linguistic similarity affects chatbot performance, focusing on integrating African American English (AAE) into virtual agents to better serve the African American community. We develop text-based and spoken chatbots using large language models and text-to-speech technology, then evaluate them with AAE speakers against standard English chatbots. Our results show that while text-based AAE chatbots often underperform, spoken chatbots benefit from an African American voice and AAE elements, improving performance and preference. These findings underscore the complexities of linguistic personalization and the dynamics between text and speech modalities, highlighting technological limitations that affect chatbots' AA speech generation and pointing to promising future research directions.
arxiv_record.authors: Sarah E. Finch, Ellie S. Paek, Ikseon Choi, Jinho D. Choi
arxiv_record.title: Finding A Voice: Exploring the Potential of African American Dialect and Voice Generation for Chatbots

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes AAVE-speaking users' preference for SAE chatbots. v2 retains that finding for text but makes modality dependence central: African American voices can improve spoken-chatbot reception. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion accordingly expand the contributions from dialect generation to dialect-and-voice personalization.

C2.justification: v2 introduces hypotheses connecting poor high-intensity ratings to excessive phonetic rewriting, speech limitations to SAE-oriented TTS training, and SAE preference to historical technological expectations. It also acknowledges partially different evaluator cohorts across modalities. v1's attitude-based interpretation and specific recommendation for optional dialect customization are removed.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly discloses temperature zero, five-beam Llama decoding, F5 defaults, exact source-audio identifiers, and stated release of reference clips. Sections 3.2 and 4.4 document audio processing and participant eligibility, while Appendix D supplies tagging examples and a prompt. The text-generation settings are newly documented, not established changes to the earlier procedure.

E1.justification: The five SODA dialogue domains remain. v2 adds spoken-dialogue evaluation using African American and Standard American voices, with reference audio from the Corpus of Regional African American Language and LibriSpeech. It also introduces a 90-text linguistic-feature identification test set, expanding both modality and task coverage.

E2.justification: The text comparison retains GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-3.5, Llama3.1-70B, and the SAE control. The new speech comparison introduces an SAE/Standard American voice baseline and an SAE/African American voice condition alongside dialect variants. Section 4.3 additionally compares GPT-4o and Claude for feature tagging, substantially expanding the comparison design.

E3.justification: v2 adds a five-condition speech evaluation with eight evaluators and speech-specific metrics, plus feature-tagger testing on 90 texts containing 136 labels and analysis of 250 translated responses per chatbot. For text evaluation, v1 reports 95 retained dialogues, including 41 double-rated; v2 describes 100 dialogues with at least half double-rated without reconciling these accounts. Appendix E also explicitly reverses Offensiveness scores.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 2 add analysis of phonetic, morphological, syntactic, and semantic changes across models and dialect strengths. Section 7 adds a qualitative consistency check using evaluators who participated in both modalities. Conversely, v1's attitude-stratified analysis in Figure 2 and its accompanying subjectivity discussion are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals around human-rating means; applying that practice to speech does not introduce a new uncertainty procedure. However, v2 removes v1's reported inter-annotator agreement range of 0.11–0.36, reducing reliability reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds feature-identification accuracies of 91% for Claude versus 86% for GPT, linguistic-feature distributions, and speech ratings showing benefits from an African American voice on several conversational measures. Existing text means also change between v1 Figure 1 and v2 Figure 3, while attitude-stratified results disappear. The changed sample account prevents interpreting the text updates as established same-setting gains.

M1.justification: The original prompted SAE-to-AAVE text transformation is substantially retained. Section 3.2 adds an F5 text-to-speech pipeline conditioned on reference voices, with text normalization, sentence segmentation, audio concatenation, and speaker cues. This introduces a substantive speech-generation component.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, AAVE terminology largely becomes AAE, and the title and author list change. The original Approach and Results and Discussion organization becomes a subdivided chatbot-design section, expanded experiments, and separate discussion. References move before the reorganized appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds a pipeline diagram, feature-distribution chart, speech-result panels, and speech-evaluation interface. The retained text-results figure uses darker colors, distinct markers, reordered panels, and horizontal SAE reference lines instead of separate baseline points. Prompt, metric, and example tables are relocated or restructured, with the response examples expanded.

R1.justification: Related work gains substantial AAE linguistic background and a dedicated accented-speech discussion, including Green, Wolfram, and Pinhanez and colleagues. New speech-generation and linguistic-resource references support positioning the work around dialect features and accent-enabled chatbots evaluated by their intended users.

T1.justification: The dialect-transformation mapping E(I, Da, Db) to O is retained with equivalent terminology. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and v2's linguistic background and TTS descriptions do not introduce new mathematical definitions or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis of the conclusions: feature analysis examines what the models actually change, and the speech comparisons show that the negative text findings do not apply uniformly across modalities. The added implementation details also improve reproducibility. Removing attitude-stratified results and agreement statistics, and leaving text-sample changes unexplained, weakens transparency; nevertheless, the gains in measurement and support for a more qualified central conclusion outweigh those losses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SODA-based dialect-chatbot research. The original methods and experiments can be matched despite the expanded title and added speech study. The main text, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 reports original text-chatbot results, an additional spoken-chatbot evaluation with eight evaluators, and feature-tagging accuracy and linguistic-feature analyses.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report an original human evaluation of three LLM families at three dialect intensities against an SAE control, involving 12 evaluators and 95 retained dialogues.

arxiv_record.abstract: While many advanced LLMs are designed to handle long sequence data, we can still observe notable quality degradation even within the sequence limit. In this work, we introduce a novel approach called Scaling to Emphasize Attention for Long-context retrieval (SEAL), which enhances the retrieval performance of large language models (LLMs) over long contexts. We observe that specific attention heads are closely tied to long-context retrieval, showing positive or negative correlation with retrieval scores, and adjusting the strength of these heads boosts the quality of LLMs in long context by a large margin. Built on this insight, we propose a learning-based mechanism that leverages generated data to emphasize these heads. By applying SEAL, we achieve significant improvements in long-context retrieval performance across various tasks and models. Additionally, when combined with existing training-free context extension techniques, SEAL extends the contextual limits of LLMs while maintaining highly reliable outputs.
arxiv_record.authors: Changhun Lee, Minsang Seok, Jun-gyu Jin, Younghyun Cho, Eunhyeok Park
arxiv_record.title: SEAL: Scaling to Emphasize Attention for Long-Context Retrieval

C1.justification: The central claims of inexpensive attention scaling, improved retrieval and compatibility with context extension remain. v2 removes the abstract's explicit claim of considerable out-of-domain improvement and the conclusion's generalization claim, while prioritizing synthetic rule-based retrieval and retaining LongBench as additional validation.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the broad generalization interpretation with task-dependent transfer: scales learned on word-extraction tasks can harm variable tracking, motivating category-specific training. Its mechanism explanation omits v1's dominant-MLP account and the caveat that pruning effects might reflect format understanding. New limitations discuss memory requirements for longer training sequences and task-dependent learning-rate tuning.

D1.justification: v2 specifies selection of the 50 longest triviaqa_e samples for LongBench, documents RULER data generation and learning rates, and explains offline-merging axes and grouped-query attention. Most existing optimizer, hardware, sample-generation and training-budget information is retained. Conversely, v1's explicit LongBench-specific learning rates are omitted.

E1.justification: v2 adds RULER variable tracking, common word extraction and frequent word extraction, substantially extending task requirements beyond the previous evaluations. Line retrieval, Needle-in-a-Haystack, MMLU and LongBench document QA remain represented. Naming triviaqa_e for LongBench training supplies previously missing documentation rather than establishing a dataset replacement.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 adds one-shot prompting for LongChat-7B and Vicuna-13B. LoRA/DoRA line-retrieval comparisons are reduced from five models to those two; the Mistral-7B, Vicuna-7B and LongChat-13B comparison rows disappear. The five-model Needle-in-a-Haystack LoRA/DoRA comparison remains in Appendix G, so that relocation is not a comparator removal.

E3.justification: New RULER protocols introduce Llama-3.1-8B, 200 evaluation samples per task, testing up to 64K and variable-length training samples. The one-shot comparison uses a 1K-token example and maximum task lengths of 30K/15K, versus 31K/16K in the primary table. Mistral SEAL-C's reported Needle-in-a-Haystack learning rate changes from 4e-4 in v1 Appendix A to 4e-2 in v2 Table 4; rerunning is not established.

E4.justification: v2 replaces line-retrieval-to-LongBench transfer evaluation with a RULER task-to-task transfer analysis. It also removes the MLP-specific direct-effect analysis from the retained retrieval error case. The pruning experiments, MMLU check and sample-count/learning-rate ablations remain; moving the latter to Appendix E does not add an analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new RULER evaluation sample count describes evaluation size, not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds RULER, one-shot and cross-task transfer results, including Llama-3.1-8B's 64K CWE scores of 0.1 for baseline and 95.7 for SEAL-C. LongBench SEAL-H averages change from 33.52/26.23 to 33.25/26.05, while its out-of-domain rows disappear. Parameter counts also change, including 13B SEAL-C from 207.7K to 204.8K. Primary baseline/SEAL line-retrieval scores remain unchanged; the shorter-context comparison is not a same-setting improvement.

M1.justification: Both versions generate task-formatted training examples and learn head-wise or channel-wise attention-output scales. Offline merging already appears in v1. v2's expanded merging explanation, including grouped-query attention, documents implementation rather than establishing a changed procedure. SEAL-L/SEAL-D correspond to the retained LoRA/DoRA comparators.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, motivation and method explanations. It nests qualitative analysis within experiments, creates separate comparison sections, relocates LongBench discussion to Appendix D and reorganizes the appendices. These changes substantially alter the narrative and structure of retained material.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 2–4 are reorganized or redrawn, including an offline-merging diagram and replacement of flattened head plots with three-dimensional plots. The context-extension table becomes Figure 6, the full Needle-in-a-Haystack comparison moves to Appendix G, and new RULER and transfer displays are added.

R1.justification: The research context is substantially narrowed toward synthetic retrieval benchmarks, with circuit-analysis and context-extension discussion partly redistributed. v2 adds RULER, GQA and Llama 3 references while removing Wu et al.'s retrieval-head work and much of the hallucination, RAG and chain-of-thought background. LongBench's publication update represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 2 introduces a formal transferability metric: summed score changes across lengths normalized by the baseline score range. The existing direct-effect equation is retained with clearer unembedding-weight notation. Neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation and qualifies applicability through harder RULER tasks, a newer long-context model, a relevant prompting comparator and explicit negative-transfer evidence. These address gaps in v1's support for broad retrieval and generalization claims. LongBench data-selection details and practical limitations also improve transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of MLP-specific analysis, several line-retrieval comparator results and some reproducibility details.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SEAL and share identifiable methods, experiments and results. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive rewriting and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and additionally reports RULER evaluations, cross-task transfer measurements and one-shot prompting comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original pruning experiments, retrieval evaluations, context-extension experiments, LongBench and MMLU results, and sample-count/learning-rate analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Most progress in recent coder models has been driven by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while the potential of reinforcement learning (RL) remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the lack of reliable reward data/model in the code domain. In this paper, we address this challenge by leveraging automated large-scale test-case synthesis to enhance code model training. Specifically, we design a pipeline that generates extensive (question, test-cases) pairs from existing code data. Using these test cases, we construct preference pairs based on pass rates over sampled programs to train reward models with Bradley-Terry loss. It shows an average of 10-point improvement for Llama-3.1-8B-Ins and 5-point improvement for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Ins through best-of-32 sampling, making the 7B model on par with 236B DeepSeek-V2.5. Furthermore, we conduct reinforcement learning with both reward models and test-case pass rewards, leading to consistent improvements across HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench, and LiveCodeBench (V4). Notably, we follow the R1-style training to start from Qwen2.5-Coder-base directly and show that our RL training can improve model on HumanEval-plus by over 25\% and MBPP-plus by 6\% for merely 80 optimization steps. We believe our results highlight the huge potential of reinforcement learning in coder models.
