C1.justification: The abstract and central synthesis/reward-training/RL contributions remain. v4 adds an introductory claim of leading RM-Bench performance, including Chat, removes the claim to the first large-scale verifiable code-training dataset, and frames novelty more specifically around combining synthesis with reward-model and RL training.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive limitations concerning incorrect reference solutions, insufficient edge-case coverage and noisy rewards despite passing tests. It also interprets RM-Bench results as generalization beyond coding and explains specific RL regressions and improvements in Appendix A.4. These extend the earlier, narrower reward-hacking discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2/Table 9 explicitly identifies the backbones and preference-generation models for both reward-model sizes. Appendix A.3 adds a reference-program-only synthesis prompt. Existing training hyperparameters, hardware information and access identifiers are retained.

E1.justification: v4 retains HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench and LiveCodeBench and adds RM-Bench evaluations covering Code, Chat, Math and Safety. This substantially extends evaluation beyond coding performance to reward judgments across multiple domains.

E2.justification: The RL comparison replaces its DeepSeek-V2.5 row with RLEF-8B/70B, PPOCoder-7B, StepCoder-7B, CodeGemma-7B and DSTC-33B (v1 Table 3; v4 Table 4). DeepSeek-V2.5 remains elsewhere. The new RM-Bench comparison also includes Nemotron-340B and additional InternLM and Skywork variants.

E3.justification: Core training budgets and generation settings remain unchanged. v4 adds a random audit of 40 questions with five tests each, dataset pass-rate profiling and RM-Bench scoring by domain/difficulty. Table 1 revises the filtered corpus size from 89,422 to 87,149; the PDFs do not establish reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained filtering, backbone and base-model RL ablations, v4 adds direct human validation of synthesized tests, dataset difficulty analysis in Table 2, and three HumanEval case studies in Appendix A.4. These substantially expand analysis of reliability, successes and failures.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new audit reports raw outcomes and sampling details without uncertainty estimation; generated-candidate counts do not represent repeated experimental runs.

E6.justification: v4 adds RM-Bench averages of 72.2 and 76.1 for the 7B and 32B reward models, three invalid tests among 200 audited tests, dataset pass-rate statistics and comparator/case-study results. Original model scores largely remain unchanged, but summary gains are revised, including the Llama/32B reranking average gain from 10.7 to 9.0.

M1.justification: The synthesis/filtering pipeline, preference-selection thresholds, Bradley-Terry reward training, scalar reward head and Reinforce++ tuning remain unchanged. The additional prompt and model-role tables provide implementation disclosure without establishing a revised algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction is compressed and refocused, the conclusion and RL-related-work discussion are rewritten, dataset construction becomes a Methodology subsection, and two related-work sections move into the expanded appendix. These changes substantially reorganize the narrative alongside widespread copyediting.

P2.justification: v4 adds four tables covering dataset pass rates, RM-Bench, model roles and another prompt, plus three illustrated code-comparison figures. Existing result tables gain comparator rows, captions move below tables, and table sizing and placement change substantially. Figure 1 is retained.

R1.justification: v4 adds substantial positioning against automated test-generation work, including CodeT, Algo and Clover, and expands coding-RL discussion beyond CodeRL to PPOCoder, RLEF, StepCoder and DSTC. The earlier general code-model and reward-model reviews are preserved in Appendix A.1.

T1.justification: The Bradley-Terry formulation, PPO ratio/objective, best-of-N selection and preference-selection equation are retained. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs, and v4 introduces no substantive mathematical derivation.

improvement.justification: The human audit directly examines synthesized-test reliability, while relevant RL comparisons, RM-Bench evaluation, clearer prior-work distinctions and concrete limitations address important validation and positioning gaps in v1. Together these substantially strengthen the paper. The audit remains small and reporting defects persist: v4 Table 8 states a 2.4 gain despite displayed averages of 54.0 and 57.6. These flaws limit some summaries but do not outweigh the broader improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ACECODER. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated and newly added content to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds original test-case auditing, dataset analysis, RM-Bench evaluations and HumanEval case studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original reward-model evaluations, reinforcement-learning results and filtering/backbone ablations in Tables 2–6.

arxiv_record.abstract: We introduce Agentic Reasoning, a framework that enhances large language model (LLM) reasoning by integrating external tool-using agents. Agentic Reasoning dynamically leverages web search, code execution, and structured memory to address complex problems requiring deep research. A key innovation in our framework is the Mind-Map agent, which constructs a structured knowledge graph to store reasoning context and track logical relationships, ensuring coherence in long reasoning chains with extensive tool usage. Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive exploration of the Web-Search agent, leading to a highly effective search mechanism that surpasses all prior approaches. When deployed on DeepSeek-R1, our method achieves a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) among public models and delivers performance comparable to OpenAI Deep Research, the leading proprietary model in this domain. Extensive ablation studies validate the optimal selection of agentic tools and confirm the effectiveness of our Mind-Map and Web-Search agents in enhancing LLM reasoning. The code is at: https://github.com/theworldofagents/Agentic-Reasoning
arxiv_record.authors: Junde Wu, Jiayuan Zhu, Yuyuan Liu, Min Xu, Yueming Jin
arxiv_record.title: Agentic Reasoning: A Streamlined Framework for Enhancing LLM Reasoning with Agentic Tools

program_record.Abstract: We introduce Agentic Reasoning, a framework that enhances large language model (LLM) reasoning by integrating external tool-using agents. Agentic Reasoning dynamically leverages web search, code execution, and structured memory to address complex problems requiring deep research. A key innovation in our framework is the Mind-Map agent, which constructs a structured knowledge graph to store reasoning context and track logical relationships, ensuring coherence in long reasoning chains with extensive tool usage. Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive exploration of the Web-Search agent, leading to a highly effective search mechanism that surpasses all prior approaches. When deployed on DeepSeek-R1, our method achieves a new state-of-the-art (SOTA) among public models and delivers performance comparable to OpenAI Deep Research, the leading proprietary model in this domain. Extensive ablation studies validate the optimal selection of agentic tools and confirm the effectiveness of our Mind-Map and Web-Search agents in enhancing LLM reasoning. Our code and data are publicly available.
program_record.Title: Agentic Reasoning: A Streamlined Framework for Enhancing LLM Reasoning with Agentic Tools

C1.justification: v1 broadly claims superiority over existing models and emphasizes test-time scalability and potential verifier/reward-model use. v2 instead emphasizes SOTA among public models, comparability to OpenAI Deep Research, and a superior Web-Search design supported by ablations. The verifier/reward-model contribution is dropped from the main claims, with test-time computing relegated to future work.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning tool synergy, redundancy between Knowledge Refinement and reranking, and Mind-Map's prevention of reasoning drift and repeated mistakes. Its new limitations section expands earlier warnings about tool inaccuracies to computational overhead, sequential latency, missing source-credibility verification, and hallucination propagation. The appendix adds an explanation based on communicating uncertain agent outputs.

D1.justification: v2 Section 3.1 newly specifies reasoning and agent models, generation parameters, Bing retrieval depth, Cohere reranking thresholds and iteration limits, Python version, and default pass1 reporting. The appendix supplies the human-rating rubric, and the research-question total is disclosed. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the code repository link is unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds Humanity's Last Exam, GAIA, and FreshWiki, extending evaluation to broader expert subjects, general assistant tasks requiring browsing and tools, and Wikipedia-style article generation. GPQA, professional research questions in finance/medicine/law, and the Werewolf and reasoning examples remain.

E2.justification: The GPQA comparator set changes: several Qwen2.5 and plain-RAG rows disappear, while DeepSeek-R1 and o3-mini baselines appear and o1 replaces o1-preview. The professional deep-research comparison expands beyond Gemini to DirectGen, RAG, RAgent, Search-O1, and STORM. Appendix comparisons additionally evaluate Read-agent, MemoryBank, MemGPT, Perplexity Deep Research, GPT Deep Research, and direct API calling.

E3.justification: Professional research evaluation changes from expert pass/fail rates to four 1-5 ratings. New experiments introduce ROUGE/entity-recall evaluation, latency measurements, memory/API controls, and GPQA analysis grouped by reasoning length and tool calls. The GPQA Extended comparison is removed. The newly stated total of 56 research questions is a disclosure, not evidence that the original sample increased.

E4.justification: v2 adds toolbox and tool-combination ablations, search-component ablations, and Mind-Map comparisons across reasoning lengths. The appendix adds alternative-memory, efficiency, and agent-versus-API analyses. Werewolf gains a without-Mind-Map control. The earlier standalone analysis advocating tool-count-based test-time selection is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports statistical uncertainty, confidence intervals, significance tests, seeds, or statistical replication counts. The plots and tables continue to present point estimates. v2's discussion of agents expressing confidence concerns model behavior, not uncertainty estimation for experimental results.

E6.justification: v2 adds HLE accuracy of 23.8%, GAIA average accuracy of 66.13%, FreshWiki scores, human ratings, and numerous ablation and timing results. Original GPQA values 88.1/58.3/79.6 are retained and labeled QwQ-based; the new 94.5/73.7/80.5 values use DeepSeek-R1 and are not a same-configuration improvement. GPQA Extended results disappear. Werewolf's 72% win rate remains, with a newly reported 36% without Mind-Map.

M1.justification: The three-agent architecture remains, but the Web-Search procedure is substantially revised. v1 Section 2.4 describes contextual summarization of retrieved pages; v2 Section 2.3 introduces query breakdown, relevance reranking, threshold-triggered query refinement, and RAG. Section 3.4.2 explicitly selects this combination and excludes separate Knowledge Refinement from the final design.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten, and the introduction gains an explicit contribution list. The preliminary formalism and Main Findings section disappear; their surrounding narrative is reorganized into expanded experimental analyses. New implementation, related-work, limitations, and appendix sections substantially change the document structure. The title and author block also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds a front-page HLE table and numerous benchmark, rating, ablation, and efficiency tables. The GPQA table gains an overall column and revised structure. New toolbox and Mind-Map bar charts replace the earlier tool-call/pass-rate presentation. The workflow, medical, and riddle illustrations are largely retained, while the Werewolf display is reduced from two graphs to one.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated Related Work section positioning the framework against AutoGPT, LangChain, hierarchical planning, and task-specific agents. It expands the claimed research gap to agent integration, delegation, and tool synergy. New benchmark, retrieval, clustering, and memory-system references further broaden the positioning beyond v1's introductory discussion.

T1.justification: v1 Section 2.1 defines the task mapping and a joint autoregressive probability factorization for reasoning and answer generation. This formal preliminary section is removed from v2 and is not relocated to its appendix. Neither version contains substantive theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 provides little direct testing of its tool-selection and memory explanations and sparse implementation information. v2 substantially addresses these deficiencies through component ablations, alternative-memory and API controls, explicit implementation settings, and a documented human-rating rubric. Its limitations discussion also improves qualification of the claims. Reporting weaknesses remain: uncertainty is still absent, and Section 7.2.2 incorrectly claims faster performance than Perplexity despite Table 8 showing 6.8 versus 3.1 minutes. These issues limit confidence but do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidential support and reproducibility information.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Agentic Reasoning, with matching core components, examples, and retained results. The text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no separate appendix; v2's Section 7 appendix was included in the assessment.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark evaluations, human ratings, tool and memory ablations, and efficiency comparisons, including additional experiments in the appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPQA evaluations, expert-assessed deep-research pass rates, tool-use analyses, and a Werewolf experiment.

arxiv_record.abstract: Providing Language Models (LMs) with relevant evidence in the context (either via retrieval or user-provided) can significantly improve their ability to provide better-grounded responses. However, recent studies have found that LMs often struggle to fully comprehend and utilize key evidence from the context, especially when it contains noise and irrelevant information, an issue common in real-world scenarios. To address this, we propose SelfElicit, an inference-time approach that helps LMs focus on key contextual evidence through self-guided explicit highlighting. By leveraging the inherent evidence-finding capabilities of LMs using the attention scores of deeper layers, our method automatically identifies and emphasizes key evidence within the input context, facilitating more accurate and grounded responses without additional training or iterative prompting. We demonstrate that SelfElicit brings consistent and significant improvement on multiple evidence-based QA tasks for various LM families while maintaining computational efficiency. Our code and documentation are available at https://github.com/ZhiningLiu1998/SelfElicit.
arxiv_record.authors: Zhining Liu, Rana Ali Amjad, Ravinarayana Adkathimar, Tianxin Wei, Hanghang Tong
arxiv_record.comments: Accepted by ACL 2025. 21 pages, 5 figures, 13 tables
arxiv_record.title: SelfElicit: Your Language Model Secretly Knows Where is the Relevant Evidence

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of training-free, efficient attention-based evidence highlighting that improves contextual QA. The conclusion retains the 5.0%–11.7% improvement claim. Revised grounding terminology and descriptions of additional analyses do not redefine the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations concerning attention redistribution, information lost through filtering, incomplete evidence selection, and declining evidence attention in final layers. Its limitations replace the discussion of repeated input encoding with threshold selection and adaptation. The noise discussion also removes the unresolved TK% statement and emphasizes adaptive evidence selection.

D1.justification: Appendix A and new Table 5 disclose dataset-specific context sources and average/maximum token lengths, including use of the Llama-3.1 tokenizer for counting. Existing sample counts, model access references, implementation framework, segmentation details, decoding settings, and code link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The four original datasets and existing distractor setting are retained. Appendix B.6 adds a HotpotQA scenario where some supplied contexts contain no supporting evidence, extending evaluation to answer rejection without introducing a new source corpus.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparators remain. Appendix B.7/Table 11 adds Filco, a trained context-filtering comparator, and crosses SELFELICIT/Filco evidence selection with highlighting/filtering. Table 9 also adds beginning- and end-attached evidence comparisons. These substantially expand the comparisons supporting the design.

E3.justification: Original validation splits, sample counts, model checkpoints, greedy decoding, and QA metrics remain unchanged. New protocols include replacing contexts for randomly selected 50% of HotpotQA samples and measuring rejection accuracy, plus averaging attention across all layers and heads before and after highlighting. These are additional experimental procedures, not reported revisions to the original evaluations.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether highlighting increases attention to evidence, whether evidence placement or filtering affects accuracy, and whether the method preserves rejection of unsupported questions. Appendix C.1 adds a failure case repaired by lowering the threshold. Original layer, threshold, token-versus-sentence, and distractor analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing attention plots and point-estimate reporting are retained; the new randomized context-replacement experiment adds no seed or repeated-run information.

E6.justification: Original per-dataset Table 1 scores remain unchanged, but swapped average EM/F1 rankings are corrected: Llama3.1-8B Base changes from 4.75/4.38 to 4.38/4.75. Tables 7 and 9–11 add substantial results for attention, alternative strategies, Filco, and unsupported questions. In the new unanswerable setting, rejection accuracy is 91.25 for Base and 92.86 for SELFELICIT.

M1.justification: Equations (1)–(4), Algorithm 1, and the prompting procedure retain the same attention aggregation, sentence selection, and highlighting method. The default remains the last 50% of layers with alpha = 0.5. Additional variants are evaluated as comparisons; dynamic threshold selection remains future work.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section hierarchy are retained. Editing concentrates on the introduction, robustness discussion, and limitations, with added acknowledgments and appendix subsections. Existing analyses and examples are largely preserved through renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands displayed evidence through new dataset-statistics, attention-change, strategy-comparison, and unanswerability tables, plus paired threshold-failure callouts. Existing figures remain, with several displays relocated. Original full-context Tables 7–8 become Tables 12–13 without changing their examples.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around attention sorting, SnapKV, Filco, and DoLa. Section 5 explicitly distinguishes sentence-level evidence highlighting from document-level attention ranking and trained filtering, while Appendix C.2 connects findings to layer-wise factuality research. The bibliography and general-AI citations also expand considerably.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and attention-scoring equations are unchanged. Appendix C.2 adds qualitative reasoning about evidence use across layers, without introducing mathematical assumptions, propositions, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct measurements of highlighting's effect on attention, comparison with trained context filtering, and an explicit no-evidence test. v2 addresses these gaps and adds a concrete failure analysis, substantially strengthening validation and clarifying applicability. Ranking corrections also improve reporting accuracy. There are localized weaknesses: Appendix B.5 overstates the HotpotQA advantage of in-context highlighting despite Table 9 showing 69.8 for beginning-attached evidence versus 69.5 in-context, and the repeated-encoding limitation disappears. These shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SELFELICIT and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–C. Retained material can be matched reliably despite expanded appendices and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds attention measurements, strategy comparisons, an unanswerable-question experiment, and a threshold-related failure case.

before.justification: v1 reports original QA evaluations across six language models and four datasets, alongside attention analyses, robustness tests, and appendix ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent work in computational psycholinguistics has revealed intriguing parallels between attention mechanisms and human memory retrieval, focusing primarily on vanilla Transformers that operate on token-level representations. However, computational psycholinguistic research has also established that syntactic structures provide compelling explanations for human sentence processing that token-level factors cannot fully account for. In this paper, we investigate whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis between models and humans. Our experiments demonstrate that TG's attention achieves superior predictive power for self-paced reading times compared to vanilla Transformer's, with further analyses revealing independent contributions from both models. These findings suggest that human sentence processing involves dual memory representations -- one based on syntactic structures and another on token sequences -- with attention serving as the general memory retrieval algorithm, while highlighting the importance of incorporating syntactic structures as representational units.
arxiv_record.authors: Ryo Yoshida, Shinnosuke Isono, Kohei Kajikawa, Taiga Someya, Yushi Sugimoto, Yohei Oseki
arxiv_record.title: If Attention Serves as a Cognitive Model of Human Memory Retrieval, What is the Plausible Memory Representation?

C2.justification: Transformer's advantage is reinterpreted through noun-triggered semantic retrieval rather than possessive-pronoun antecedent retrieval. Section 5.1 replaces the strategic retrieval of constituents within composed phrases with an emphasis on COMPOSE's role in verb retrieval. v2 also qualifies the algorithmic-level positioning and explains Appendix F's dependence on excluding Transformer's NAE.

D1.justification: v2 adds a reproduction-code link, identifies the corrected Natural Stories release, and clarifies top-layer NAE calculation and word-to-token indexing in Appendix D. Hyperparameters, hardware, computational cost, and software-version disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions train on BLLIP-LG and evaluate English self-paced reading times from Natural Stories. The corrected dataset release retains the same task and population coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain Transformer, TG−comp, and CLT. The appendix comparisons also retain their comparator membership; RNNG remains the parser used to generate alternative structures.

E3.justification: Section 3.2 switches to a Natural Stories release explicitly described as correcting data misalignment, revising the evaluation data underlying the central reading-time analyses. Retained observations change from 724,883 to 725,875. Training budgets, filtering rules, regression controls, and evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The COMPOSE ablation and POS analyses retain their designs but provide substantially revised evidence: TG−comp's unique contribution under the full controls disappears, and its former POS-specific advantages disappear or reverse (Section 5.1, Figure 4). The CLT control and supplementary experiments remain present with updated results.

E5.justification: Table 2 changes its stated p-value-summary scope from across random seeds to seeds achieving significance. The three-seed design, means and standard deviations, significant-seed counts, standard errors, and statistical tests are otherwise retained.

E6.justification: Table 1's TG/Transformer ΔLogLik values change from 96.3/35.2 to 76.6/42.8. TG−comp's unique-contribution test in Section 5.1 changes from p<0.001 to p=0.478. POS findings and Tables 3 and 6–8 also change substantially. These updated results use corrected evaluation data, preventing interpretation as same-setting model performance changes.

M1.justification: The architectures, training objectives, COMPOSE/STACK mechanisms, NAE aggregation procedure, and parallel-parsing approach are retained. Corrected formulas and clearer token indexing do not establish a change to the implemented method.

P1.justification: v2 separates cue-based retrieval into its own background subsection, expands the dataset-selection rationale, refines word/token terminology, and updates affiliations and acknowledgments. The main section sequence and Appendices A–G remain, with Appendix F retitled.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses a central data-validity problem by using the corrected Natural Stories release and updating the main and appendix results and interpretations accordingly. arxiv_record.abstract: Data augmentation is an essential technique in natural language processing (NLP) for enriching training datasets by generating diverse samples. This process is crucial for improving the robustness and generalization capabilities of NLP models. However, a significant challenge remains: \textit{Insufficient Attention to Sample Distribution Diversity}. Most existing methods focus on increasing the sample numbers while neglecting the sample distribution diversity, which can lead to model overfitting. In response, we explore data augmentation's impact on dataset diversity and propose a \textbf{\underline{D}}iversity-\textbf{\underline{o}}riented data \textbf{\underline{Aug}}mentation framework (\textbf{DoAug}). % \(\mathscr{DoAug}\) Specifically, we utilize a diversity-oriented fine-tuning approach to train an LLM as a diverse paraphraser, which is capable of augmenting textual datasets by generating diversified paraphrases. Then, we apply the LLM paraphraser to a selected coreset of highly informative samples and integrate the paraphrases with the original data to create a more diverse augmented dataset. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on 12 real-world textual datasets. The results show that our fine-tuned LLM augmenter improves diversity while preserving label consistency, thereby enhancing the robustness and performance of downstream tasks. Specifically, it achieves an average performance gain of \(10.52\%\), surpassing the runner-up baseline with more than three percentage points.
arxiv_record.authors: Zaitian Wang, Jinghan Zhang, Xinhao Zhang, Kunpeng Liu, Pengfei Wang, Yuanchun Zhou
arxiv_record.title: Diversity-oriented Data Augmentation with Large Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the central claims: diversity-oriented paraphrasing with DPO and coreset selection improves diversity while preserving coherence and downstream performance. The headline 10.52% average gain remains. Additional supporting experiments and the sixth diversity metric do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 develops new interpretations of component roles: sampling chiefly affects latent diversity, while DPO affects lexical diversity, and fine-tuning is argued necessary relative to cheaper alternatives. It adds metric-choice rationale and default coreset recommendations. Limitations now acknowledge restricted reasoning and multilingual coverage, human/model evaluation biases, and the exclusion of Arabic, replacing several statements that these evaluations were absent.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code link, dataset access locations, the exact paraphrasing prompt, adapter-training/merging details, and the 20,000-source-by-five-paraphrase composition of SFT data. Appendix D newly explains baseline sample selection and matching of dataset sizes. Most learning rates, epochs, hardware, software versions, and training times were already documented in v1.

E1.justification: The twelve English classification datasets remain. v2 Appendix M adds CSQA and CODAH multiple-choice reasoning tasks and Twitter sentiment evaluation in English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese. These substantially extend task and language coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds AEDA to the main and GPT-2/T5 comparisons, Code-Mixed to the new multilingual experiment, and temperature/prompt alternatives in the DPO-replacement study. The original eleven baselines remain. Llama-based implementations of AugGPT and other prompting baselines were already disclosed in v1 Appendix C.

E3.justification: v2 adds unique 3-grams, excludes invalid words from lexical diversity, and changes Table 2 from average ranks to normalized-score averages. New protocols include human evaluation of 200 samples per dataset and metric comparison on 1,000 sources with 5,000 paraphrases. The low-resource comparison revises reported counts from 600 original plus 600 augmented samples to 800 plus 400, and pruning-ratio labels change. These revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds experiments testing whether higher temperature or diversity prompts can replace DPO, and examines Euclidean-versus-cosine selection agreement, correlation, and distributions in Appendices G–H. Human paraphrase-validity checks and lexical ablation results also expand the analyses. Existing generation-count, coreset, architecture, and low-resource studies largely remain.

E5.justification: Both Table 1 captions report means and standard deviations over ten random seeds. v2 Appendix D newly specifies that methods use matching seeds, while Appendix C reiterates the run count. Appendix G also introduces Pearson correlation estimation for the metric comparison. No increase in repeated runs or new confidence intervals is reported.

E6.justification: Retained accuracy entries in Tables 1 and 4 are unchanged, with AEDA results added. Table 3 corrects DoAug's Yelp accuracy from 59.67 to 56.57. Raw diversity results change, including DoAug distance from 9.5308 to 9.6430, alongside revised evaluation reporting. New findings include 95% human-assessed validity, metric correlation of 0.96, and DPO-replacement, reasoning, and multilingual results. These additions do not demonstrate a same-setting improvement over v1.

M1.justification: Both versions use supervised paraphraser training, Euclidean-distance preferences, DPO, selective coreset augmentation, and distance-based output selection. Newly explained adapter merging does not establish a procedural change. Algorithm 1 corrects S_select to S_retain, matching the procedure already described in v1 Section 3.4.

P1.justification: v2 divides experimental settings into numbered subsections, relocates metric formulas to Appendix A, expands dataset and implementation explanations, and reorganizes the appendices. It also adds acknowledgments and corresponding-author identification. Most introductory, methodological, and concluding prose is retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds a conceptual illustration and several analytical and benchmark figures, expands diversity displays to six metrics, and separates normalized and raw diversity tables. Existing plots are rearranged, pruning axes and mislabeled architecture-comparison metrics are corrected, and appendix plots are compressed. The original framework diagram is retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for CSQA, CODAH, multilingual benchmarks, and additional AI/LLM applications. The related-work discussion and positioning against existing augmentation methods remain substantially unchanged. Publication updates for works such as LoRA, back-translation, and CCS are bibliographic changes rather than new prior art.

T1.justification: Appendix A adds the mathematical definition of the newly evaluated unique-3-gram measure, 3-gram(S) = |G3|. The optimization formulation, LoRA/DPO equations, and existing diversity and affinity formulas remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of the central diversity-and-coherence argument: human checks supplement LLM-only judgments, replacement controls test the need for DPO, and reasoning/multilingual experiments address v1's narrow evaluation scope. Some new protocols remain underspecified, and Appendix K retains a stale 'twice the size' statement after correcting sample counts, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DoAug research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds human validation, metric comparisons, DPO-replacement experiments, and reasoning and multilingual evaluations.

arxiv_record.abstract: In-context machine translation (MT) with large language models (LLMs) is a promising approach for low-resource MT, as it can readily take advantage of linguistic resources such as grammar books and dictionaries. Such resources are usually selectively integrated into the prompt so that LLMs can directly perform translation without any specific training, via their in-context learning capability (ICL). However, the relative importance of each type of resource, e.g., dictionary, grammar book, and retrieved parallel examples, is not entirely clear. To address this gap, this study systematically investigates how each resource and its quality affect the translation performance, with the Manchu language as our case study. To remove any prior knowledge of Manchu encoded in the LLM parameters and single out the effect of ICL, we also experiment with an enciphered version of Manchu texts. Our results indicate that high-quality dictionaries and good parallel examples are very helpful, while grammars hardly help. In a follow-up study, we showcase a promising application of in-context MT: parallel data augmentation as a way to bootstrap a conventional MT model. When monolingual data abound, generating synthetic parallel data through in-context MT offers a pathway to mitigate data scarcity and build effective and efficient low-resource neural MT systems.

program_record.Abstract:
In-context machine translation (MT) with large language models (LLMs) is a promising approach for low-resource MT, as it can readily take advantage of linguistic resources such as grammar books and dictionaries.
Such resources are usually selectively integrated into the prompt so that LLMs can directly perform translation without any specific training, via their in-context learning capability (ICL).
However, the relative importance of each type of resource, e.g., dictionary, grammar book, and retrieved parallel examples, is not entirely clear.
To address this gap, this study systematically investigates how each resource and its quality affect the translation performance, with the Manchu language as our case study. 
To remove any prior knowledge of Manchu encoded in the LLM parameters and single out the effect of ICL, we also experiment with an enciphered version of Manchu texts.
Our results indicate that high-quality dictionaries and good parallel examples are very helpful, while grammars hardly help.
In a follow-up study, we showcase a promising application of in-context MT: parallel data augmentation as a way to bootstrap a conventional MT model. 
When monolingual data abound, generating synthetic parallel data through in-context MT offers a pathway to mitigate data scarcity and build effective and efficient low-resource neural MT systems.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: dictionaries and relevant parallel examples help most, grammar and CoT offer little benefit, in-context learning explains much of performance, and synthetic data can improve low-resource NMT. New evidence supports these retained claims.

C2.justification: Appendices D–F add localized interpretations concerning masked grammar benefits, English vocabulary mismatch as a possible cause of low overlap metrics, and linguistic or metric explanations for Chinese results. Section 5.3 interprets the nonsignificant human-score difference between original and enciphered outputs. The existing generalization and CoT limitations remain essentially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix H supplies detailed human-rating instructions and scoring examples; Appendix F identifies the Chinese resources and Jieba implementation. These improve documentation of the added evaluations. Appendix C's generation and fine-tuning hyperparameters and the code/data access statement remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds Manchu-to-Chinese evaluation using GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3. v1 already used Manchu-Chinese material to construct English data but did not evaluate Chinese outputs. This extends target-language coverage while retaining the original Manchu-English coverage.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained experiments is unchanged: the same Llama3 sizes, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, and prompting controls remain. The new human and Chinese evaluations reuse existing models or variants rather than introduce additional comparison methods.

E3.justification: Section 5.3 introduces a substantial new evaluation protocol: three bilingual experts score adequacy from 0 to 100 for three GPT-4o variants on 33 randomly selected sentences, producing 99 anonymized, randomly ordered items. Appendix F also introduces Jieba segmentation for Chinese evaluation. Existing automatic-evaluation and training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds a targeted control testing grammar without retrieved parallel examples, addressing possible masking of grammar benefits. Appendix E adds a vocabulary-overlap diagnostic, finding 25% unmatched English test subwords versus 3% for Manchu. Existing component ablations, model-size analyses, and output examples are retained.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without these statistical assessments. v2 adds 1,000-sample bootstrap significance tests for component comparisons in Appendix G, plus human-score normalization, inter-rater Pearson correlation, and Wilcoxon rank-sum tests in Section 5.3. These introduce substantive statistical support without establishing any increase in model-training runs.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–6, Figures 2–3, and matched appendix examples retain their results. Substantial new outcomes include human adequacy scores of 29.04, 56.12, and 64.47 for direct, enciphered, and original prompting respectively (Table 7), and Chinese BLEU scores of 5.21 for GPT-4o and 9.28 for DeepSeek-V3 (Table 9). Grammar-control, vocabulary-overlap, and significance findings are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The morphological analyzer, dictionary retrieval, BM25 examples, grammar and CoT components, character-substitution procedure, and mT5 augmentation method remain unchanged. The Chinese experiment applies the existing pipeline; replacing 'encryption' with 'encipherment' is terminology editing.

P1.justification: v2 contains localized copyediting, replaces encryption terminology with encipherment, retitles Section 5, and adds Section 5.3 and Appendices D–H. Output examples move from Appendix D to I. The existing narrative and main section order are largely preserved.

P2.justification: v2 adds four tables covering human scores, vocabulary overlap, Chinese translation, and significance tests, plus boxed rater instructions. Existing figures and example-table designs are retained, with caption edits, renumbering, and page reflow rather than a substantial visual redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references for transfer learning, human assessment, forward translation, and Chinese evaluation. Section 5.2 newly positions the cipher experiment relative to Yuan et al. (2024) and Marmonier et al. (2025). The overall research positioning remains stable; NLLB and BLOOM bibliographic updates do not constitute new baselines.

T1.justification: The mathematical prompt formulation and character-substitution mapping are retained. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the added statistical procedures do not introduce new theoretical results.

improvement.justification: v1 relied on automatic scores and illustrative examples; v2 adds blinded expert adequacy assessment, component-level bootstrap tests, and a control addressing whether parallel examples mask grammar benefits. Together these substantially strengthen validation of the central empirical claims. The human sample remains small at 33 sentences, and the Chinese test set is not clearly specified, limiting broader conclusions, but the gains in support for the main study are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Manchu in-context translation study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching, including the relocation of v1 Appendix D to v2 Appendix I.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds expert human assessments, Manchu-to-Chinese results, vocabulary analysis, and a grammar-order control.

before.justification: v1 reports original component ablations, comparisons across LLMs, character-substitution experiments, and mT5 data-augmentation results in Sections 4–6 and the appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to solve complex reasoning tasks by generating intermediate reasoning steps. However, most existing approaches focus on hard token decoding, which constrains reasoning within the discrete vocabulary space and may not always be optimal. While recent efforts explore continuous-space reasoning, they often require full-model fine-tuning and suffer from catastrophic forgetting, limiting their applicability to state-of-the-art LLMs that already perform well in zero-shot settings with a proper instruction. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach for continuous-space reasoning that does not require modifying the LLM. Specifically, we employ a lightweight fixed assistant model to speculatively generate instance-specific soft thought tokens as the initial chain of thoughts, which are then mapped into the LLM's representation space via a trainable projection module. Experimental results on five reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our method enhances LLM reasoning performance through supervised, parameter-efficient fine-tuning. Source code is available at https://github.com/xuyige/SoftCoT.
arxiv_record.authors: Yige Xu, Xu Guo, Zhiwei Zeng, Chunyan Miao
arxiv_record.title: SoftCoT: Soft Chain-of-Thought for Efficient Reasoning with LLMs

C1.justification: V2's introduction adds priority claims that the work first systematically identifies and addresses the forgetting issue and provides the first lightweight soft-thought approach preserving prior knowledge. The central method and effectiveness claims in the abstract and conclusion remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 explains weak assistant-size effects through the assistant's supporting role, interprets Qwen3 results as evidence of broader applicability, and incorporates LoRA results into the catastrophic-forgetting argument. The limitations concerning explicit reasoning paths and unverified scaling to larger backbone models remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New Appendix A specifies hardware, optimizer, learning rate, weight decay, batch sizes, epochs, checkpoint selection, and token-count settings. Appendix C supplies assistant instructions and concrete special-token names. V2 also documents Coconut's LoRA adaptation and adds code/data access information plus announcements of logs and checkpoints, substantially reducing v1's reproducibility gaps.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8K, ASDiv-Aug, AQuA, StrategyQA, and Date Understanding with the same task coverage. The added Qwen3 and assistant-size experiments use these existing datasets; they change model configurations rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds LoRA Fine-Tuning to both main backbone comparisons and adds Coconut to the Qwen2.5 comparison in Table 3. It also removes Zero-Shot CoT-Unk from the self-consistency comparison in Table 4, while retaining it in the main tables. These changes substantially strengthen the fine-tuning comparisons.

E3.justification: New configurations include Qwen3-8B, Qwen2.5 assistants of 0.5B, 1.5B, and 7B, and rank-16 LoRA for the added baseline. Dataset counts, accuracy evaluation, and the existing one-versus-ten-chain self-consistency design remain unchanged. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments were retuned.

E4.justification: V2 adds an assistant-size sensitivity study in Section 5.3.2 and expands self-consistency analysis from GSM8K to all five datasets, with further tests on Qwen3. Appendix C adds a SoftCoT worked example alongside the retained baseline examples. This substantially broadens the supplementary validation beyond v1's analyses.

E5.justification: Table 4 adds uncertainty values to self-consistency results that previously had only point accuracies, including the retained ten-chain GSM8K comparison. Five-seed reporting and the single-run ±0.00 convention already appeared in v1. The PDFs do not establish an increase in repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: V2 adds baseline results, assistant-size results, and Qwen3 results across all five datasets. Existing SoftCoT scores in Tables 2 and 3 remain unchanged. In the retained GSM8K ten-chain comparison, SoftCoT changes from 90.98 to 90.63 and Assist-CoT from 90.54 to 90.43; these are revised reported results, not improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The frozen assistant, trainable projection, frozen reasoning LLM, and training loss are retained. However, v1 Equation 8 uses the fixed LLM task prompt, whereas v2 uses Iassist despite using ILLM in Equation 6. The PDFs do not resolve whether this represents a training-input change or a notation error.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized introduction and baseline rewrites, refines terminology and notation, renames analysis headings, and adds acknowledgements. The original prompt appendix becomes Appendix C after new implementation and Qwen3 appendices. Most existing prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: Table 4 changes from a compact two-column comparison into a full-width table with five paired dataset groups and uncertainty values. V2 adds Tables 5–7, extends Tables 2–3, and expands the appendix example panels. Figures 1 and 2 retain their content with sizing and placement changes.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for GLM, LoRA, a prompt-engineering survey, AdamW, Transformers, and Qwen3, and strengthens its priority positioning. The main related-work taxonomy and discussion of Coconut, CCoT, and Heima remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Neither version introduces theorems or proofs. The prompt optimization, hidden-state extraction, linear projection, and language-modeling formulation are retained. Explicit concatenation notation and renamed symbols do not establish new mathematical reasoning; the training-input ambiguity is addressed under M1.

improvement.justification: V1 omitted essential training and assistant-prompt details; v2's Appendices A and C fill much of that reproducibility gap. Added fine-tuning controls, assistant-size tests, and broader self-consistency and Qwen3 evaluations substantially strengthen empirical scrutiny. The Equation 8 ambiguity, single-run baselines, and unisolated catastrophic-forgetting explanation remain limitations, but the gains in reproducibility and validation are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SoftCoT, with matching authors, architecture, datasets, and retained experiments. Their complete main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds LoRA comparisons, assistant-size experiments, and Qwen3 evaluations, including Appendix B.

before.justification: V1 reports original SoftCoT evaluations on five reasoning datasets, including backbone comparisons, thought-token sensitivity, and self-consistency experiments in Tables 2–4 and Figure 2.

arxiv_record.abstract: To compare autoregressive language models at scale, we propose using log-likelihood vectors computed on a predefined text set as model features. This approach has a solid theoretical basis: when treated as model coordinates, their squared Euclidean distance approximates the Kullback-Leibler divergence of text-generation probabilities. Our method is highly scalable, with computational cost growing linearly in both the number of models and text samples, and is easy to implement as the required features are derived from cross-entropy loss. Applying this method to over 1,000 language models, we constructed a "model map," providing a new perspective on large-scale model analysis.
arxiv_record.authors: Momose Oyama, Hiroaki Yamagiwa, Yusuke Takase, Hidetoshi Shimodaira
arxiv_record.title: Mapping 1,000+ Language Models via the Log-Likelihood Vector

Our method is highly scalable, with computational cost growing linearly in both the number of models and text samples, and is easy to implement as the required features are derived from cross-entropy loss. Applying this method to over 1,000 language models, we constructed a "model map," providing a new perspective on large-scale model analysis.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same principal contributions: scalable log-likelihood model representations, their relationship to KL divergence, mapping over 1,000 models, and predicting benchmark performance.

C2.justification: V2 explains the grouped-versus-random prediction difference through model-family leakage and interprets the L-versus-Q comparison as evidence that centered coordinates already encode performance information. It also proposes interpolation for efficient model exploration and updates the limitations to acknowledge related models carrying different type labels.

D1.justification: V2 adds a first-page code-and-data repository link, identifies GroupKFold as the splitting implementation, and documents enabling torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) for interpolation experiments.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same 10,000-text corpus with 17 categories, 1,018-model collection, 996-model prediction subset, and six benchmark tasks. The interpolation additions change model configurations and analyses within this coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds mean log-likelihood as an explicit performance-prediction reference in Table 3 and ridge regression using uncentered L as a comparison with Q in Table 9. V1's corresponding prediction experiment lacked these comparisons.

E3.justification: The main prediction evaluation changes from random five-fold splits to model-type-based GroupKFold splits. Appendix J also replaces 1,000 sampled interpolation-evaluation texts with all 10,000 texts and adds a Mistral base-model configuration alongside Llama-2.

E4.justification: New controls in Appendix K.3 test whether random splits inflate prediction accuracy and whether replacing centered Q with uncentered L matters. Appendix J extends the weight-grid analysis to Mistral and adds a direct test of estimating merged models' mean log-likelihoods through interpolation.

E5.justification: V1 already averages predictions over five seeded splits and reports correlation means and standard deviations in Table 6. V2 retains this reporting practice in Tables 7–9; the changed settings, additional comparisons, and numerical values do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the prediction results under the revised split protocol: 6-TaskMean Pearson/Spearman correlations change from 0.976/0.978 to 0.953/0.960, not a same-setting performance decline. V2 also reports new baseline and control results and interpolation correlations, including Pearson r=0.969 for Llama-2 and 0.973 for Mistral in Figure 20.

M1.justification: Appendix J introduces an auxiliary procedure estimating merged-model log-likelihoods by interpolating source-model log-likelihoods, evaluated through their means. The main log-likelihood coordinates, double centering, distance calculation, and ridge-regression objective remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and appendices A–L are retained. Local revisions expand Sections 5.3 and 6.3, extend Appendix J, add Appendix K.3, clarify terminology, and update author contact information.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 3, 8, and 9 and Figures 19–20. It also reformats nearest-neighbor tables and the dendrogram in bits per byte, adjusts map sizing and captions, and relocates several displays while retaining the overall presentation structure.

R1.justification: Related work adds Horwitz et al.'s model-atlas study and Zhuang et al.'s EmbedLLM. The perplexity discussion adds Liu et al. (2023a), Fang et al. (2025), and Thrush et al. (2025). These are focused additions rather than a substantial repositioning of the contribution.

T1.justification: Appendix J adds the mathematical definition of the interpolated log-likelihood estimator in Equation 43. The central KL approximations, assumptions, coordinate identities, and proofs in Appendices B–F remain unchanged apart from equation numbering.

improvement.justification: Model-type grouping materially addresses v1's stated concern that closely related models could inflate benchmark-prediction accuracy. The grouped-versus-random controls and mean-likelihood/L-versus-Q comparisons substantially strengthen this central empirical application, while the code-and-data link improves reproducibility. Residual overlap across type labels remains acknowledged, and the new interpolation evidence supports mean likelihoods more directly than downstream task prediction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–L support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material and reordered model-list entries.

after.justification: The original empirical study is retained and extended with prediction controls, Mistral interpolation experiments, and estimated-versus-observed mean log-likelihood results.

before.justification: Sections 4–6 report original model-mapping analyses, benchmark-score prediction, empirical KL-divergence validation, and weight-interpolation experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: LMs' alignment with human reading behavior (i.e. psychometric predictive power; PPP) is known to improve during pretraining up to a tipping point, beyond which it either plateaus or degrades. Various factors, such as word frequency, recency bias in attention, and context size, have been theorized to affect PPP, yet there is no current account that explains why such a tipping point exists, and how it interacts with LMs' pretraining dynamics more generally. We hypothesize that the underlying factor is a pretraining phase transition, characterized by the rapid emergence of specialized attention heads. We conduct a series of correlational and causal experiments to show that such a phase transition is responsible for the tipping point in PPP. We then show that, rather than producing attention patterns that contribute to the degradation in PPP, phase transitions alter the subsequent learning dynamics of the model, such that further training keeps damaging PPP.
arxiv_record.authors: Tatsuya Aoyama, Ethan Wilcox
arxiv_record.title: Language Models Grow Less Humanlike beyond Phase Transition

C1.justification: The central phase-transition explanation and abstract are retained. The introduction and conclusion refine the regularization claim toward delaying the transition and PPP peak, and more explicitly favor the Dynamics Hypothesis over attributing degradation to persistent specialized heads.

C2.justification: v1 treats incomplete suppression largely as a possible explanation for residual degradation. v2 explicitly documents incomplete suppression, explains why absolute PPP comparisons must consider language-model loss, and proposes SAS scaffolding and attention competition as possible explanations of asymmetric head interactions. It also adds qualified comparisons with brain-alignment dynamics.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code/data availability link and a substantial hyperparameter table covering architecture, parameter counts, learning rate, weight decay, warmup and scheduling. It newly specifies the 0.1 breakthrough threshold and gaze-duration outcome, and documents Gaussian-noise implementation. These disclosures materially improve reproducibility without establishing changes to existing training settings.

E1.justification: Both versions retain CC100 training, Dundee, MECO, Provo and Natural Stories reading data, and BLiMP and synthetic-sequence evaluations. The added controls and analyses use existing coverage. Brain-alignment results discussed in v2 are attributed to other studies.

E2.justification: Experiment 3 adds one comparator family: Gaussian Noise Injection, evaluated at sigma = 0.05 and 50 alongside NoReg and the existing syntactic and copying regularization variants. The original comparison methods remain.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends Experiment 3's evaluation design by analyzing validation loss versus PPP separately before and after phase transition, using PS for transition timing except UAS for copy-suppressed models. It also introduces Gaussian-noise control settings. Figure 1 changes the reported Pythia batch size from 2,048 to 1,024; this reporting revision does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix K examines how suppressing SAS affects induction heads and how suppressing induction heads affects SAS, including downstream BLiMP and ICL behavior. Section 6 and Appendix N add analyses of loss–PPP relationships around phase transition, while Gaussian-noise controls test nonspecific perturbation. The original head ablations and suppression checks are retained.

E5.justification: Beyond the existing correlation significance reporting, v2 adds 10,000 within-word permutations for comparisons against NoReg (Appendix I/Table 3) and Fisher-z weighted pooling of correlations across models (Figure 4). These are substantial additions to statistical assessment. The permutation p-values are explicitly reported without multiple-testing correction.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical entries are unchanged, but v2 adds Gaussian-noise outcomes, cross-head interaction findings, permutation p-values and transition-specific loss–PPP results. For example, new Figure 4 reports pooled Dundee correlations of -0.976 before transition and 0.416 afterward. Original regularization results are retained in expanded Figures 16–17.

M1.justification: The syntactic and copying regularization objectives, pattern-preserving head ablation and core scoring procedures are retained. PMS becomes PS without changing its definition. Gaussian noise injection is an added comparison condition, rather than a revision to the proposed suppression methods.

P1.justification: Experiment 3 and the conclusion are substantially rewritten around transition delay and loss–PPP relationships. The discussion gains thematic subsections, hypotheses are reorganized as 1/2a/2b, and the original absolute-PPP discussion moves into an expanded appendix structure. Terminology and explanations are also revised throughout.

P2.justification: New main Figures 3–4 replace the earlier main-text displays, which survive as expanded appendix Figures 17 and 16. v2 adds interaction and validation-loss plots and Tables 2–4, revises legends and axes, and distinguishes positive and negative significant correlations by color in Table 1. These substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The foundational related-work account remains. v2 adds discussion of brain-alignment studies by AlKhamissi et al. and Nakagi et al., supporting references for small-model research, and explicit novelty claims about studying SAS in decoder-only models and observing both specialized-head types together.

T1.justification: The UAS attention-scale argument changes from claiming approximately 0.002 expected attention for every j > i in v1 Appendix B to averaging over j > i in v2 Appendix C. It also changes j < i to j <= i in the preceding expression. This is a limited mathematical revision; the central definitions and objectives remain.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central mechanism claim. Compared with v1's emphasis on absolute PPP improvements, it adds perturbation controls, examines loss–PPP dependence, tests statistical significance and investigates incomplete suppression directly. These additions support a more precise interpretation of transition delay and expose limits of the regularization evidence. The new implementation details also improve reproducibility. Full causal isolation remains unresolved, but the gains address important evidential and interpretive weaknesses.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support a reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds Gaussian-noise controls, head-interaction analyses, permutation tests and analyses of loss–PPP relationships.

before.justification: v1 reports original reading-time prediction experiments, attention-head ablations and regularized GPT2 training, with additional empirical results in its appendices.

arxiv_record.abstract: Many challenging reasoning tasks require not just rapid, intuitive responses, but a more deliberate, multi-step approach. Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) highlights an important shift from the "System 1" way of quick reactions to the "System 2" style of reflection-and-correction problem solving. However, current benchmarks heavily rely on the final-answer accuracy, leaving much of a model's intermediate reasoning steps unexamined. This fails to assess the model's ability to reflect and rectify mistakes within the reasoning process. To bridge this gap, we introduce FINEREASON, a logic-puzzle benchmark for fine-grained evaluation of LLMs' reasoning capabilities. Each puzzle can be decomposed into atomic steps, making it ideal for rigorous validation of intermediate correctness. Building on this, we introduce two tasks: state checking, and state transition, for a comprehensive evaluation of how models assess the current situation and plan the next move. To support broader research, we also provide a puzzle training set aimed at enhancing performance on general mathematical tasks. We show that models trained on our state checking and transition data demonstrate gains in math reasoning by up to 5.1% on GSM8K.
arxiv_record.authors: Guizhen Chen, Weiwen Xu, Hao Zhang, Hou Pong Chan, Chaoqun Liu, Lidong Bing, Deli Zhao, Anh Tuan Luu, Yu Rong
arxiv_record.title: FINEREASON: Evaluating and Improving LLMs' Deliberate Reasoning through Reflective Puzzle Solving

C1.justification: The training contribution broadens from demonstrated mathematical benefits and suggested wider utility to an explicit claim of transfer to general problem-solving in the introduction and conclusion. The central benchmark contribution and headline puzzle and GSM8K claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 develops the transfer interpretation through harder-problem gains, subject-specific benefits, and examples of verification and correction, arguing that unsolvable states teach transferable backtracking skills. It adds the limitation that correctness evaluation ignores solution efficiency. Conversely, v1's Section 4.2 interpretation of the execution gap as shortcut-seeking is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix A.2 expands exact prompt documentation from Sudoku alone to all four puzzle categories, substantially improving reproducibility. Appendix A.5 newly states that transition errors are classified automatically. Training hyperparameters and access links remain, although the hardware description loses specificity: '8 H20 (120 GB)' becomes '8 GPUs (120 GB)'.

E1.justification: Section 5.5 adds actual training and evaluation on MMLU, covering 57 tasks across STEM, humanities, social sciences, and other subjects. This substantially broadens coverage beyond the retained four puzzle categories and mathematical benchmarks.

E2.justification: Tables 2–5 retain identical comparator membership. The new MMLU experiment extends the existing untrained-model, task-only-training, and mixed-training comparison design to another benchmark without introducing a distinct comparison method.

E3.justification: v2 adds an unsolvable-training-ratio sweep at 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8, specifies an 80% task-data mixture for MMLU, and reviews 20 corrected examples. Existing puzzle sample counts, zero-shot prompting, training hyperparameters, and 1024-token limits are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses examine unsolvable-training proportions, transfer across MATH difficulty levels and MMLU categories, and verification/self-correction in model outputs (Tables 6, 11, 12, and 28). Tables 18–27 additionally provide concrete cases for the existing error categories; the original error distributions and scaling analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new results follow the existing reporting practice; the 20-example qualitative review is not repeated-run uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Existing quantitative results are retained. New MMLU comparisons report task-only versus mixed accuracies of 41.1 versus 44.9 for 1.5B and 61.2 versus 64.2 for 7B (Table 7). v2 also adds unsolvable-ratio results, subgroup outcomes, and model-output cases, including a MATH Level 3 decline from 675 to 661 correct answers despite gains at other levels.

M1.justification: The DFS puzzle decomposition, minimal moves, state-checking and state-transition procedures, and GRPO training approach remain unchanged. Additional prompt documentation and experiments with training mixtures do not introduce a new algorithm.

P1.justification: v2 tightens introductory and methodological prose, renames behavior-analysis sections, organizes Section 5 into numbered subsections, and regroups the appendix. Affiliations and acknowledgments are expanded. The main narrative order and substantial portions of the original exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds quantitative displays for the new analyses and extensive full-width prompt and error-example tables, culminating in the annotated, side-by-side output comparison in Table 28. Existing figures are retained, with caption and axis-label refinements and some relocation, including Figure 7.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations including Reasoning Paths Optimization, PuzzleVQA, critic-guided planning, and science-question-answering and chart-understanding work. The positioning around intermediate reasoning versus final-answer evaluation remains largely unchanged. Publication updates to existing references do not represent new cited works.

T1.justification: The formal puzzle-state representation, subtree-solvability criterion, and minimal-move definitions are unchanged. No new theoretical assumptions, propositions, or proofs are introduced; mathematical calculations in added model outputs serve as case evidence.

improvement.justification: v1's transfer evidence was confined to mathematical accuracy. v2 substantially strengthens this contribution through MMLU evaluation, controlled unsolvable-state mixing, and analyses of where gains occur and how outputs differ. Complete prompt coverage also resolves an important reproducibility gap. The small qualitative sample and absent uncertainty estimates still limit mechanistic conclusions, and hardware specificity decreases slightly, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FINEREASON. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite the expanded appendix in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds MMLU experiments, training-mixture ablations, subgroup results, and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original puzzle evaluations, error analyses, and GRPO training experiments evaluated on GSM8K and MATH.

arxiv_record.abstract: Inference-Time Scaling has been critical to the success of recent models such as OpenAI o1 and DeepSeek R1. However, many techniques used to train models for inference-time scaling require tasks to have answers that can be verified, limiting their application to domains such as math, coding and logical reasoning. We take inspiration from how humans make first attempts, ask for detailed feedback from others and make improvements based on such feedback across a wide spectrum of open-ended endeavors. To this end, we collect HelpSteer3 data to train dedicated Feedback and Edit Models that are capable of performing inference-time scaling for open-ended general-domain tasks. In our setup, one model generates an initial response, which are given feedback by a second model, that are then used by a third model to edit the response. We show that performance on Arena Hard, a benchmark strongly predictive of Chatbot Arena Elo can be boosted by scaling the number of initial response drafts, effective feedback and edited responses. When scaled optimally, our setup based on 70B models from the Llama 3 family can reach SoTA performance on Arena Hard at 92.7 as of 5 Mar 2025, surpassing OpenAI o1-preview-2024-09-12 with 90.4 and DeepSeek R1 with 92.3.

Section 6 attributes human-preferred improvements to factuality, coherence, and conciseness; the original limitations discussion is retained.

D1.justification: V2 documents public access to HelpSteer3 with a CC-BY-4.0 license, a model collection, and the generated distillation data, which lacked corresponding access information in v1. It also supplies the new 8B distillation checkpoint and learning rate, describes the CritiqueLLM English-output instruction, and clarifies that Table 8's compute figures concern 70B models.

E1.justification: General, STEM, Coding, and Multilingual coverage and the three evaluation benchmarks remain unchanged. HelpSteer3 names the existing data. The human study samples additional prompts from the retained General category; the 8B and Gemma experiments change model configurations rather than task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix K, Table 9 adds step-by-step prompting and CritiqueLLM feedback followed by Nemotron Self-Edit as evaluated comparison methods. The original baseline and ablation comparisons remain.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a human evaluation using 50 prompts, three raters per prompt from eight in-house annotators, randomized response order, and an invalid-response exclusion rule. It also adds 8B distillation, Gemma-2-27B-IT evaluation, and controlled 8B-versus-70B Feedback/Edit experiments without RL. These substantially expand evaluation design while retaining the original benchmark protocols.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of Feedback/Edit model capacity, transfer to a non-Llama response model, and whether automated gains translate into human preferences. These extend v1's component and scaling ablations with important applicability and validation checks, including negative results for 8B Feedback/Edit models.

E5.justification: The new human study specifies an aggregation procedure that averages three independent ratings and rounds to the nearest preference category. Existing AlpacaEval standard errors and Arena Hard 95% confidence intervals remain unchanged in practice; no uncertainty interval or significance test accompanies the human-study findings.

E6.justification: Substantial new results supplement unchanged original scores, including the headline 92.7 Arena Hard result. The human study reports 16 improvements, 21 ties, and 7 degradations among 44 retained comparisons.

arxiv_record.abstract: LLMs have achieved remarkable fluency and coherence in text generation, yet their widespread adoption has raised concerns about content reliability and accountability. In high-stakes domains, it is crucial to understand where and how the content is created. To address this, we introduce the Text pROVEnance (TROVE) challenge, designed to trace each sentence of a target text back to specific source sentences within potentially lengthy or multi-document inputs. Beyond identifying sources, TROVE annotates the fine-grained relationships (quotation, compression, inference, and others), providing a deep understanding of how each target sentence is formed. To benchmark TROVE, we construct our dataset by leveraging three public datasets covering 11 diverse scenarios (e.g., QA and summarization) in English and Chinese, spanning source texts of varying lengths (0-5k, 5-10k, 10k+), emphasizing the multi-document and long-document settings essential for provenance. To ensure high-quality data, we employ a three-stage annotation process: sentence retrieval, GPT-4o provenance, and human provenance. We evaluate 11 LLMs under direct prompting and retrieval-augmented paradigms, revealing that retrieval is essential for robust performance, larger models perform better in complex relationship classification, and closed-source models often lead, yet open-source models show significant promise, particularly with retrieval augmentation. We make our dataset available here: https://github.com/ZNLP/ZNLP-Dataset.
arxiv_record.authors: Junnan Zhu, Min Xiao, Yining Wang, Feifei Zhai, Yu Zhou, Chengqing Zong
arxiv_record.title: TROVE: A Challenge for Fine-Grained Text Provenance via Source Sentence Tracing and Relationship Classification
